title: ENH/BUG: Utilize `_values_for_json` in `Series.to_json`
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  ExtensionArrays can define a `_values_for_json` method if the standard numpy array with `object` dtype returned by `__array__` is not serializable because the objects themselves are not serializable. However this method is only utilized for `DataFrame.to_json` trough `BlockManager.column_arrays`:  https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/core/internals/managers.py#L1249-L1251  In `Series.to_json` no path leads to the `_values_for_json` method and nearly always `__array__` is utilized. Therefore some ExtensionArrays are only JSON serializable if they are in a `DataFrame` and not a `Series`, which in my opinion also could be considered a bug.  ### Feature Description  In short modify the `objToJSON.c` file to also call `_values_for_json` for pandas `Series`.  With the help of GitHub Copilot I was able to trace the issue to the `get_values` function, specifically the following lines: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/353763e607745e6fad90fed89efe97bd1f87ebae/pandas/_libs/src/vendored/ujson/python/objToJSON.c#L201-L213  - In `201` we are effectively calling `Series.values` and assign it to `values`. - If the `Series` and therefore `values` is not empty `values` now is a numpy array or ExtensionArray. - Next in `205` it is checked if `values` has a `__array__` attribute and if so calls it, that is also the path mentioned above that leads potentially to the numpy array of object dtype with not serializable objects in it. - At last in `210` if none of the checks above worked it is checked if `values` is already a `np.ndarray` (and only that, so no subclass) and if not dereferences `values` and tries to create the array somewhere up the stack (if I understand it correctly).  My proposal would be to add another check after the empty check

title: ENH: Add coerce errors functionality to pandas.Series.apply
body: ### Feature Type  - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  I would like to use pandas.Series.apply without creating helper functions to coerce errors.   Currently if I am applying a function to a series that I know could raise errors (for example, trying to make each item in series of strings into an int), I have to write a small helper function to coerce errors into None or other.  I would like pandas.Series.apply to have a new parameter called errors, with possible values of 'raise' and 'coerce', similar to pandas.to_datetime.   ### Feature Description  Adds a new parameter to pandas.Series.apply, to coerce errors.  Pseudocode implementation: ``` def apply(self):     func = self.func     if self.errors == "coerce":         def safe_func(val):             try:                 return func(val)             except Exception:                 return np.nan         results = [safe_func(val) for val in self.values]     else:         results = [func(val) for val in self.values]     return results ```  Example usage: ``` s = pandas.Series(['1', '2', 'N/A']) s = s.apply(lambda x: int(x), errors = 'coerce') ```  ### Alternative Solutions  Write helper functions when necessary: ``` def coerce_to_int(x):     try: return int(x)     except: return None s = pandas.Series(['1', '2', 'N/A']) s = s.apply(coerce_to_int) ```  This is viable but requires the user to write many helper functions.   ### Additional Context  _No response_

body: A small nit, but `Index` uses the same repr as `float("nan")` while `Series/DataFrame` uses a hardcoded `"NaN"` repr (in a `na_rep` argument)    ```python In [1]: import pandas as pd  In [2]: pd.Index([1, float("nan")]) Out[2]: Index([1.0, nan], dtype='float64')  In [3]: pd.Series([1, float("nan")]) Out[3]:  0    1.0 1    NaN dtype: float64  In [4]: pd.DataFrame([1, float("nan")]) Out[4]:       0 0  1.0 1  NaN ```  It would be nice if this was consistent

title: Hosting of the pandas website and documentation

title: BUG: mask(inplace=True) gives where() results in EA recursive path
body: `DataFrame.mask(cond, other, axis, inplace=True)` produces incorrect results (equivalent to `where()`) when `other` is a Series with ExtensionArray values.  ```python import pandas as pd import numpy as np  df = pd.DataFrame({"A": [1, 2, 3], "B": [4, 5, 6]}) ser = pd.Series(pd.array([7, pd.NA, 9])) mask = np.ones(df.shape, dtype=bool) mask[1, :] = False  df.mask(mask, ser, axis=0)            # correct: replaces rows 0, 2 df.mask(mask, ser, axis=0, inplace=True)  # wrong: replaces row 1 (where() semantics) ```  The cause is a double negation in `NDFrame._where`. `mask()` passes `~cond`, then `_where` negates again (`cond = -cond if inplace`) before reaching the EA recursive path at `generic.py:10095-10120`. The recursive `_where` calls are non-inplace, so they interpret the double-negated cond with where semantics, producing the wrong result.  The non-EA path (which goes through `putmask`) is not affected.

title: ENH: Proposal for pd.col() for multi-column and regex column selection
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  `pd.col()` currently only supports selecting a **single column**, even though its behavior allows expressions to be chained in ways that naturally suggest multi-column operations should also work.  The function is defined as:  ```python def col(col_name: Hashable) -> Expression: ```  Internally it constructs an `Expression` whose evaluation function does:  ```python def func(df: DataFrame) -> Series:     if col_name not in df.columns:         raise ValueError(...)     return df[col_name] ```  This always returns a **Series**, meaning `pd.col()` is fundamentally single-column oriented.  ### Inconsistent behavior with lists  Passing a list currently does not raise a clear error:  ```python pd.col(["price", "discount"]) ```  The expression is created successfully, but when evaluated it produces:  ```python df[["price", "discount"]]   # returns a DataFrame ```  This creates inconsistent behavior when chaining operations such as:  ```python df.assign(total=pd.col(["price", "discount"]).sum()) ```  because the expression now operates on a **DataFrame instead of a Series**. body: There is one remaining TODO item in the string dtype tracker issue for the actual implementation (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/54792):  > Ensure dtype=str/ astype(str) works as an alias when the future mode is enabled (and any other alias which will currently convert the input to strings, like "U"?)  The Python `str` is already an alias for the `"str"` /  `pd.StringDtype(na_value=np.nan)`, but so the remaining question is: what to do with the other aliases that currently "kind of" give you strings.  Summary of the current behaviour when using numpy's fixed-width unicode string dtype (`np.dtype("U")`, and its aliases like `np.str_`, `"U"`, `"unicode"`, `"str_", ...):  - `Series(.., dtype="U")` constructor: converts all data to strings while preserving missing values as-is, but then returns the result as object dtype   - here, we end up calling `lib.ensure_string_array` with the default of `skipna=True`  - `DataFrame(.., dtype="U")` constructor seems to be consistent with Series - `.astype("U")` method: converts all data to strings, _including_ stringifying the missing values, and then returns the result as object dtype   - here, we end up calling `lib.ensure_string_array` (in `_astype_nansafe`) with `skipna=False`, causing those missing values to be stringified   - (this is the behaviour we originally also had for `astype(str)`, but that is something we fixed for 3.0; before that was essentially also a alias of the numpy dtype) - when passing an actual numpy array of this dtype to the Series constructor, at that point we actually _do_ convert it to our '"str"` dtype and no longer returning it as object-dtype Series - `pd.array(..., dtype="U")` constructor: converts all data to strings, including stringifying the missing values. title: DEPR: deprecate set_eng_float_format
body: Claude wrote this at my request. ## Proposal Deprecate `pd.set_eng_float_format()` in favor of using `pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(...))` directly. Human Update Or just deprecate without an alternative. I haven't seen any evidence that anyone uses this. ## Rationale `set_eng_float_format` is a legacy convenience function (added in v0.5.0) that is a thin wrapper around `set_option`: ```python def set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=False): set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy, use_eng_prefix)) ``` It is the only top-level `pd.set_*` function that exists outside the options API, making it an odd outlier in the public API. This was already identified in #15610, where the consensus was to integrate this into the options machinery or deprecate it. **Evidence of minimal usage:** - **GitHub code search** yields ~30 results for `set_eng_float_format` outside pandas-dev/pandas. The vast majority are vendored copies of pandas, type stubs, or re-exports (xorbits, modin, Apache Beam, pyparallel, pandas-stubs, etc.). Only **2** results are actual user code calling this function. - **Stack Overflow** has **zero** questions or answers mentioning `set_eng_float_format`. - **Only 2 bug reports** have ever been filed against this function in the pandas issue tracker (#11981 in 2016, #15610 in 2017). The replacement is straightforward and equally concise: ```python # Before pd.set_eng_float_format(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True) # After from pandas.io.formats.format import EngFormatter pd.set_option("display.float_format", EngFormatter(accuracy=3, use_eng_prefix=True)) ``` This keeps `EngFormatter` available (it is not being deprecated), removes a one-off top-level function that doesn't fit the options API pattern, and simplifies the public API surface. Closes #15610.

title: API: Add reduction methods to ExtensionArray subclasses
body: The subclasses of `ExtensionArray` implemented within pandas can support various reductions, but many do not have specific reduction methods defined, e.g. `.mean()`. We should fill these out for better API consistency.  The only method that should be added to `ExtensionArray` itself is `count`, as this can be implemented for all EAs via `ExtensionArray.isna`.  I'm already working on this.

title: DEPR: float_precision in read_csv
body: We have "high" (the default), "legacy", and "round_trip". When it was introduced in #8044, using the "high" precision apparently came with a performance penalty, but that changed by 2017 (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/17154#issuecomment-319917647) so the default was changed from "legacy" to "high" in #36228. I can't think of any reason why anyone would use "legacy". I'm not aware of anyone who uses this parameter at all. Let's deprecate it and simplify the code+API. Update: I patched the code to always use precision="high" to see whether it broke any tests. Aside from a test specifically asserting that "legacy" is _inaccurate_, the only test that broke was `test_precise_conversion` (4 cases out of 42) where we parse `1.700000000000000177635684` to `1.7`. I'm fine with this level of rounding (though I think using `fast_float` might improve it to `1.7000000000000002` which is what pyarrow gives). I'd also be OK with saying "round_trip" level precision is only for the python engine (though that engine also gives 1.7)

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  Hello,  Function allowing to get attributes on time index like `.month`, `.year` are 10 times slower when the time index is built from a `ZoneInfo` instead of a `pytz.timezone`.  With pandas 2.2.3, 3.0.1 or from main, with the use of ZoneInfo: ```bash $ python -m timeit -n 200 -s 'import pandas as pd; from zoneinfo import ZoneInfo' 'pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31 23:59:59", freq="1min", tz=ZoneInfo("Europe/Paris")).month' 200 loops, best of 5: 119 msec per loop ```  With pandas 2.2.3, 3.0.1 or from main with pytz and dztada installed, with the use of pytz timezone: ```bash $ python -m timeit -n 1000 -s 'import pandas as pd;from pytz import timezone' 'pd.date_range("2024-01-01", "2024-12-31 23:59:59", freq="1min", tz=timezone("Europe/Paris")).month' 1000 loops, best of 5: 11.3 msec per loop ```  Same behavior with `year`, `day`, `hour` and `minute` but I didn't check others.    ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 0691c5cf90477d3503834d983f69350f250a6ff7 python                : 3.11.14 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Linux OS-release            : 6.17.0-14-generic Version               : #14~24.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Jan 15 15:52:10 UTC 2 machine               : x86_64 processor             : x86_64 byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : en_US.UTF-8 LOCALE                : en_US.UTF-8  pandas                : 2.2.3 numpy                 : 2.4.2 pytz                  : 2025.2 dateutil              : 2.9.0.post0 pip                   : 24.0 Cython                : None sphinx                : None IPython

title: ENH: add Expression for index
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  I wish I could replace the `(lambda df: ...)` even when that lambda expression contains the term `df.index`.  ### Feature Description  Add a pre-build expression, which could be defined as  ``` from pandas.core.col import Expression  def get_index(df: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.Index:     return df.index  pd_index = Expression(func = get_index, repr_str="Index") ```   ### Alternative Solutions  Expose `Expression` so that users can define `pd_index` as above, without going against the documented intent of the library.  ### Additional Context  I ran into this trying to re-write expressions such as ``` yield (             normaliser.inverse_transform(predicted_q)             .to_frame("quantity")             .assign(forecast_time=lambda df, t_this=t_this: df.index - t_this)  # type: ignore[misc] ) ``` using the new pandas syntax.

title: PERF: DataFrame.describe() calls Series.reindex() N times instead of once
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  When DataFrame.describe() processes a DataFrame with many columns, there's an inefficient pattern where Series.reindex() is called for each column. ```python col_names = reorder_columns(ldesc) d = concat(     [x.reindex(col_names) for x in ldesc],  # reindex() called N times     axis=1,     ignore_index=True,     sort=False, ) ``` With N columns, Series.reindex() is called N times. Instead of aligning the index individually for each Series, we can concat first and reindex the entire DataFrame once to achieve the same result.    ``` python import timeit import numpy as np import pandas as pd  def bench_describe(n_cols: int, n_rows: int = 100, repeat: int = 5) -> float:     np.random.seed(42)     df = pd.DataFrame(np.random.randn(n_rows, n_cols))     _ = df.describe()     times = timeit.repeat('df.describe()', globals={'df': df}, number=3, repeat=repeat)     return min(times) / 3 * 1000  for n_cols in [10, 100, 1000, 10000]:     print(f"{n_cols:>5} cols: {bench_describe(n_cols):>8.1f} ms") ``` main branch: ```    10 cols:      4.7 ms   100 cols:     44.1 ms  1000 cols:    445.9 ms 10000 cols:   4558.1 ms ``` Expected output after fix: ```    10 cols:      4.2 ms   100 cols:     40.2 ms  1000 cols:    408.0 ms 10000 cols:   4102.4 ms ``` describe's performance is improved by about 10%.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : e04b26f375035e5106cb913e47b6db612f4ebb11 python                : 3.13.0 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 11 Version               : 10.0.26100 machine               : AMD64 processor             : Intel64 Family 6 Model 183

title: Suggestion: link a RAG / LLM debugging checklist (WFGY Problem Map) in the docs
body: Hi pandas team,  thank you for maintaining such a foundational library. pandas is often the first stop for people who are building data workflows that later feed into LLM or RAG systems (corpus cleaning, chunking, metadata enrichment, offline evaluation, and so on).  I maintain an MIT-licensed project called **WFGY Problem Map**, which is a 16-question diagnostic checklist for RAG / LLM pipelines in production. It focuses on data and retrieval failure modes (ingestion gaps, chunking pathologies, vector store issues, evaluation leaks, etc), not on model weights.  Why I think this might be relevant for pandas users: - Many real-world RAG systems start from pandas DataFrames (documents, logs, event streams) before anything is embedded or indexed. - Several of the 16 failure modes are about how tabular and semi-structured data are transformed and filtered before they reach a retriever. - The checklist is tooling-agnostic and can be applied no matter whether people use pandas alone or in combination with other frameworks.  For credibility: the same checklist has already been included in a few curated / academic ecosystems such as - ToolUniverse by Harvard MIMS Lab   - Multimodal RAG Survey by QCRI LLM Lab   - Rankify (University of Innsbruck)  Suggestion:  If you think it could be useful for your users, would you consider adding a small link in your docs or resource section such as  > “RAG / LLM debugging checklist: WFGY Problem Map (16 failure modes)”   > https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY/blob/main/ProblemMap/README.md  Project home: https://github.com/onestardao/WFGY  Thanks again for all your work on pandas and for considering this small suggestion.  Best,   PSBigBig

title: ENH: `series.argsort(stable=True)` currently does nothing
body: ### Feature Type  - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas   - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Hi, the method `pandas.Series.argsort` has an argument `stable` that currently does nothing.  I am aware that it is documented that this argument does nothing. But I must ask why?  The current method is already able to perform stable sorts using `kind='stable'`. So if the `stable` argument must be present, why not have it actually do something?  Of course it might conflict with the `kind` argument, e.g. if `kind='quicksort'` is specified, but there are already plenty of methods in Pandas where such arguments can potentially conflict with each other. What's important is that these complications are well-documented, which already seems to be case in the rest of the library.  The fact that this argument exists adds a lot of confusion, particularly for anyone trying to use it by glancing through method signatures or using their IDE autocomplete.  ### Feature Description  ``` if stable is True:     kind = 'stable' ```  ### Alternative Solutions  The argument could be removed, though perhaps there are reasons for which it hasn't already been.  Otherwise, I think it would be great if a warning message could be presented if anyone tries to use this argument (setting it to anything other than `None`). This way any confusion can be immediately resolved without someone having to think to check the documentation for what seems like a very straightforward argument.  ### Additional Context  There is also an `order` argument, which is similarly confusing, but probably a bit harder to change.

title: API: PeriodIndex(dt64_data) depends on container for data
body: ``` data = np.arange(5).view("M8[D]").astype("M8[ns]") dti = pd.DatetimeIndex(data) assert dti.freq is None  pd.PeriodIndex(dti)             # <- raises bc no freq pd.PeriodIndex(pd.Series(dti))  # <- infers freq="D"  ```  PeriodIndex goes through period_array -> PeriodArray._from_datetime64 -> dt64arr_to_periodarr.  When no freq is specified, this does  ```     if freq is None:         if isinstance(data, ABCIndex):             data, freq = data._values, data.freq         elif isinstance(data, ABCSeries):             data, freq = data._values, data.dt.freq ```  In the Series case we get `data.dt.freq`, which uses `inferred_freq` instead of `freq` (which is always `None` inside a Series).  I think we should consider this inconsistency a bug and always use data._values.freq.

title: PERF: loc/iloc setitem with list-of-lists unnecessarily round-trips through object array
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  When using `df.loc[:, cols] = value` (or df.iloc) with a 2D list-of-lists on a mixed-dtype DataFrame, two things happen that are unnecessarily slow: 1. np.ndim(value) constructs a temporary array just to check dimensionality ``` elif np.ndim(value) == 2:     # TODO: avoid np.ndim call in case it isn't an ndarray, since     #  that will construct an ndarray, which will be wasteful     self._setitem_with_indexer_2d_value(indexer, value) ``` 2. `_setitem_with_indexer_2d_value` round-trips through an object array ``` if not is_array_like(value):     value = np.array(value, dtype=object) # ... for i, loc in enumerate(ilocs):     value_col = value[:, i]     if is_object_dtype(value_col.dtype):         value_col = value_col.tolist()     self._setitem_single_column(loc, value_col, pi) ```  For a list-of-lists, the full sequence is: - np.array(value, dtype=object) — O(n) element-by-element boxing into Python objects - value[:, i] — slice an object column - is_object_dtype(...) → True - value_col.tolist() — convert right back to a Python list  So the data goes list → object array → list for every column, which is pure waste.  Reproducible example  ``` import pandas as pd import numpy as np import timeit  # Mixed dtypes force the split path where the issue occurs df = pd.DataFrame({     "a": np.zeros(1_000_000),     "b": np.zeros(1_000_000, dtype=int),     "c": np.zeros(1_000_000), })  val_list = np.random.randn(1_000_000, 2).tolist() val_arr = np.array(val_list)  t_list = timeit.timeit(lambda: df.loc.__setitem__((slice(None), ["a", "c"]), val_list), number=10) t_arr = timeit.timeit(lambda: df.loc.__setitem__((slice(None), ["a", "c"]), val_arr), number=10)  p

title: API: PeriodArray._from_sequence(ints)
body: We have three constructors for a PeriodArray: PeriodIndex(...).array, periodarray, and PeriodArray._from_sequence.  I'm finding they have slightly different behaviors that I am trying to align (_from_sequence will be canonical).  The first difference is integers:  ``` ser = pd.Series([1, 2, 3])  >>> pd.PeriodIndex(ser, freq="D") PeriodIndex(['1-01-01', '2-01-01', '3-01-01'], dtype='period[D]')  >>> pd.core.arrays.period_array(ser, freq="D") <PeriodArray> ['1-01-01', '2-01-01', '3-01-01'] Length: 3, dtype: period[D]  >>> pd.core.arrays.PeriodArray._from_sequence(ser, dtype="period[D]") TypeError: 1  >>> ser.astype("period[D]")   # goes through _from_sequence TypeError: 1 ```  I don't see any clear reason why the last two don't work. title: BUG: test_assignment_not_inplace incorrectly xfailed due to wrong assertion
body: @jbrockmendel asked [claude] to open this.  ## Summary  `tests/computation/test_eval.py::TestOperations::test_assignment_not_inplace` is marked `xfail` with reason `"Unknown: Omitted test_ in name prior."` The test was previously named without a `test_` prefix so pytest never collected it. When it was renamed, it started failing — but the failure is due to a bug **in the test itself**, not in pandas.  ## The bug  The test checks that `df.eval("c = a + b", inplace=False)` does **not** modify `df` in place. However, the final assertion compares `df` (2 columns) against `expected` (3 columns, including `"c"`):  ```python actual = df.eval("c = a + b", inplace=False) expected = df.copy() expected["c"] = expected["a"] + expected["b"] tm.assert_frame_equal(df, expected)  # wrong: compares `df` instead of `actual` ```  This assertion would only pass if `df` *was* modified in place — the exact bug the test was meant to guard against (GH#9297).  ## Fix  - Remove the `xfail` marker - Replace `tm.assert_frame_equal(df, expected)` with `tm.assert_frame_equal(actual, expected)` - Add a check that `df` is unchanged, e.g. `assert list(df.columns) == ["a", "b"]`

title: DEPR: Period "freq" -> "unit"
body: Discussed in last week's meeting and before that in #61897, but before pulling the trigger on the rest of this (#64155 and more) I decided to write up The Whole Thing:  ### Motivation  There are 2 longstanding issues with the Period/PeriodDtype/PeriodArray/PeriodIndex API I'd like to address:  1) "freq" means something different in the Period context than it does for DatetimeIndex/TimedeltaIndex (xref #47227)  2) Period.freq being a DateOffset makes users incorrectly expect that *all* DateOffsets have associated Periods (xref #5091, #12379, etc)  To fix this, I propose to change (with deprecation cycle) the Period classes to use "unit" instead of "freq", with unit being a string analogous to Timestamp.unit/DatetimeIndex.unit.  This will include:  - The `freq` keyword in Period, PeriodIndex, PeriodDtype - The `freq` attribute in Period, PeriodIndex, PeriodDtype, PeriodArray - The `freq` keyword in `pd.period_range`, `Timestamp.to_period`, `DatetimeArray.to_period`, `DatetimeIndex.to_period`, `Series.to_period`, `DataFrame.to_period` - `asfreq` -> `as_unit` (matching DatetimeIndex, TimedeltaIndex, Timestamp, Timedelta) - The `freqstr` attribute for the Period classes. - (maybe?) deprecate allowing Offset objects for the "unit" keyword   ..NB: All units supported by Timestamp ("s", "ms", "us", "ns") will be supported by Period, but not vice-versa. Period also supports ["m", "h", "D", "M", "W-SUN", ..., "Q-JAN", ..., "Y-JAN", ...]   ### User Impact  In most places where users currently use `obj.freq`, the string `obj.unit` will work just fine.  The exceptions that come to mind are:  1) Specifying `freq=obj.unit` in functions like `pd.date_range`, `PeriodIndex.to_timestamp` in a subset of cases where `obj.unit` will not be recognized by `to_offset` (mainly "M", "Q-ABC", "Y-ABC")  2) Arithmetic with adding `period + period.freq` will not work with `period.unit`.  `period + 1` is a viable alternative, as is `period + np.timedelta64(1, period.unit)` in non-hyphenated cases.

title: API: Period subtraction
body: ATM Period subtraction gives an Offset object.  Subtraction with PeriodDtype array gives an object dtype array of Offsets:  ``` per1 = pd.Period("2016-01-01", "M") per2 = pd.Period("2017-01-01", "M")  left = pd.Series([per1]) right = pd.Series([per2])  >>> left - right 0    <-12 * MonthEnds> dtype: object ```  A better result in this example would be a `timedelta64[M]` dtype.  There are two problems with this:  1) we don't support e.g. timedelta64[M].  We either raise or convert it to timedelta64[s]. 2) Not all Period units have a matching timedelta64 unit.  The outliers are   a) "B" (which is deprecated)   b) "W-SUN", "W-MON",... for which "W" is the timedelta64 unit.   c) "Y-JAN", "Y-FEB", ... for which "Y" is the timedelta64 unit.   d) "Q-JAN", ... for which we would need to use "3M" (or ask numpy to add "Q"; in 2023 I discussed this briefly with seberg and he seemed open to it)  Our lack of support for the lower-unit td64 dtypes seems like the harder problem.  Adding that support for td64 without adding it for dt64 is liable to cause problems, and adding it for dt64 (especially dt64tz) would cause its own problems.  So I'm not sure if this is worth pursuing, but soliciting opinions.

If none or more were returned, .item() would return a value error.   The workaround for now is to do rewrap the array in a series object  ``` person = pd.Series(df.query("userName == 'Johnny1234'")['person'].unique()).item() ```  ### Expected Behavior  We would expect the following response ``` # 'John' ```  ### Installed Versions  <details>  <summary>Installed Versions</summary>  ``` INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 366ccdfcd8ed1e5543bfb6d4ee0c9bc519898670 python                : 3.12.4 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Linux OS-release            : 6.17.0-14-generic Version               : #14~24.04.1-Ubuntu SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Jan 15 15:52:10 UTC 2 machine               : x86_64 processor             :

title: PERF: Avoid drop_duplicates(keep=False) in DataFrame.__getitem__ for single-column access
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  Observed (before fix): With n = 1000000 columns, 1000 accesses can take on the order of several seconds because each access builds a new Index via drop_duplicates(keep=False).  https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/main/pandas/core/frame.py#L4162-L4169   ```code import pandas as pd import timeit  # DataFrame with many columns and duplicate names; one column "key" appears once n = 1000000 cols = ["a"] * (n - 1) + ["key"] df = pd.DataFrame(0, index=range(10000), columns=cols)   # Repeated single-column access (e.g. in a loop or pipeline) def access():     for _ in range(100):         _ = df["key"]   # Current state: each df["key"] calls columns.drop_duplicates(keep=False) → O(n) + allocation  sec = timeit.timeit(access, number=10) print(f"1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): {sec:.2f}s") ```  Output  ``` 1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 8.69s ```  Expected: Single-column access when the key appears once should not rebuild the Index on every access; runtime should be much lower (e.g. well under 1 second for 1000 accesses).  Suggested Fix  ``` if not is_mi:     try:         loc = self.columns.get_loc(key)         if isinstance(loc, int):             return self._get_item(key)     except (KeyError, InvalidIndexError):         pass elif is_mi and self.columns.is_unique and key in self.columns:     return self._getitem_multilevel(key) ```  Output would be  ``` 1000 accesses (100 iters × 10 runs): 0.04s ```   ### Installed Versions  <details>   INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 4ce8e340d5b579c11290d855a7e99e646289555d python                : 3.12.2 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Darwin OS-release

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd examples=['ga',           'Áa',           '永a',           '🐍a'] for t in examples:     objects = pd.Series([t], dtype=object)     strs = pd.Series([t], dtype=str)     print('python:', t.find('a'),            'pandas with object type:', objects.str.find('a')[0],           'pandas with string type:', strs.str.find('a')[0],                     ) ```  ### Issue Description  `str.find` appears to be indexing its result based on bytes rather than characters. In the example, the basic python `str` type, and a `Series` using the `object` `dtype`, `find('a')` is `1` for all the example strings, as expected. With a `Series` using the new `str` `dtype`, the result is 1, 2, 3, and 4 respectively. Note that encoded in UTF-8, Á takes two bytes, 永 takes three, and 🐍 takes four, so I suspect it's counting bytes instead of characters. `len` gives a result of 2 regardless of dtype.  ### Expected Behavior  The result of `str.find` shouldn't change depending on dtype.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : cc9e131258c3f6a2df793c3876ea708e192b4875 python                : 3.13.12 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 11 Version               : 10.0.26200 machine               : AMD64 processor             : Intel64 Family 6 Model 140 Stepping 1, GenuineIntel byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : None LOCALE                : English_United States.1252  pandas                : 3.1.0.dev0+1

title: API/BUG: support for operations with custom objects / object dtype
body: Consider the following dummy example of a custom Python object that supports some arithmetic operations:  ```python class MyObject:     def __init__(self, val):         self.val = val     def __add__(self, other):         if hasattr(other, "dtype"):             return NotImplemented         return MyObject(self.val + other)     def __radd__(self, other):         if hasattr(other, "dtype"):             return NotImplemented         return MyObject(other + self.val)     def __repr__(self):         return f"<MyObject({self.val})>" ```  Working with such objects in pandas containers generally works, i.e. we defer to the scalar operation and assemble the results:  ```python # operation of scalar/arr/series with numeric other arr = np.array([MyObject(1), MyObject(2)]) ser = pd.Series([1, 2])  print(ser + arr[0]) print(ser + arr) print(ser + pd.Series(arr)) print(arr[0] + ser) print(arr + ser) print(pd.Series(arr) + ser) ```  When the other operand were strings, this worked in pandas 2.x as well:  ```python # operation of scalar/arr/series with string (object) other arr = np.array([MyObject("a"), MyObject("b")]) ser = pd.Series(["1", "2"])  print(ser + arr[0]) print(ser + arr) print(ser + pd.Series(arr)) print(arr[0] + ser) print(arr + ser) print(pd.Series(arr) + ser) ```  However, this case no longer works in pandas 3.0 with the default `str` dtype.  We specifically fixed this for `pathlib.Path` objects for the scalar case (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/61940 / https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/62229), but then got a report for such objects in a Series (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63832). But in the end, while we can "fix" this again specifically for Path objects, this is a more general issue with any generic Python object. title: ENH: Nearest_in_time fill for time series data
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  While working with time series data, I ran into a case where missing values needed to be filled using observations that were closest in time, rather than only forward or backward. pandas currently offers ffill / bfill and numeric interpolation, but neither fits this use case well.  The data was irregularly sampled and contained a mix of numeric measurements and categorical state columns. Forward or backward fill was too directional, and interpolation was not applicable to categorical data and also introduced new values.  What I needed was a way to fill missing values by looking at the nearest observations in time, regardless of direction, and to optionally consider more than one nearby point, with closer observations having more influence.  There does not seem to be a built-in, time-aware way in pandas to express this kind of nearest-neighbor imputation during preprocessing.  ### Feature Description  Assume we have a numeric time series indexed by timestamps. title: ENH: Allow merge to override columns
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  I wish that merge would be able to solve column name conflicts by allowing to override one value. This is especially useful for jupyter notebooks when I have cells that perform a pd.merge() and have the resulting df be the same variable as one of the inputs:  ```python df = pd.merge(df, otherdf, **otherargs) ```  If I rerun a cell containing such a merge, the dataframe columns are changed. There are two possible workarounds, the first is to just never assign to the same name, the other one is this:  ```python df = pd.merge(df.loc[:,~df.columns.isin(otherdf.columns), otherdf, **otherargs) ```  ### Feature Description  Add a new parameter to the pd.merge() function to allow overriding columns:  ```python def merge(left, right, override: str | None=None, **kwargs):     """     Parameters     ----------     override: {"left","right",None}         default: None         If not None suffix will be ignored and the columns of the specified dataframe         will override the other one in case of a conflict     """ ```  ### Alternative Solutions  Alternatively override could be a bool and it will always override the left dataframe  ### Additional Context  I am happy to make a pull request if you are okay with having this feature included

title: ENH: Determination of result "flavor" when based on multiple input flavors
body: In various places, we may want to determine the dtype flavor* for newly created columns when based on multiple input flavors. A list of areas is at the bottom.  The implementation (a function in `core.dtypes`) could take an array, Series, or DataFrame and determine the proper flavor. If the input is a single flavor, then this is trivial. We'd need to decide what the rule is in case of multiple flavors.  Option 1: `pyarrow` -> `nullable` -> `numpy` (or any of the 5 other permutations as suboptions)  If there are any `pyarrow` then go with that; if no `pyarrow` and there are `nullable` then go with that, and finally only have `numpy` if all columns are `numpy`. I think we'd want to consider `str` dtype (whether backed by pyarrow or numpy) as being `numpy` for the purposes of this. This might be problematic when the data has only `str` columns, but I don't see a better alternative.  *flavor may not be the appropriate term here, I recall some objections to its usage in the past.  <details>  <summary>Areas</summary>  - In `pivot_table` [ref](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/63979#discussion_r2755700009) - In apply/agg/transform/map when a UDF is returning all scalars. Here, the input columns are to be used, which can in some cases be more than 1.  </details>

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  In `pandas/_libs/tslibs/offsets.pyx`, several offset classes access private member variables (e.g., _offset, _normalize, _n, _weekmask, _holidays, _calendar) through their property accessors (e.g., self.offset, self.normalize) instead of directly accessing the private variables (e.g., self._offset, self._normalize). This is inconsistent with other private variable access patterns in the same file (e.g., self._n is typically accessed directly) and introduces unnecessary property method call overhead in performance-sensitive code paths. Classes potentially affected: ``` BusinessDay BusinessHour CustomBusinessDay CustomBusinessHour CustomBusinessMonthBegin CustomBusinessMonthEnd ```  Other offset classes inheriting from BusinessMixin or BaseOffset  Common patterns to address: ``` self.offset → self._offset self.normalize → self._normalize self.holidays → self._holidays self.weekmask → self._weekmask self.calendar → self._calendar ```  Expected behavior: Private variables should be accessed directly within class methods rather than through property accessors for consistency and minor performance improvement.   ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 4ce8e340d5b579c11290d855a7e99e646289555d python                : 3.12.2 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Darwin OS-release            : 25.2.0 Version               : Darwin Kernel Version 25.2.0: Tue Nov 18 21:09:41 PST 2025; root:xnu-12377.61.12~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6031 machine               : arm64 processor             : arm byteorder             : little LC_ALL                : None LANG                  : C.UTF-8 LOCALE

title: ENH: Allow `np.ndarray` in `check_result_array` for certain `dtype`
body: ### Feature Type  - [ ] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Aggregations are using `check_result_array` to verify that the aggregation operation reduced the dimension. To do so it checks that the given `obj` is not a `np.ndarray` and if so the expected `dtype` is at least `object`. The expected `dtype` hereby is the `dtype` of the `group` before the aggregation. This can be an issue if the actual aggregated `obj` is expected to still be an `np.ndarray` but the expected `dtype` is not `object`.  `_aggregate_series_pure_python` calls `check_result_array(res, group.dtype)` to verify result of aggregation: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/433b140936aadec0f42c46e4e827f6f545569bbc/pandas/core/groupby/ops.py#L986-L1005  `check_result_array`: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/433b140936aadec0f42c46e4e827f6f545569bbc/pandas/core/groupby/ops.py#L81-L89  ### Feature Description  The `dtype` parameter in `check_result_array` lets us know what the `dtype` of the `group` was. title: BUG: refs not set when creating DataFrame from Series/Index with StringDtype and infer_string=False
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd from pandas import DataFrame, Series, Index import pandas._testing as tm from pandas.tests.copy_view.util import get_array  with pd.option_context("infer_string", False):     obj = Series(["a", "b"], dtype="str")     df = DataFrame(obj, dtype="str")      assert tm.shares_memory(get_array(obj), get_array(df, 0))  # OK     assert not df._mgr._has_no_reference(0)  # AssertionError ```  ### Issue Description  When creating a DataFrame from a Series or Index with dtype="str" via DataFrame(obj, dtype="str"), the underlying memory is shared with the source, but the copy-on-write reference (refs) is not passed to the block. As a result, df._mgr._has_no_reference(0) returns True even though the block is shared, so the CoW reference tracking is wrong. Other dtypes (e.g. int64, object) set refs correctly in the same situation.  ### Expected Behavior  When the DataFrame shares memory with the source Series/Index, refs should be set so that _has_no_reference(0) is False.  ``` python obj = Series(["a", "b"], dtype="str") df = DataFrame(obj, dtype="str")  assert tm.shares_memory(get_array(obj), get_array(df, 0)) assert not df._mgr._has_no_reference(0) # refs present → CoW can trigger correctly  ```  ### Installed Versions  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 366ccdfcd8ed1e5543bfb6d4ee0c9bc519898670 python                : 3.13.7 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Windows OS-release            : 11 Version               : 10.0.26200 machine               : AMD64 processor             : I

title: BUG: Handling of `None` column name in `from_records()` is now all-NaN instead of values
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  dict_data = [     {'fieldA': 'X', 'fieldB': 'Y', None: ['1000']},     {'fieldA': 'Z', 'fieldB': '', None: ['900']} ]  pd.DataFrame.from_records(dict_data) ```  ### Issue Description  Using that example list-of-dicts, which is the result of an incorrect CSV file read with `csv.DictReader()`:  On Pandas 3.0.0, the output just has a **NaN column name** with **NaN values**, which doesn't seem useful.: ```   fieldA fieldB  NaN 0      X      Y  NaN 1      Z         NaN ```  Even if that last field was not an array, and just `None: '1000'` and `None: '900'`, the result is still the same NaN column name with NaN values.    ### Expected Behavior  It should have `None` as the column name and the values should be present.  While it may be more consistent with the behaviour of the `columns` param of DataFrame.from_records() _"(any names not found in the data will become all-NA columns)"_ - the column name is already different and it's a breaking change wrt how this used to be handled when no column param is provided:  On version 2.3.3, the result of that same code is: ```   fieldA fieldB    None 0      X      Y  [1000] 1      Z          [900] ```  which can be used to inform the end user of the missing header/extra column. When it's NaN _name and values_, nothing can done with it except to inform the end user "there probably an extra column".  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 366ccdfcd8ed1e5543bfb6d4ee0c9bc519898670 python                : 3.13.11 python-bits

title: BUG: Conversion from numpy masked arrays to pandas array does not preserve missing values
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python >>> import numpy as np >>> import pandas as pd  >>> a = np.ma.array([1, 2, 3, 4], mask=[False, True, False, True]) >>> # mask is ignored completely >>> pd.array(a) <IntegerArray> [1, 2, 3, 4] Length: 4, dtype: Int64 >>> # mask is handled correctly, but type is converted to float >>> pd.Series(a) 0    1.0 1    NaN 2    3.0 3    NaN dtype: float64  >>> b = np.ma.array(['foo', 'bar', 'baz', '42'], mask = [False, True, False, True]) >>> pd.array(b) <StringArray> ['foo', 'bar', 'baz', '42'] Length: 4, dtype: string >>> pd.Series(b) 0    foo 1    NaN 2    baz 3    NaN dtype: str ```  ### Issue Description  Numpy [masked arrays](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/maskedarray.generic.html#what-is-a-masked-array) can be used to define numpy arrays with missing values, similar to pandas extension arrays. However, conversion to `pd.array` does not handle missing values. Conversion to `pd.Series` does, but does not preserve the correct type in all cases.    fyi @flying-sheep @ilan-gold  ### Expected Behavior  ```python >>> pd.array(a) <IntegerArray> [1, <NA>, 3, <NA>] Length: 4, dtype: Int64  >>> pd.array(b) <StringArray> ['foo', <NA>, 'bar', <NA>] Length: 4, dtype: string  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 366ccdfcd8ed1e5543bfb6d4ee0c9bc519898670 python                : 3.12.9 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Linux OS-release            : 6.18.6-arch1-1 Version               : #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Sun, 18 Jan 2026 00:34:07 +0000 machine               : x86_6

title: BUG: AttributeError: 'ArrowStringArray' object has no attribute 'item'
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd  # Pandas object that contains only 1 unique value: s = pd.Series(["foo", "foo"]) s.unique() # pandas 2.3.3: # array(['foo'], dtype=object) # # pandas 3.0.0: # <ArrowStringArray> # ['foo'] # Length: 1, dtype: str  # Retrieve the unique value as a scalar s.astype(object).unique().item() # pandas 2.3.3 or 3.0.0: 'foo'  # Retrieve the unique value as a scalar s.unique().item(): # pandas 2.3.3: 'foo' # pandas 3.0.0: AttributeError: 'ArrowStringArray' object has no attribute 'item' ```  ### Issue Description  In pandas 2.3.3 and earlier `(...).unique().item()` worked as a way to get a single unique value that appeared in a Series —or DataFrame column, or as the result of other operation that resulted in a Series. This was concise and preferable to, for instance, `(...).unique()[0]` because it would raise an exception if earlier code produced a *non*-unique Series.  With pandas 3.0.0, when the dtype of the Series is `str`, the result of `.unique()` is ArrowStringArray, which [lacks an `.item()` method](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/reference/api/pandas.arrays.ArrowStringArray.html).  If this is a deliberate breaking change, then I would expect that (a) it would be mentioned in [the relevant section of the release notes](https://pandas.pydata.org/pandas-docs/stable/whatsnew/v3.0.0.html#other-api-changes); and/or (b) version < 3.0.0 would give some kind of DeprecationWarning to draw attention to expected breakage with the release of 3.0.0. title: ENH: Data Entropy & Information Loss Tracking for DataFrame Transformations
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Pandas does not provide any method to measure the information loss which occurs when DataFrame transformations are applied.   Data resolution decreases permanently through common operations because users cannot observe this reduction which results from rounding and binning and aggregation and encoding and filtering and deduplication. Users create data compression that exceeds proper limits which leads to the loss of valuable information without their awareness.   I want pandas to provide users with information loss measurements which show how transformations affect data processing because this will help them choose preprocessing methods and identify excessive operations which will improve their data pipeline trust.  ### Feature Description  The system will start tracking operational data transformations through its mandatory tracking system which will record every DataFrame transformation that occurs.   The feature would:  - The system will calculate entropy values at the column level using Shannon entropy for discrete data and histogram-based entropy for continuous data.  - The system will measure information loss through its normalized entropy difference calculation which compares two different states.  - The system will track information loss from operations that occur within a monitoring environment.  Example API:        with df.track_information() as info:            df["price"] = df["price"].round(0)            df["age_group"] = pd.cut(df["age"], bins=5)          info.report()  Conceptual implementation        def entropy(series):           if is_discrete(series):               p = value_counts(series) / len(series)               return -sum(p * log2(p))           else:                bins = adaptive_bins(series)                p = histogram(series, bins) / len(series)

title: BUG: Inconsistent BOM handling in pd.read_csv with encoding='utf-8'
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import pandas as pd import io  # CSV with UTF‑8 BOM bytes_data = b"\xef\xbb\xbfName,Age\nJohn,25" bio = io.BytesIO(bytes_data)   df_c = pd.read_csv(bio, encoding="utf-8") print(repr(df_c.columns[0]))  # 'Name'  bio.seek(0) # but different behaviour in text wrapper stream = io.TextIOWrapper(bio, encoding='utf-8')  print(repr(stream.read())) # '\ufeffName,Age\nJohn,25'  ```  ### Issue Description  When reading a UTF-8 encoded CSV that contains a BOM, specifying `encoding='utf-8'` pandas strips the BOM from the first column header and textwrapper leaves it as an invisible `\ufeff` character. The outcome depends on the parsing, but this behaviour is undocumented and inconsistent.  ### Expected Behavior  I expected `encoding='utf-8'` either to always keep the BOM (requiring `utf-8-sig` to remove it) or to always strip it, regardless of parser. At minimum, the documentation should clarify how BOMs are handled across engines when using `encoding='utf-8'`.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  Replace this line with the output of pd.show_versions()  </details>

[x] I have confirmed this issue exists on the main branch of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  Using `groupby.agg` with a named aggregation which doesn't actually use relabeling is much slower (for small dfs) than the same operation without a named aggregation   ```python In [1]: import numpy as np    ...: import pandas as pd    ...:    ...:    ...: def generate_data(n_rows: int) -> pd.DataFrame:    ...:     # Random date range within 2024    ...:     date_range = pd.date_range(start="2024-01-01", end="2024-12-31", freq="D")    ...:     dates = np.random.choice(date_range, size=n_rows)    ...:    ...:     # Random number of users and values    ...:     num_users = np.random.randint(1, 100, size=n_rows)    ...:     values = np.random.uniform(1.0, 1000.0, size=n_rows)    ...:    ...:     # Create DataFrame    ...:     df = pd.DataFrame({"date": dates, "num_users": num_users, "value": values})    ...:     return df    ...:    ...:    ...: def named(df: pd.DataFrame):    ...:     return df.groupby("date").agg(    ...:         **{"num_users": ("num_users", "sum"), "value": ("value", "sum")}    ...:     )    ...:    ...:    ...: def unnamed(df: pd.DataFrame):    ...:     return df.groupby("date").agg({"num_users": "sum", "value": "sum"})    ...:  In [2]: df = generate_data(10**3)  In [3]: %timeit named(df) 1.21 ms ± 61.5 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000 loops each)  In [4]: %timeit unnamed(df) 365 μs ± 6.41 μs per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1,000 loops each) ```  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874 python                : 3.12.9 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Darwin OS-release            : 24.6.0 Version

title: BUG: Inconsistent NaN detection based on Series dtype, to_numeric dtype_backend, None vs np.nan, strings in orig list
body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ```python import numpy as np import pandas as pd import pyarrow as pa # Create 'float' Series with numeric and np.nan (or None) ser = pd.Series([1, np.nan], dtype=np.float64) # Passing either dtype_backend results in failure to find nulls for backend in ['numpy_nullable', 'pyarrow']:     s = pd.to_numeric(ser, dtype_backend=backend)     assert 0 == s.isna().sum() # should be 1     assert 2 == s.dropna().size # should be 1  # See 54 different in df_failures under the Full Testing section ```  ### Issue Description  The `.isna()` and `.dropna()` methods do not always find nulls in float and float-like Series. This includes Series that have been passed to `pd.to_numeric`. The behavior depends on...   - The `dtype_backend` of `to_numeric`   - Whether the original data were numbers, strings, or mixed   - The `dtype` of the Series when it was created      Please, see the **Full testing** section below for combinations.  This is tagged with `to_numeric`, but given some of the behavior happens even before `to_numeric` is called, it may be more of a general pandas issue.  # Reproduction  steps  There are several variations that will reproduce the issue as shown in the Full Testing section; this is just one example:    1. Create a list that has only numbers and `np.nan` values 2. Create a pandas Series from the list with `dtype=np.float64` 3. Use `pd.to_numeric()` on that Series with one of the `dtype_backend` options     - You must pass either `'numpy_nullable'` or `'pyarrow'` 4. Check the number of nulls with `pd.isna().sum()` and see it returns `0`

title: Cleanup: Add type: ignore comments for comparison-overlap in datetimes.py
body: ## Description  Following up on #58475, which was closed after the team decided against  implementing type-safe constructors for `Timestamp`/`Timedelta`.  While that decision is sound, it leaves some mypy warnings in the codebase  that could be cleaned up with minimal `type: ignore` comments.  ## Current State  Running mypy on latest main (commit 0771efc5a0) shows: ``` pandas\core\arrays\datetimes.py:2973: error: Non-overlapping identity check  (left operand type: "Timestamp", right operand type: "NaTType") pandas\core\arrays\datetimes.py:2981: error: Non-overlapping identity check  (left operand type: "Timestamp", right operand type: "NaTType") ```  ## Proposed Solution  Add `# type: ignore[comparison-overlap]` comments to these specific lines: ```python # Line 2973 if start is not NaT:  # type: ignore[comparison-overlap]     start = start.as_unit(unit)  # Line 2981   if end is not NaT:  # type: ignore[comparison-overlap]     end = end.as_unit(unit) ``` ## Alternatives Considered I considered using `typing.cast(object, start)` to make the check valid, but `type: ignore` seemed less verbose for a known false positive. I am happy to implement whichever pattern the team prefers. ## Context  This is NOT proposing to reopen #58475 or implement the rejected constructors.  This is simply cleaning up the expected mypy warnings that result from the  team's decision to keep the current type system.  ## Environment - pandas: 2.3.0.dev0+1847.g0771efc5a0 - Python: 3.14.0 - mypy: 1.19.1  I'm happy to submit a PR if this approach is acceptable.

title: ENH: Add high-level "themes" or "presets" to Styler API
body: ## Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ## Problem Description   Currently, using df.style to create common visualization patterns (like financial formatting, data bars, or heatmaps) is verbose. body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example  ``` sh  pip install pandas pyreadstat ```  ``` python import pandas as pd import pyreadstat  source_df = pd.DataFrame([[1,2.0,"a"],[3,4.0,"b"]], columns=["v1", "v2", "v3"]) column_labels = ["Variable 1", "Variable 2", "Variable 3"] pyreadstat.write_sav(source_df, "spss_data.sav", file_label="test", column_labels=column_labels)  read_df = pd.read_spss("spss_data.sav") print(read_df.attrs) # contains creation_time and modification_time keys with datetime values # read_df.attrs.clear() # enabling this line allows parquet writing to succeed read_df.to_parquet("spss_data.parquet") # crashes ```  ### Issue Description  Possibly not strictly a pandas bug, possibly pyarrow, possibly pyreadstat, but pandas is the project linking it all together.  Pandas leans on pyreadstat to process spss files and pyarrow to write parquet files.  pyreadstat generates a metadata dictionary which pandas assigns to `attrs` in `pandas.io.spss.read_spss`. This dict contains `creation_time` and `modification_time` keys of `datetime.datetime`, which crash json.dumps when metadata is created from `attrs` during writing of a parquet file in `pyarrow.pandas_compat.construct_metadata`.  ### Expected Behavior  Parquet writing should succeed for a dataframe created from an spss file.  ### Installed Versions  <details>  INSTALLED VERSIONS ------------------ commit                : 9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874 python                : 3.13.3 python-bits           : 64 OS                    : Linux OS-release            : 5.15.153.1-microsoft-standard-WSL2 Version

title: ENH: `Timestamp.round`: officially accept `Timedelta` arguments
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  `Timestamp.round` should accept arbitrary `Timedelta`, so that we don't need to stringify types.  This actually already works at runtime, because internally [`Timestamp.round`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.Timestamp.round.html) parses the `freq` argument with [`pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset`](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/reference/api/pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset.html) but it is not documented:  ```python import pandas as pd  freq = "1h30min" offset = pd.Timedelta(freq)  dt = pd.Timestamp.now() dt.round(freq)  # ✅️ (documented) dt.round(offset)  # ✅️ (undocumented) dt.round(str(offset)) # ❌️ fails ```  If accepted, one should also consider patching `pandas.tseries.frequencies.to_offset` so that it gives identical results when passing a `Timedelta` versus casting that timedelta to string. In fact, it seems like internally it should probably just cast the string to timedelta first before processing it further.   ### Feature Description  1. Update documentation / type-hints of `Timestamp.round` to allow `Timedelta` argument 2. title: String dtype: differences in regex operations because of engine (Python vs RE2)
body: One area where there can be significant behaviour differences depending on the string dtype backend being used (https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63105) is for regex operations:  - The Python str object-dtype based implementation uses the Python stdlib `re` module, which I think was generally based on the PCRE engine but has diverged from it. - On the other hand, for the pyarrow-backed string dtype, the Arrow C++ / pyarrow library uses the [RE2](https://github.com/google/re2) engine.  And unfortunately, there are lots of different regular expression engines with slight differences in behaviour and supported features (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comparison_of_regular_expression_engines).  We already encountered a few differences: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/60833 (RE2 not supporting look-around assertions), https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63385 (RE2 not supporting `\Z`), https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/62653 (replace with groups).  RE2 explicitly says to "not not support constructs for which only backtracking solutions are known to exist. Thus, backreferences and look-around assertions are not supported."  There is probably not an easy definitive list of differences, but @rhshadrach found the (old) https://swtch.com/~rsc/regexp/regexp3.html#caveats article from the RE2 author listing a bunch. That also shows an example where it results in different behaviour and not raising an error (because of an unsupported feature), with `$` matching a ending newline differently:  ``` ser = pd.Series(["a\n"]) print(ser.str.contains(r'a$')) # 0    False # dtype: bool print(ser.astype(object).str.contains(r'a$')) # 0    True # dtype: bool ```  Update: the description in the Python bindings of RE2 might give a quite good overview (although it does not mention the above difference), as those bindings specifically mimic the stdlib `re` module except for behaviour differences because of being RE2 (https://pypi.org/project/google-re2/,

body: ### Pandas version checks  - [x] I have checked that this issue has not already been reported.  - [x] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [latest version](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/whatsnew/index.html) of pandas.  - [ ] I have confirmed this bug exists on the [main branch](https://pandas.pydata.org/docs/dev/getting_started/install.html#installing-the-development-version-of-pandas) of pandas.   ### Reproducible Example (Updated)  I have managed to isolate the issue to a minimal reproducible example. Any scientific notation string where the exponent causes a 32-bit signed integer overflow (wrapping to negative) triggers the crash.  ```python import pandas as pd  # The exponent '3000000000' (3 billion) exceeds INT_MAX (2.14 billion) # but is within the parser's digit limit (max_digits=17). # This causes an integer overflow in the C parser. s = pd.Series(["1E3000000000"])  print(f"Pandas version: {pd.__version__}") print("Attempting to crash...")  # This triggers SIGSEGV immediately res = pd.to_numeric(s, errors='coerce') print(res) ```  ### Issue Description The Python interpreter crashes with a **Segmentation Fault (SIGSEGV)** when parsing specific strings that look like scientific notation.  The crash occurs in `precise_xstrtod` within `pandas/_libs/pandas_parser`.  ### Root Cause Analysis  Based on the GDB trace and source code analysis, this is a **Signed Integer Overflow leading to an Out-of-Bounds Read**.  1.  **Integer Overflow**:     In `precise_xstrtod` (tokenizer.c), the variable `n` (used to parse the exponent) is typically declared as `int` (32-bit signed).     The input exponent `3000000000` is parsed. Since this exceeds `INT_MAX` (2,147,483,647), it overflows and is interpreted as a **negative number** (specifically `-1294967296` in 32-bit representation).  2.  **Bypassing Bounds Checks**:     The code likely contains checks like `if (exponent > 308)`. Since the overflowed exponent is now negative, it bypasses this check and enters the logic path

title: ENH: Create `.rdiff()`, like `.diff()` but reversed, like `.rsub()` and `.sub()`
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  Firstly, it's easy enough to get the behaviour I want by using other methods, so this is just a suggestion if you want it. By all means ignore if it would be more effort than it's worth. Hopefully it has non-trivial uses, but I can't think of any :P  I wanted to find gaps in a Series of integers, similar to [this SO question](https://stackoverflow.com/q/66021881/4518341 "How to detect gaps between integer sequence in pandas?"). All the answers use some variation of `s.shift(-1) - s - 1`, so I thought, it'd be more elegant to write that using `Series.diff`, but if you do `.diff(-1)`, you get negatives (when the Series is sorted ascending), so you have to invert it after: `s.diff(-1)*-1 - 1`. Or you can do `.diff(1).shift(-1)`.  What would be cleaner is to have a method `.rdiff()` that does the equivalent of `s.shift(-1) - s`, which I guess you could call the "reverse difference". As a bonus, this would create a symmetry: `.diff()` and `.rdiff()` like `.sub()` (subtract) and `.rsub()` (reversed subtract - or "reflected" subtract [according to the Python docs](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__rsub__)).  ### Feature Description  If `x.diff(n)` does the equivalent of `x - x.shift(n)`, `x.rdiff(n)` does the equivalent of `x.shift(-n) - x`.  In actual fact, [`Series.diff` uses `algorithms.diff`](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874/pandas/core/series.py#L3134C1-L3134C56), which [gets pretty complicated](https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/blob/9c8bc3e55188c8aff37207a74f1dd144980b8874/pandas/core/algorithms.py#L1339), so I'm glossing over the details.  ### Alternative Solutions  As said above, this is easy enough to accomplish using other methods.  ### Additional Context  _No response_

title: DEPR: Series.round and Series.clip on non-numeric and non-object dtypes
body: Ref: https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63444  Prior to the PR linked to the above issue, `Series.round` would raise on only object dtype and be a no-op on other dtypes that did not support rounding. The behavior is also the same for `Series.clip`.  ```python ser = pd.Series(pd.Categorical([1.234], categories=[1.234]))  print(ser.abs()) # TypeError: Object with dtype category cannot perform the numpy op absolute  print(ser.round()) # 0    1.234 # dtype: category # Categories (1, float64): [1.234]  print(ser.clip()) # 0    1.234 # dtype: category # Categories (1, float64): [1.234]  ser = pd.Series(["a"], dtype=str)  print(ser.abs()) # pyarrow.lib.ArrowNotImplementedError: Function 'abs_checked' has no kernel matching input types (large_string)  print(ser.round()) # 0    a # dtype: str  print(ser.clip()) # 0    a # dtype: str ```  I think we should deprecate `Series.round` and `Series.clip` from being a no-op. The corresponding DataFrame methods are to still be no-ops on such columns.

title: ENH: Add .center() method to DataFrame/Series for inspecting middle rows.
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  I wish I could use pandas to inspect the middle rows of a DataFrame or Series using a simple method like .center(), analogous to .head() and .tail().  ### Feature Description  def center(self, n: int = 5):     """     Return the middle n rows.          Parameters     ----------     n : int, default 5         Number of rows to select.          Returns     -------     type of caller         The subset of the DataFrame or Series.     """     total_len = len(self)          # Edge case: If the requested window is larger than the data, return the whole object     # (consistent with .head() and .tail() behavior)     if n >= total_len:         return self          # Calculate the middle index     mid_idx = total_len // 2          # Determine start index (integer division handles odd/even n automatically)     start = max(0, mid_idx - (n // 2))          # Determine end index     end = start + n          return self.iloc[start:end]   ### Alternative Solutions  # Manual slicing with iloc mid = len(df) // 2 df.iloc[mid - 2 : mid + 3]   ### Additional Context   This feature addresses a gap in the API symmetry. head() allows inspection of the start, and tail() allows inspection of the end. center() would complete the inspection triad, making it intuitive to check the interior of the dataframe without leaving the method-chaining syntax.

title: ENH: first-class UUID support
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas - [ ] Changing existing functionality in pandas - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  A lot of people want to use UUID arrays, so we should provide first-class support.  If you want to play around with it, I prototyped this functionality here: https://pypi.org/project/pandas-uuid/  ### Feature Description  I suggest to do something similar as for `{Arrow,}StringArray`, i.e. have a dyad of `ExtensionArray` types, one backed by numpy and one by pyarrow.  They don’t need a lot of features except for comparison (`self == other` / `self == elem`) and membership tests (`self.__contains__(elem)`/`elem in self` and `self.isin(other)`).  The numpy variant needs to be backed by a `np.void(16)`/`"V16"` array, since [`np.bytes_`/`"S"`](https://numpy.org/doc/stable/reference/arrays.scalars.html#numpy.bytes_) has special treatment of null bytes, whereas numeric types (like UUIDs) assign no special meaning to them.  ### Alternative Solutions  - We could use `MaskedArray` as base for the numpy-backed variant to allow missing values in both cases. - We could just force people to rely on pyarrow for this functionality, but I feel that wrapping `np.void(16)` is simple enough. People didn’t like adding the pyarrow dependency for basic functionality, so I assume you want to keep adding basic features that don’t rely on pyarrow. - We could keep the `pandas-uuid` package around, see [here](https://icb-pandas-uuid.readthedocs-hosted.com/en/latest/#pandas-integration) for its limitations.  ### Additional Context  - Turns out the following issue isn’t actually a blocker if we have the `ExtensionDtype` report its `kind` to be `"O"`: #54810  - We should test that things like this work by default: #59132

title: ENH: Add an opt in operation report for time memory and copy behavior
body: ### Feature Type  - [x] Adding new functionality to pandas  - [x] Changing existing functionality in pandas  - [ ] Removing existing functionality in pandas   ### Problem Description  I want a reliable way to understand why a single pandas operation is slow or uses far more memory than I expect. When a merge, groupby, sort, or rolling call suddenly takes minutes or crashes with out of memory, pandas completes the work or fails without telling me what path it took, how many temporary arrays were created, or where the time went. That leaves me guessing, rewriting code, and trying different dtypes and arguments until something improves.  External profilers can show Python level hotspots, but they do not answer the pandas specific questions I need in the moment. I need something that can tell me whether a join built a large hash table, whether groupby spent most of its time building the grouper, whether a sort triggered large copies, and whether Copy on Write forced unexpected materialization. With that information I could make simple changes like adjusting key dtypes, choosing observed or sort settings, reducing columns earlier, or validating join cardinality. Without it, debugging performance and memory spikes is slow, fragile, and hard to reproduce.  ### Feature Description  A practical way to build this is to introduce an opt in collector that wraps a single pandas operation and produces a compact report. When diagnostics are turned off, nothing happens apart from one cheap check, so there is no meaningful overhead in normal use.  The public entry point can be pd.diagnostics.report(func, *args, **kwargs) with an optional context manager for the same behavior. Internally, the wrapper sets a thread local reference to the active collector, starts wall time measurement and optional memory tracking, executes the operation, then stops tracking and clears the thread local. After the call completes, the collector freezes the captured metrics into a DiagnosticsReport object,

title: BUG: specifying unit in to_datetime when parsing strings causes different error behaviour
body: Consider the case of "mixed" iso strings. Nowadays that gives an error, but you can then specify `format` to indicate you know it is all ISO strings:  ```python >>> pd.to_datetime(["2025-01-01T00:00:00.000000", "2025-01-01T01:00:00"]) ... ValueError: time data "2025-01-01T01:00:00" doesn't match format "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%f". You might want to try:     - passing `format` if your strings have a consistent format;     - passing `format='ISO8601'` if your strings are all ISO8601 but not necessarily in exactly the same format;     - passing `format='mixed'`, and the format will be inferred for each element individually. You might want to use `dayfirst` alongside this.  >>> pd.to_datetime(["2025-01-01T00:00:00.000000", "2025-01-01T01:00:00"], format="ISO8601") DatetimeIndex(['2025-01-01 00:00:00', '2025-01-01 01:00:00'], dtype='datetime64[us]', freq=None) ```  Strangely, passing a `unit` (which is generally ignored when not parsing numeric input), the error is not given, and it parses the input fine by default, but also gives ns instead of us:  ```python >>> pd.to_datetime(["2025-01-01T00:00:00.000000", "2025-01-01T01:00:00"], unit="s") DatetimeIndex(['2025-01-01 00:00:00', '2025-01-01 01:00:00'], dtype='datetime64[ns]', freq=None) ```  cc @jbrockmendel

title: API: comparing time series with index of different unit should work
body: Taking the example from https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/issues/63417, but opening a separate issue to focus on just the behaviour with mismatching unit, regardless of performance issues.  pandas generally aligns on the index in all operations, _except_ for comparison operations, where we raise an error for mis-aligned indices (_"Can only compare identically-labeled Series objects"_).   But currently, two DatetimeIndex with the same values but different unit is apparently considered as "not identical", and thus you get errors like this:  ```python dti = pd.date_range("2016-01-01", periods=3) ser = pd.Series(1, index=dti) ser2 = pd.Series(1, index=dti.as_unit("ns"))  >>> ser == ser2 ... File ~/scipy/repos/pandas/pandas/core/series.py:6656, in Series._cmp_method(self, other, op)    6653 res_name = ops.get_op_result_name(self, other)    6655 if isinstance(other, Series) and not self._indexed_same(other): -> 6656     raise ValueError("Can only compare identically-labeled Series objects")    6658 lvalues = self._values    6659 rvalues = extract_array(other, extract_numpy=True, extract_range=True)  ValueError: Can only compare identically-labeled Series objects ```  With pandas 3.0, since we now no longer default to nanoseconds in all cases (typically microseconds, but also other resolutions depending on how you created the timestamp data), I assume this would be more common.   And generally, my feeling is that the above comparison should Just Work?  cc @pandas-dev/pandas-core
