title: watch with deep: true incorrectly collects parent dependencies
body: ### Vue version  3.5.13  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://play.vuejs.org/#  ### Steps to reproduce  ```js const obj = reactive({ nested: { foo: 1 } });  watch(   () => obj.nested.foo,   (newValue, oldValue) => {     console.log("watch triggered newValue, oldValue: ", newValue, oldValue);   } );  watch(   () => obj.nested.foo,   (newValue, oldValue) => {     console.log("watch deep triggered newValue, oldValue: ", newValue, oldValue);   },   { deep: true } );  obj.nested = {   foo: 1, }; ```  When using watch with the deep: true option, the getter execution triggers dependency collection for the entire object tree, including parent properties, instead of only the target property. This causes the callback to be triggered when a parent property (e.g., obj.nested) is modified, even though the target property (e.g., obj.nested.foo) itself has not changed.   ### What is expected?  The callback should only be triggered when obj.nested.foo changes, not when the parent property (obj.nested) is modified, as the target property has not changed.  ### What is actually happening?  When deep: true is set, modifying the parent property obj.nested triggers the watch callback, even though obj.nested.foo has not changed.  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  _No response_

title: `defineCustomElement` looses provide context configured by `configureApp` on HMR
body: ### Vue version  3.5.12  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-kennhm?file=src%2FApp.ce.vue  ### Steps to reproduce  1. Open the reproduction link 2. Remove the comment in `App.ce.vue` after the app is running  If you create a custom element with `defineCustomElement` and provide something in the app via `configureApp` the provided context gets lost when a HMR occurs.  ### What is expected?  The provide context should be kept  ### What is actually happening?  The provide context will be lost  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  This is happening because when the custom element will be mounted a VNode will be created that will be linked to the app via `_ceVNode` (see https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/06310e82f5bed62d1b9733dcb18cd8d6edc988de/packages/runtime-dom/src/apiCustomElement.ts#L423). But when a HMR occurs a new VNode will be created (see https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/06310e82f5bed62d1b9733dcb18cd8d6edc988de/packages/runtime-dom/src/apiCustomElement.ts#L523) which isn't linked to the app anymore and doesn't have its context.  A possible solution would be to link the newly created VNode with the app or to not create a new VNode on every HMR. Here is a snippet of a custom definition of `defineCustomElement` which I did which worked for me: ```ts const vnode = createVNode(AppComponent, this._props); // @ts-expect-error: Isn't typed vnode.ce = (instance: ComponentInternalInstance) => {     // @ts-expect-error: Isn't typed     instance.ceReload = (newStyles: string[] | undefined) => {         styleElements.forEach((styleElement) => {             this._shadowRoot?.removeChild(styleElement);         });         styleElements =             newStyles?.map((style) => {                 const styleElement = document.createElement("style");                 styleElement.textContent = style;                 this._shadowRoot?.appendChild(styleElement);                 return styleElement;             }) ?? []

title: Synchronous watchers can fail to fire
body: ### Vue version  3.5.12  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://play.vuejs.org/#  ### Steps to reproduce  Click the "test" button. The value stays false because the watcher runs. Click the "test" button again and the value changes to true because the watcher does not run.  ### What is expected?  The watcher should run every time the value changes.  ### What is actually happening?  The watcher seems to remember the value as being "true" when the value is set to "false" within its watch callback.  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  Finally upgrading to Vue 3 and this behavior change caused a bug. In our usage, the watch callback is an edge trigger only when the value switches from true to false in some circumstances, so the watch function being called within itself was expected and handled correctly. I'm guessing this is some known trade-off for a performance optimization but wanted to call it out just in case.  The [docs](https://vuejs.org/guide/essentials/watchers.html#sync-watchers) contain this warning:  > Sync watchers do not have batching and triggers every time a reactive mutation is detected. It's ok to use them to watch simple boolean values, but avoid using them on data sources that might be synchronously mutated many times, e.g. arrays.  But that doesn't mention anything about cases where the watcher could fail to fire on a valid change.

Setup element with a class and put it to teleport (teleport target should be outside current component tree, but inside shadow tree) 3. Set some css properties of the class to ```v-bind``` values in SFC of component containing teleport  In the linked example I set an element with class ```v-bind-fail``` to have red background using v-bind. But it is white.  ### What is expected?  ```v-bind``` styles are applied to teleported dom element.  ### What is actually happening?  ```v-bind``` styles are not applied to teleported dom element.  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  ```v-bind``` is implemented using ```var(--some-hash) ``` custom properties. Values for those provided by inline style attributes. When some part of a component is inside teleport tag those style attributes duplicated there. At least normally so. When teleport target is inside shadow dom styles aren't duplicated.   From my perspective v-bind implementation expects teleport to be used with selectors only, but it can be used with ```HTMLElement``` variable which can point to shadow tree element. title: Prop type inference for `typeof Symbol()` is incorrect and breaks Vue runtime checks
body: ### Vue version  3.5.12  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://play.vuejs.org/#  ### Steps to reproduce  1. Export a symbol in a typescript file `a.ts` ```ts // a.ts export const MySmbol = Symbol(); ``` 2. In a Vue file `Comp.vue` with `<script setup lang="ts">` import and use the symbol as prop type and default: 3. Update the prop type to be a union of the symbol type and some other inferable type, e.g., `boolean`. 4. Use the symbol as default value: ```vue // Comp.vue <script setup lang="ts"> import { MySmbol } from "./a";  withDefaults(defineProps<{   value?: typeof MySmbol | boolean; }>(), { value: MySymbol }); </script>  <template>   renders </template> ``` **==> Check the JS output, and you can see that only the `boolean` type of the type union is inferred:** ```  props: {     value: { type: [Boolean], default: MySymbol }   }, ``` 5. Switch to `Prod` mode 6. Create a second component, import and use the first component: ```vue // App.vue <script setup> import Comp from "./Comp.vue"; </script>  <template>   <Comp /> </template> ``` 7. Switch to `DEV` mode. **==> Now you will get the error: `can't convert symbol to string`**  **Why is the DEV mode switching relevant?** We are building a component library and there we use symbols as explicit defaults for special default behaviors. This issue was only encountered when a user tried to develop (in dev mode) using the compiled lib (in prod mode).  See also: https://github.com/SchwarzIT/onyx/issues/1

'' : null"   ></vue-custom-element> ``` updates the non-hyphenated attribute correctly, but the hyphenated attribute is always set to `foo-bar=""` in the HTML document, which is interpreted as `true`.  ```vue <vue-custom-element   :foo="booleanValue"   :foo-bar="booleanValue" ></vue-custom-element> ``` sets both attributes correctly on vue custom-elements, but ```vue <native-custom-element   :foo="booleanValue"   :foo-bar="booleanValue" ></native-custom-element> ``` sets both attributes to either `"true"` or `"false"` in the HTML document, which is always interpreted as `true` by the native custom-element because the attribute is present. This can cause hydration errors or potentially disrupt future functionality. This warning is factually incorrect. The [relevant spec](https://html.spec.whatwg.org/#the-table-element) says that a `

title: Recursive sync watcher stops tracking computed
body: ### Vue version  3.5.6  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://play.vuejs.org/#  ### Steps to reproduce  Just click the button.  ### What is expected?  The rendered values should be `1`.  ### What is actually happening?  The rendered values are `6`.  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  This changed in 3.5.6. In 3.5.5 and earlier it renders `1`, as expected.  I found this while investigating #11956. I still don't know what causes the memory leak, but after staring at #11944 for a bit I noticed the potential problem I've reported here.  This is what I believe is happening...  When a `computed` is notified, the `NOTIFIED` flag gets set for both `ComputedRefImpl` and its `dep`. These are queued in a batch. When `endBatch()` is called it handles the `dep` first, clearing the `NOTIFIED` flag from the `dep` and then calling `trigger()`. But the `NOTIFIED` flag is still set for the `ComputedRefImpl`, so it can't be notified while `trigger()` is running.  I used `watch` with `flush: 'sync'` in the reproduction, as that was the most direct way to take advantage of the mismatched flags. I'm not sure whether there's a more 'normal' way to hit this timing issue.

body: ### Vue version  3.5.4  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://play.vuejs.org/#  ### Steps to reproduce  1. Create a div with class `foo` and an inner div with class `bar`. 2. title: vue 3.5 propsDestructure 破坏了现有的响应式原则
body: ### Vue version  3.5.3  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://blog.vuejs.org/posts/vue-3-5#reactive-props-destructure  ### Steps to reproduce  vue3 围绕着两种响应式数据结构，分别是 ref 和 reactive，但 propsDestructure 出现却破坏了这一点，我将从一下几个方面阐述我的观点以及提出个人的建议：  1. 破坏了 vue3 现有的响应式原则 ```ts const { count = 0, ...rest } = defineProps<{   count?: number   message?: string   disabled?: boolean }>() ``` 上述代码中，count 看上去只是一个类型为数字的变量(它并不是 ref 和 reactive 中的一种)，但它因为最终会被编译成 props.count 而具备响应式。单从代码的角度看上去似乎是增加了一种响应式数据结构，但又无法直接分辨这一数据结构与普通数据结构的差别。   2. 依赖关系变复杂，失去可读性和增加了维护成本 ``` // 虽然在 vue2.x 中的我们需求提前确定依赖关系，但也增加了代码的可读性和减少了维护成本 // 过去 const computedRef = computed(() => {   // 清晰明了的依赖关系   const { count, message, disabled } = props   // ... })  // 现在 const computedRef = computed(() => {    //  count, message, disabled 与其他普通的变量混杂在一起，依赖关系变得复杂   // ... })  // 这一问题同样也出现在 watchEffect 中， 这一行为意味着我们更难直接从繁杂的代码中一一理清依赖关系 // ref 能一定程度解决这一点是因为我们可以通过查看它的类型知道它是否是一个响应式数据 ``` **vue 的维护者不应该一味的追求代码的书写方便而丢失可读性，书写的人只为了一时爽，但后期维护者以及维护的成本该怎么办**   3. [梦回 $() 宏](https://cn.vuejs.org/guide/extras/reactivity-transform#destructuring-with)  在 vue3.4 中废弃了 $() 来创建响应式变量，而如今它似乎又出现在 defineProps() 中  [$()](https://github.com/vuejs/rfcs/discussions/369#discussioncomment-5059028) 的出现确实给开发者带来便利，但它被废弃的其中一个原因就是解构出来的变量与普通变量无法进行很好的区分，导致在使用时很难去理清整个依赖链。    ### What is expected?  为解决以上问题，有几点建议：  1. 对于开发者而言，在 vue3 中解构响应式数据而丢失响应是一个根本性问题，它不应该只针对于 props。而是针对所有响应式数据。 ```ts const { count = 0, ...rest } = defineProps() const {} = useAttrs() ```  2.  丢失响应是关键，应该利用现有的两种响应式数据结构 ref 和 reactive 来实现 ```ts const { count = 0, ...rest } = defineProps<{   count?: number   message?: string   disabled?: boolean }>() ``` 上述代码中，count 应该是一个 ref 类型，rest 应该是一个 reactive 对象  **toRefs 最大的问题在剩余属性不是一个  reactive 对象而是一个由 ref 属性组合而成的普通对象, 因为缺乏可以修改 destructure trap ，所以无法从根本上解决此问题。因此，toRefs 很少被使用（事实上可以移除该 api）** ```ts // rest 不是一个 reactive object 而是一个 {[key: string]: Ref<any>} const { count, ...rest } = toRefs(props) ```  3. 实现一个类似 $() 的宏 ```ts const { id, class, style, ...rest} = $(useAt

title: Vue 2 migration build WATCH_ARRAY triggers on deep value modification
body: ### Vue version  3.4.38 (compat)  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://stackblitz.com/edit/vitejs-vite-cpcesj?file=src%2FApp.vue  ### Steps to reproduce  1. Create a new project with the Vue 2 migration build 2. Create an array with object elements (e.g. `[{foo: 0}, {foo: 1}]`) and add a watch on it 3. Replace the array (`arr = [...arr]`) 4. Mutate the array (`arr.push({foo: 2})`) 5. Modify the contents of one of the elements (`arr[0].foo++`)  ### What is expected?  The watch should be triggered when the array is replaced or mutated, but should not be triggered when the contents of the array elements are modified ([Vue 2 repro](https://vue2-sfc-playground.vercel.app/#))  ### What is actually happening?  The watch is triggered in all three cases, on replacement, mutation, and deep modification  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  The compat is implemented [here in createWatcher](https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/fe2ab1b/packages/runtime-core/src/componentOptions.ts#L863-L881), and it's implemented by doing a deep traversal of array values. The Vue 2 behavior can be reproduced by instead calling `array.slice(0, 0)` there, which creates a reactive dependency on `TrackOpTypes.ITERATE`. The internal [shallowReadArray](https://github.com/vuejs/core/blob/fe2ab1b/packages/runtime-core/src/componentOptions.ts#L878) function may also be more appropriate to call in internal code.

body: ### Vue version  https://github.com/vuejs/core/commit/52cdb0f991dc154ae32a2900874d5dbc4e078565  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://play.vuejs.org/#  ### Steps to reproduce  1. (On Chrome devtools) Trigger GC and take initial heap snapshot. 2. Click "Toggle" button twice (Text disappears and appears again) 3. (On Chrome devtools) Trigger GC again and take second heap snapshot. 4. Compare 3. and 1.  ### What is expected?  There is no detached DOM node.  ### What is actually happening?  There are detached DOM nodes that disappeared on step 2. It is retained by the old vnode in the scope of `<Transition>` render function via `postClone` callback of `resolveTransitionHooks`.  ![スクリーンショット 2024-09-03 9 50 51](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/e3298146-0f5f-4a55-bdc6-5807181215da)   ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  The detached nodes will be released when a next leave transition. So memory usage does not increase forever. But this behavior always keep some detached nodes which makes harder to find actual memory leak. In addition, since it keeps unused DOM tree in memory, it can be a problem under an environment where memory usage is restricted like mobile app's WebView.

body: ### Vue version  3.4.25  ### Link to minimal reproduction  https://github.com/orgs/vuejs/discussions/11752  ### Steps to reproduce  抱歉，用 issue 来提 new feature request  在现有的语法种，我们可以通过 toRefs 去解构 reactive 对象： ```ts const reactiveObj = reactive({ name: 'name',  age:  10,  sex: 0}} const { name, age,  ...restObj } = toRefs(reactiveObj ) ``` name  和 age 被解构，并且是 ref 类型，这表现的得很好，且符合预期。 关键在于 restObj，它并非是一个 reactive 类型，而是由多个 ref 构成的普通对象 很可惜，js 缺乏 ‘能重写解构细节’ 的内置 symbol 。  但借助编译器，我们可以实现这一点： ```ts const reactiveObj = reactive({ name: 'name',  age:  10,  sex: 0}} const { name, age,  ...restObj } = defineDestruct(reactiveObj ） const attrs = useAttrs() const { a , b, c } = defineDestruct(attrs) // 解构 attrs ``` 同样的 ：name 和 age 被解构成一个 ref 类型(这是需要的，如果将其解构成一个基础数据类型，并通过标记的方法在起他地方使用时转为 ref ，会增加开发者的心智负担) **这里最重要的是 restObj  会被转化一个 reactive 对象， 类似于 reactive({ sex: 0 })**   当然，我们可以重写 defineProps 来实现对 props 的解构 ```ts const { name, age,  ...restObj } = defineProps(reactiveObj ） ``` restObj  同样是一个 reactive 对象，但 defineProps 太过于局限，比如：我要解构 attrs 等其他 reactive 对象时将无从下手，又会陷入解构后无法保持响应式的苦恼  ### What is expected?  no response  ### What is actually happening?  no response  ### System Info  _No response_  ### Any additional comments?  _No response_

title: `--set key={}` produces a list with one empty string instead of an empty list
body: ### What happened?  `--set key={}` sets `key` to a list with one empty string (`[""]`) instead of an empty list.  - Templates see a non-empty list: `len` is 1, `if` and `with` are true, and `toYaml` renders `- ""`. - `--set-string key={}` gives the same result. - `--set-file key={}` fails, because it tries to read a file with an empty name.  ### What did you expect to happen?  An empty list: the same value that `key: []` gives in a values file, and that `--set-json key=[]` gives today.  Why a list:  - In `--set`, braces are the list syntax. The docs ([The Format and Limitations of `--set`](https://helm.sh/docs/intro/using_helm/#the-format-and-limitations-of---set)) say "Lists can be expressed by enclosing values in `{` and `}`". So `{a,b}` is `[a, b]`, `{a}` is `[a]`, and `{}` is the list with no items. - The same docs section promises an empty array for `--set name=[]`. But square brackets are not list syntax in a `--set` value, and `name=[]` gives the string `"[]"`. - `[""]` is not useful to anyone: it is a non-empty list whose only item is an empty string.  Why this is a bug and not a behavior change:  - The syntax stays the same: braces still mean a list. - A `--set` list still replaces the chart value as a whole, as it does today. Only the extra empty item goes away. - Every non-empty list parses exactly as before, including `{a}`, `{a,b}` and `{a,}`. - The current output of `--set key={}` was already called "not correct" in a review on #31331, and #31061 was labeled `bug`.  That review also mentioned an empty map. An empty list keeps a single meaning for braces in `--set`. An empty map would also be merged with a map default from the chart, instead of replacing it. That would change what `--set key={}` does today on such keys.  Cause: `valList` in `pkg/strvals/parser.go` appends the last item when it reaches `}`, even when nothing was read, so `{}` yields one empty item.  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  `foo/Chart.yaml`:

title: Post delete hook health checks
body: ### What would you like to be added?  The health checking for resources has been reworked to use kstatus, which is great as it adds wider support for resources. Currently health checking is partially applied to post delete hooks, meaning that it only runs for pods and jobs.  I would like to expand the health checking in hooks to support more kinds of resources.  ### Why is this needed?  I think my use case may be a bit unique, but I do not think I am the only one who would need this. My project Spegel creates a daemonset and each pod changes the hosts Containerd mirror configuration, so that it works with Spegel. The old configuration is persisted, so that during uninstall I can revert it back. For this to be possible I need to run a pod on every node during the post uninstall hook. Once its done the daemonset should be removed.  https://github.com/spegel-org/spegel/blob/main/charts/spegel/templates/post-delete-hook.yaml  On its own this does not currently work, as Helm considers the daemonset healthy right after apply, causing it to be deleted. Instead of waiting for all pods to be healthy. To solve this currently I have an additional pod which implements the waiting logic that kstatus would otherwise implement. Waiting for all daemonset pods are ready before reporting a healthy state.  I think that there are more projects out there that would want to run a daemonset as part of a uninstall so that they can also revert configuration. The current complexity is probably what is stopping them from implementing it.

title: Add machine-readable output to helm lint
body: ### What would you like to be added?  What would you like to be added?  It would be useful for helm lint to support machine-readable output.  For example:  ```bash helm lint ./chart --output json ```  The default output could stay exactly as it is today, with structured output only enabled when requested.  The JSON could expose the information Helm already has for each lint finding, such as the severity, message, chart, and related file or path when available.  Ideally, using structured output wouldn't change the existing exit-code behavior of helm lint.  ### Why is this needed?  helm lint is commonly used as part of CI, but its output is mainly designed for people reading it in a terminal.  If a CI pipeline wants to turn lint findings into annotations, summaries, or another report format, it currently has to parse the human-readable console output.  That works, but it ties automation to formatting that wasn't really intended to be an API and may change over time.  Having a structured format would make it much easier to integrate helm lint with CI systems and other tooling, while keeping the current experience unchanged for normal CLI use.

title: Simplify or fix the http.DefaultTransport clone fallback in registry NewTransport
body: Split out of #31386, where @ogulcanaydogan noted this as "the Go 1.20-era cloner fallback in `pkg/registry/transport.go`". It is unrelated to the oras-go workarounds that issue tracked, so filing it separately.  `NewTransport` in `pkg/registry/transport.go`:  ```go func NewTransport(debug bool) *retry.Transport { 	// clone http.DefaultTransport so mutations (e.g. TLS config) are not 	// reflected globally 	transport := http.DefaultTransport 	if t, ok := transport.(*http.Transport); ok { 		transport = t.Clone() 	} 	... } ```  The type assertion dates from when `(*http.Transport).Clone` was newer and the guard was worth having. The standard library documents `http.DefaultTransport` as a `*http.Transport`, so in practice the assertion always succeeds and the fallback branch never runs — we now require Go 1.26 (#32078), so there is no supported toolchain where this differs.  Worth being precise about what the fallback actually guards, though: `http.DefaultTransport` is a package-level variable of interface type, so a caller (or an imported package) *can* reassign it to some other `RoundTripper`. If that happened, today's code silently falls through and we would wrap and hand out the shared global without cloning it — which is exactly the aliasing the comment says we are trying to avoid. So the branch is not strictly dead; it is a silent-and-wrong path rather than an impossible one.  Two reasonable directions:  1. Drop the assertion and clone `http.DefaultTransport.(*http.Transport)` directly, accepting a panic if someone has replaced it. Simplest, and fails loudly instead of silently sharing state. 2. Keep a guard but make the fallback meaningful — construct a fresh `&http.Transport{}` (or log) rather than aliasing the global.  Either is a small change; mostly this needs a decision on which behavior we want. Flagging it because the current shape reads as dead code but is not quite.

title: Remove redundant ServerAddressFromHostname call in registry Login
body: `pkg/registry/client.go` `(*Client).Login()` normalizes the credentials-store key twice:  ```go key := credentials.ServerAddressFromRegistry(host) key = credentials.ServerAddressFromHostname(key) ```  The second line was added in 6ab7aa361 ("fix: legacy docker support broken for login") to work around oras-go v2.6.0, where `ServerAddressFromRegistry("registry-1.docker.io")` returned the host unchanged instead of the canonical `https://index.docker.io/v1/`.  That was fixed upstream in oras-project/oras-go#966, released in oras-go v2.6.1:  ```go func ServerAddressFromRegistry(registry string) string { 	if registry == "docker.io" || registry == "registry-1.docker.io" { 		return "https://index.docker.io/v1/" 	} 	return registry } ```  Helm is already on oras-go v2.6.2, so `ServerAddressFromHostname` is now a no-op on the output of `ServerAddressFromRegistry` and the line can be deleted. Both Docker Hub host spellings should keep resolving to `https://index.docker.io/v1/`; the existing login tests cover this.  Scope: delete one line (plus the now-unneeded import, if nothing else in the file uses it). No `go.mod` change is needed.  Split out of #31386, which also covered the oras-go empty-credentials-file bug (oras-project/oras-go#959) — that one was fixed upstream before it needed a workaround in this tree, so this is all that is left.

title: Potential nil pointer dereference in ClientConfig
body: Hi, I analyzed the source code using Svace and found an interesting bug.  Problem  In ClientConfig(), the cert variable is initially nil and is assigned a value only when CertFile or KeyFile is provided. https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/144ca65f8501953fa8b41cd1d37c7223051c85b7/internal/tlsutil/cfg.go#L42  If no client certificate is configured, cert remains nil. However, the code later unconditionally dereferences it:  cfg = &tls.Config{     InsecureSkipVerify: opts.InsecureSkipVerify,     Certificates:       []tls.Certificate{*cert},     RootCAs:            pool, }  This dereferences a nil pointer and may result in a panic.  https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/144ca65f8501953fa8b41cd1d37c7223051c85b7/internal/tlsutil/cfg.go#L56  At the same time, operating without a client certificate is a valid TLS client configuration. A client certificate is only required when mutual TLS (mTLS) authentication is used.  Fix  The cert pointer should only be dereferenced when it is non-nil. The certificate can be added to cfg.Certificates conditionally:  cfg = &tls.Config{     InsecureSkipVerify: opts.InsecureSkipVerify,     RootCAs:            pool, }  if cert != nil {     cfg.Certificates = []tls.Certificate{*cert} }  return cfg, nil  This allows the TLS client to operate correctly without a client certificate while still using the certificate when one is configured.

Plugins installed via http (e.g. `https://github.com/jkroepke/helm-secrets/releases/download/v4.7.5/secrets-4.7.5.tgz`) or from a local path / archive still end up in the default plugins directory, aka. data   path + "plugins" (`~/.local/share/helm/plugins` on linux).  The culprit is `Path()` in `internal/plugin/installer/http_installer.go` and `local_installer.go`, which still use `helmpath.DataPath("plugins", ...)` instead of `cli.EnvSettings.PluginsDirectory` like the oci installer does.  Side note, probably deserving its own treatment : the http, local and oci installers also save the tarball (and `.prov`) copy used for verification under `helmpath.DataPath("plugins", ...)`, regardless of `HELM_PLUGINS`.  Fix proposal in #31756.  ### What did you expect to happen?  All installers honor `HELM_PLUGINS`, whatever the plugin source :)  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  ```console                                                                                                                                                                     $ export HELM_PLUGINS=/tmp/helm-plugins                                                                                                                                        $ helm plugin install https://github.com/databus23/helm-diff                                                                                                                   $ helm plugin install https://github.com/jkroepke/helm-secrets/releases/download/v4.7.5/secrets-4.7.5.tgz                                                                      $ ls $HELM_PLUGINS

title: `helm create` scaffold renders invalid label values: `helm.sh/chart` can end in `.`/`_` after `trunc 63`, and `app.kubernetes.io/version` is not sanitised at all
body: ### What happened?  The `_helpers.tpl` generated by `helm create` builds the `helm.sh/chart` label as  ``` {{- define "<CHARTNAME>.chart" -}} {{- printf "%s-%s" .Chart.Name .Chart.Version | replace "+" "_" | trunc 63 | trimSuffix "-" }} {{- end }} ```  ([`pkg/chart/v2/util/create.go#L592`](https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/fa11636b01686f16700718a03de9334bbd298500/pkg/chart/v2/util/create.go#L592) on `main`; the same text is at `pkg/chartutil/create.go:592` on `dev-v3`).  `trimSuffix "-"` only protects against a trailing dash. Kubernetes label values must match `(([A-Za-z0-9][-A-Za-z0-9_.]*)?[A-Za-z0-9])?`, so they must also not end in `.` or `_`. A valid SemVer prerelease version (`1.0.0-<branch>.<sha>` is a common CI scheme) whose 63-character cut lands on a `.`, or on the `_` that `replace "+" "_"` produces from build metadata, yields a label value the API server rejects. Every resource in the release fails with:  ``` metadata.labels: Invalid value: "demo-1.0.0-abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzabcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxy.": a valid label must be an empty string or consist of alphanumeric characters, '-', '_' or '.', and must start and end with an alphanumeric character (...) ```  Because it only triggers for particular name/version length combinations, it is hard to diagnose, and the helper is copied verbatim into a very large number of charts.  The same `labels` block also emits  ``` {{- if .Chart.AppVersion }} app.kubernetes.io/version: {{ .Chart.AppVersion | quote }} {{- end }} ```  ([`create.go#L601-L602`](https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/fa11636b01686f16700718a03de9334bbd298500/pkg/chart/v2/util/create.go#L601-L602)) with no `replace "+"`, no `trunc 63` and no trimming, so any `appVersion` longer than 63 characters or containing `+` build metadata is an invalid label value too. This half was reported before in #8975 (maintainer response: "Suggestions are welcome"), which was then closed by the stale bot without a change; the scaffold is unchanged today.  `helm lint`

title: Chart URL completion incorrectly falls back to file completion
body: ### What happened?  When completing chart arguments for commands such as `helm install`, `helm show`, and `helm upgrade`, entering a complete chart URL does not disable file completion as intended.  The `compListCharts` helper stores URL completion candidates together with their descriptions:  ```go []string{     "oci://\tChart OCI prefix",     "https://\tChart URL prefix",     "http://\tChart URL prefix",     "file://\tChart local URL prefix", } ```  It then uses those full strings for prefix matching. For example, the following comparison is performed:  ```go strings.HasPrefix(     "oci://registry.example/chart",     "oci://\tChart OCI prefix", ) ```  This returns false, so cobra.ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp and cobra.ShellCompDirectiveNoSpace are not set after the user has entered a chart URL prefix.    ### What did you expect to happen?     ```markdown Once the user has entered a chart URL prefix such as `oci://`, `https://`, `http://`, or `file://`, file completion should be disabled and the completion should not append a space. ```     ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?     1. Run completion for a command that accepts a chart reference:  ```console helm __complete install oci://registry.example/chart ```  2. Or invoke the completion helper with:  ```go compListCharts("oci://registry.example/chart", true) compListCharts("https://example.com/chart.tgz", true) ```  3. Observe that the returned directive does not include:  ```text cobra.ShellCompDirectiveNoFileComp cobra.ShellCompDirectiveNoSpace ```  The same behavior affects `https://`, `http://`, and `file://` chart URLs.    ### Helm version  <details>  ```console $ helm version `main` branch at the current repository revision. ``` </details>   ### Kubernetes version  <details>  ```console $ kubectl version Not applicable. This issue occurs during shell completion before any Kubernetes interaction. ```  </details>

title: Helm V4 hangs infinetely on "waiting for resource" when kind=Rollout expectedStatus=Current actualStatus=Unknown
body: ### What happened?  When a chart contains an Argo `Rollout` custom resource (or other CRD), running `helm install --wait` (or an upgrade with `--wait`) with Helm v4 hangs: Helm logs  ``` waiting for resource ... kind=Rollout expectedStatus=Current actualStatus=Unknown ```  and keeps polling until the `--timeout` is reached, even though the Rollout is healthy and fully rolled out. This affects Helm v4 since `v4.0.0` (observed on `v4.2.4`).  ### What did you expect to happen? title: feat(upgrade): add --force-pending flag to recover stuck releases
body: ### What would you like to be added?  Add a `--force-pending` flag to `helm upgrade` that allows operators to explicitly recover from releases stuck in a `pending-*` state (`pending-upgrade`, `pending-install`, `pending-rollback`).  When `--force-pending` is passed: 1. It prints a clear safety warning banner to `stderr` highlighting the concurrency/split-brain risks if another process is active. 2. It marks the previous stuck release revision as `failed` in release storage (preserving the previous status in the description for `helm history`). 3. It proceeds with the requested upgrade without requiring manual Kubernetes Secret manipulation or manual rollbacks.  ### Why is this needed?  When a Helm deployment process is interrupted or terminated abruptly (e.g. `SIGKILL`, CI runner crash, double `SIGINT`, or network drop during execution), the release object remains in `pending-upgrade` or `pending-install` in storage.  Subsequent upgrade attempts fail immediately with: ``` Error: UPGRADE FAILED: another operation (install/upgrade/rollback) is in progress ```  Currently, recovering from this requires manual operator intervention (finding and deleting the specific release Secret `sh.helm.release.v1.<release>.v<revision>` or executing `helm rollback`), which breaks automated CI/CD pipelines and disrupts automated deployments. A dedicated disaster-recovery flag provides an explicit, audit-logged escape hatch.

body: ### What happened?  `registry.Client.Tags` returns *normalized* semver strings rather than the tag strings as they exist in the registry. title: provenance: multi-block armored keyrings silently drop keys depending on block alignment
body: Follow-up to #32281, which added support for ASCII-armored keyrings made of several concatenated blocks (`cat a.asc b.asc > keyring.asc`). This applies once that PR is merged.  ### What happens  `loadArmoredKeyRing` (pkg/provenance/sign.go:395) loops over one `*bytes.Reader`:  ```go r := bytes.NewReader(data) for { 	block, err := armor.Decode(r) 	... } ```  Each `armor.Decode` call wraps the reader in a fresh `bufio.NewReaderSize(in, 100)` and reads ahead. Whatever is sitting in that 100-byte buffer when the block ends is discarded along with the buffer, so the next `Decode` can start *past* the following `-----BEGIN` line. It then finds no armor header, returns `io.EOF`, and the loop `break`s — with **no error** and a keyring that is silently missing keys.  go-crypto documents this explicitly:  > Decode reads a PGP armored block from the given Reader. [...] The given Reader is not usable after calling this function: an arbitrary amount of data may have been read past the end of the block.  ### When it triggers  How far the decoder over-reads is a function of the length of the *previous* block's last base64 line, which armor wraps at 64 chars — so it is effectively a per-key constant (`total_base64_len % 64`).  Generating Ed25519 keys with varying UID lengths and concatenating each one with the committed `testdata/helm-test-key.asc`:  ``` last base64 line = 32, 36, 40, 44, 48, 52, 56  ->  1 entity loaded, want 2, err == nil last base64 line = 60 (and most other lengths) ->  2 entities, OK ```  Roughly one key in nine drops the block that follows it.  `testdata/helm-mixed-keyring.asc` ends its first block on a 60-char line, where the over-read stops 2 bytes short of the next `-----BEGIN`. title: Add Helm's design philosophy to AGENTS.md for agent-assisted review
body: ## Summary Capture Helm's design philosophy in this repo and apply it during PR review. Stage 1 is one PR here. Once the authoritative source moves into the HIPs (helm/community#446), a bot keeps this repo's copy in sync.  ## Stage 1: AGENTS.md philosophy (one PR) Working from a sourced distillation of Helm's design philosophy (developer calls, maintainer PR comments, blogs, talks): - [ ] Add the philosophy to `AGENTS.md`, ordered by priority: engagement and tone first (guide, do not dictate; explain the why; offer the path that fits), then does-this-belong and behavior gates (package-manager scope and plugin boundary, backward compatibility per HIP-0004, the chart contract, charts v2-vs-v3 gating, "cross-cutting change needs a HIP"), then design principles, then context. Write it as prompts to raise for a human reviewer, not verdicts. - [ ] Confirm Copilot code review picks it up on a test PR.  `AGENTS.md`, not `.github/copilot-instructions.md`: code review reads `AGENTS.md`, this repo already consolidated its Copilot instructions there, and `AGENTS.md` is cross-tool (Claude Code and Cursor read it too). It can exceed Copilot's ~1,000-line attention window without truncation, so priority ordering keeps the review-critical principles in range while other agents read all of it.  ## Stage 3: receive the HIP-sourced sync - [ ] Accept the bot PRs that regenerate the `AGENTS.md` philosophy section from the HIPs, and retire the hand-built Stage-1 content.  ## Notes - A separate `.agents/skills/helm-philosophy/` skill was considered and dropped: with the full guide in `AGENTS.md` (which Copilot reads and Claude Code / Cursor auto-load), a skill would only duplicate always-loaded content. - Authority and the sync bot: helm/community#446.

title: helm plugin install fails when the tag resolves to an OCI Image Index
body: ### What happened?  A plugin published inside an OCI Image Index cannot be installed. The pull rejects the index root before it looks at anything inside it:  ```console $ helm plugin install oci://localhost:5099/plugins/demo:idx --plain-http --verify=false WARNING: Skipping plugin signature verification Error: failed to pull plugin from oci://localhost:5099/plugins/demo:idx: unable to retrieve manifest: sha256:c309a2f11ccd6a63d2832054ff520bfd2aa0273cd2d5a660ceebf72ad968990a: application/vnd.oci.image.index.v1+json: not found ```  Charts do not have this problem. #31776 added `ocispec.MediaTypeImageIndex` to the media types the chart pull accepts and closed #31775. The plugin pull carries its own list in `pkg/registry/plugin.go`, that list has no index entry, and so the same tag shape that a chart pulls from fails for a plugin.  The message is misleading on top of that. title: helm pull returns an arbitrary chart when the reference resolves to an OCI Image Index
body: ### What happened?  `helm pull` returns an arbitrary chart when the reference resolves to an OCI Image Index that holds more than one chart. The file lands under the name taken from the reference, and what is inside it is whichever chart won the race.  The pull copies the whole index graph and collects descriptors in `PreCopy` callbacks, then picks the config, chart and prov descriptors with a switch that keeps the last match of each kind. The graph walk is concurrent, so the order in that slice is goroutine arrival order, not index order. Each kind is picked on its own, so the config and the chart layer can come from different manifests. Nothing checks the two against each other: metadata comes from the config blob, bytes come from the layer, and the file name comes from the reference.  ### What did you expect to happen? title: Helm-internal redirection from one repository to another
body: ### What would you like to be added?  I would like to see a mechanism in helm http repositories, where `index.yaml` can act as a tombstone, pointing to a different repository url.  ### Why is this needed?  One of the easiest ways to get started publishing helm charts is using GitHub pages to host the repository. However, if one does this under their own personal name, not a GitHub organization, handing control over to maintainers or accepting co-maintainership becomes quite hard.  The main challenge I face, is that moving a repository like https://github.com/ccremer/kubernetes-zfs-provisioner into an organisation doesn't work, since GItHub only creates redirects for the repo and git access, but not GitHub pages. However, GitHub leaves the last-deployed pages up indefinitely, even if the repo is deleted. So if one would like to move the repo into an organisation, a user ideally would amend `index.yaml` with an option to point the a new repo URL, wait for GitHub pages to deploy and then move the repo to the org. And if one would have used their own webserver one would not be in this position.

body: ### What happened?  Helm v4 appears to silently ignore a valid values document when its final logical line does not end with a newline, and has a byte length that is an exact multiple of 4096.  This is reproducible with compact, single-line JSON files passed through -f/--values.  In Helm v4.x, a values file is read and passed to loader.LoadValues, and loader.LoadValues constructs a Kubernetes YAMLReader over Go's default buffered reader:  pkg/chart/v2/loader/load.go: ```go func LoadValues(data io.Reader) (map[string]any, error) {     values := map[string]any{}     reader := utilyaml.NewYAMLReader(bufio.NewReader(data))      for {         currentMap := map[string]any{}         raw, err := reader.Read()         if err != nil {             if errors.Is(err, io.EOF) {                 break             }             return nil, fmt.Errorf("error reading yaml document: %w", err)         }          if err := yaml.Unmarshal(raw, &currentMap); err != nil {             return nil, fmt.Errorf("cannot unmarshal yaml document: %w", err)         }          values = MergeMaps(values, currentMap)     }      return values, nil } ```  Go's bufio.NewReader uses a default buffer size of 4096 bytes.  The underlying issue appears to be in the interaction between LineReader.Read() and YAMLReader.Read() in Kubernetes apimachinery: kubernetes/apimachinery v0.36.0 pkg/util/yaml/decoder.go:  ```go func NewYAMLReader(r *bufio.Reader) *YAMLReader {     return &YAMLReader{         reader: &LineReader{reader: r},     } } ```  ```go  func (r *LineReader) Read() ([]byte, error) {     var (         isPrefix bool = true         err      error         line     []byte         buffer   bytes.Buffer     )      for isPrefix && err == nil {         line, isPrefix, err = r.reader.ReadLine()         buffer.Write(line)     }      buffer.WriteByte('\n')     return buffer.Bytes(), err } ```  LineReader.Read() accumulates fragments returned by bufio.Reader.ReadLine() and may return the completed final line toget

title: values keys y/yes/on/n/no/off are parsed as booleans and become "true"/"false"
body: ### What happened?  Values are parsed with `sigs.k8s.io/yaml`, which follows YAML 1.1. In that dialect the plain scalars `y`, `Y`, `yes`, `no`, `n`, `on`, `off` (plus `True`/`False`) are booleans. Used as mapping keys they become `true` or `false`, and three things follow from that.  **A template cannot read the chart's own default.** With `values.yaml` containing `nested: {x: 1, y: 2}`:  ``` {{ .Values.probe.nested.x }}  ->  "1" {{ .Values.probe.nested.y }}  ->  "" ```  **Values are dropped silently.** Eight declared keys `y, n, on, off, yes, no, true, x` arrive as three -- `true`, `false`, `x`. Five values are gone, last one wins, nothing is reported.  **`--set` does not override, it adds a second key.** `--set` is handled by strvals and never reaches a YAML parser, so the key stays a string there. Chart has `nested.y: 2`, user runs `--set probe.nested.y=99`:  ```yaml nested:   "true": 2      # the original, not overridden   "y": 99        # the override, sitting next to it   x: 1 ```  The same override through `-f` works correctly, and an ordinary key like `x` overrides correctly. The two input paths disagree with each other:  | input path | resulting keys | |---|---| | `values.yaml` / `-f` | `true`, `false`, `x` | | `--set` | `y`, `n`, `on`, `off`, `yes`, `no`, `x` |  ### What did you expect to happen?  Either both input paths produce the same key, or the chart author is told that the key they wrote is not the key they get. At the moment the data is lost quietly.  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  A Grafana dashboard pasted into values is the everyday way to hit this, since `gridPos` carries `x` and `y`:  ```console $ helm create demo && rm demo/templates/*.yaml $ cat > demo/values.yaml <<'EOF' gridPos:   h: 8   w: 12   x: 0   y: 0 EOF $ cat > demo/templates/cm.yaml <<'EOF' apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:   name: demo data:   dashboard: | {{ toYaml .Values.gridPos | indent 4 }} EOF $ helm template t ./demo ...   dash

title: Create Tag ruleset(s)
body: Helm doesn't currently make use of Github's Tag rules feature. The ruleset should match the release tag format e.g. [v4.2.3](https://github.com/helm/helm/releases/tag/v4.2.3), and [v4.2.0-rc.1](https://github.com/helm/helm/releases/tag/v4.2.0-rc.1) (release candidate). Or perhaps simply all tags.  Issue to track discussion, and implementation once agreement reached.

title: Non-collaborator PR limit
body: Github recently released the "Limit open pull requests" feature:  https://github.blog/changelog/2026-06-17-limit-open-pull-requests-for-users-without-write-access/ https://github.com/orgs/community/discussions/198851  Which is part of the family of interaction limits: https://docs.github.com/en/communities/moderating-comments-and-conversations/limiting-interactions-in-your-repository  This issue proposes enabling the "Limit open pull requests" feature, with discussion to decided what the limit should be.  The goals of enabling/limiting open pull requests are to generally reduce the PR review backlog and to help ensure as many contributions as possible can receive maintainer attention. And specifically to:  1.  reduce/prevent "spam" PRs 2. limit "work in progress" PRs (ie. PRs requiring several rounds of review from maintainers) 3. (following on from the second) encourage contributors to focus on a small number of "high quality" PRs  For discussion purposes, the likely ranges for each of the above are respectively perhaps: 100-1000, 5-10, 1-3  To be clear, Helm does (and always will) welcome contributions from the wider community. But today, the Helm maintainers can not (don't have time to) actually review every contributed PR. An outcome of this issue should be to help ensure fairness among contributors for limited maintainer review time.  Finally, the discussion may revolve around "AI contributions", as yes, AI coding assistants do make contributing easier. And easier contributions appears to have equated to more contributions (a good thing!). However, this issue is not about creating a AI contribution policy for Helm. A separate issue should be created for that.  Note: this issue is for `helm/helm` only, but the same considerations could be applied across other repos within the `helm` org.

title: Enable/use alternative PR merge strategies
body: The current (default, and in practice, the only used) method to merge PRs for the Helm repository is Github's default "merge commits".  This issue is to discuss defaulting to other PR "merge" strategies: **Rebase and merge** / **Squash and merge**.  (These are currently enabled, but current maintainer practice is to merge commits only)  The proposal is to default to **Squash and merge**, and reserve **Rebase and merge** for special situation (if that remains desirable), and eventually disable **Merge commits** entirely.  The downsides of simply merging all commits are two fold: 1. Multiple commits per logical change 1. Non-linear commit history  The first, stems from that a PR is effectively the unit of change on Github (from a contributor perspective). The (vast) majority of PRs do not logically structure/layer their commits - with often one or more initial commits, then often several more commits to respond to PR review comments.   The result is a messy git history and difficultly tracking logical change in that history to Helm's functionality over time.  Each PR contributes several dependent (ie. each commit is not a logically useful change in itself) commits to Helm's history, based upon the mainline commit from which the PR's branch was created, appearing in the mainline git history as a merge commit.  By treating each PR as the logical change (generally)(and squashing commits), Helm's history would reflect a single commit for each change. By rebasing commit(s) before PR "merge", Helm's git history would be linear. As such, **Squash and merge** is the recommend default strategy.  This would:  1. title: Helm v4 hardcodes fieldValidation=Strict on forced operations, breaking previously valid charts
body: ### What happened?  In Helm v4, forced replacement operations (such as helm upgrade --force or helm install --replace) hard-fail with an HTTP 400 Bad Request (strict decoding error) if a chart contains minor schema discrepancies, like a misplaced annotation or undocumented vendor field.  Under the hood, pkg/kube/client.go ```go updateOptions := clientUpdateOptions{     serverSideApply: true,     fieldValidationDirective: FieldValidationDirectiveStrict, // Hardcoded } ```  When ForceReplace is requested, replaceResource() explicitly appends .WithFieldValidation("Strict") to the HTTP PUT request. Because the action package (Upgrade, Install, Rollback) provides no configuration knob to override this default, stray fields become a fatal error. This breaks backward compatibility and breaks downstream controllers like Flux (helm-controller).  ### What did you expect to happen?  I expected forced replace operations on these charts to succeed, just as they did in Helm v3.  In Helm v3, the forced replace path omitted the field validation directive entirely. Without the ?fieldValidation= query parameter, the Kubernetes API server fell back to its native lenient default (Warn), silently pruning unknown fields and returning an HTTP 200 with a 299 warning header.  At a minimum, the Helm v4 SDK needs to expose FieldValidationDirective on the action.Upgrade, action.Install, and action.Rollback structs so consumers can opt-out of the Strict default for forced operations. title: Proposal: Lightweight client-only chart rendering API for Go consumers
body: ### What would you like to be added?  Helm should provide an additive, lightweight Go API for rendering charts with `helm template` semantics without linking Kubernetes clients, action configuration, storage drivers, CLI runtime, or registry support into every consumer.  The initial API should cover the client-only rendering pipeline: chart loading, dependency processing, values/schema validation, template rendering, manifest and hook sorting, CRDs, and notes. Kubernetes-backed `lookup` support should be supplied by a separate adapter. Existing `pkg/action` and `pkg/engine` APIs should remain compatible and delegate to the extracted implementation where practical.  The package boundary is important: adding an interface inside `pkg/action` or the current `pkg/engine` package does not remove their transitive dependencies from Go binaries.  The current dependency roots include:  - `internal/version/clientgo.go` blank-importing `k8s.io/client-go/kubernetes`, which forces the full clientset into the build; - `pkg/chart/common` constructing default API versions from Kubernetes schemes at runtime; - client-only engine code sharing a package with REST, discovery, and dynamic-client lookup code; - the complete rendering orchestration being private to `pkg/action` (`renderResources`); and - lightweight HTTP chart retrieval sharing dependency paths with OCI, registry, plugin, and CLI support.  I propose implementing this as a sequence of small, non-breaking PRs:  1. Extract the client-independent engine core and place Kubernetes `lookup` integration in a separate adapter package. 3. title: Release branches cleanup policy
body: Helm creates release branches (of the format `release/v<Major>.<Minor>`) for each feature (minor) release.  Currently these accumulate, with no defined policy to clean them up. Helm does not support more than a single minor release version (per-major version), except in exceptional circumstances where a security patch has been backported to a prior release branch. Effectively meaning only the last one, or two in exceptional circumstances, release branches need to be retained.  To note, release branches can be recreated from a prior release tag (if needed).  Given the lack of patching of older release branches, a suggested policy is to clean up release branches >1 year old (policy suggested for simplicity, release branches don't need to live longer than ~6 months).  Issue for discussion and agreement.

title: helm upgrade does not reconcile Deployment replicas after a failed upgrade caused by a post-upgrade hook
body:
### What happened?

Helm Upgrade Does Not Restore spec.replicas After a Failed Upgrade with post-upgrade Hook Failure

Summary

We encountered an issue when using Helm SDK (action.NewUpgrade) where a failed upgrade leaves the cluster state inconsistent with the desired state during a subsequent rollback implemented via helm upgrade.

After a successful resource update but a failed post-upgrade hook, the new revision is marked as FAILED. When performing another helm upgrade using the previous chart/version (instead of helm rollback), Helm does not generate a patch for spec.replicas, leaving the Deployment scaled to the previous value.

Environment

  • Helm: v3.16.4

  • Kubernetes: v1.28

  • Helm SDK (action.NewUpgrade)

  • Upgrade performed through Helm SDK (not using helm rollback)

  • post-upgrade hook is enabled

Steps to Reproduce

Initial Release

Revision 1:

apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment spec:   replicas: 2

Release status:

Revision: 1 Status: DEPLOYED

First Upgrade

Upgrade the Deployment from:

replicas: 2

to

replicas: 4

During the upgrade:

  1. Deployment is successfully updated.

  2. Kubernetes successfully scales the Deployment from 2 to 4 replicas.

  3. All 4 Pods become running.

  4. A post-upgrade hook fails.

title: Add support for normalizing the `version:` field to valid semver in OCI image tags
body: ### What would you like to be added?  `helm push` should have a command-line option that causes `helm` to create OCI tags using a 'normalized' version of the version string, rather than using the version string directly; for example, `v1.2.3` -> `1.2.3`.  ### Why is this needed?  Currently, when pushing to an OCI repository, the tag name created is chosen from the chart's `version:` field. While this field is meant to be semver-compliant, it is not required; `helm lint` complaints about it, but internally `helm` uses `semver.NewVersion()` from `Masterminds/semver/v3` which 'normalizes' the version string to some extent. This means that `v1.2.3` is converted to `1.2.3` internally and that is what is used for comparisons, sorting, etc. In this way, helm continues to work with these not-technically-valid semver versions.  `helm` still uses the `version:` field as-is in various places; for OCI registry pushes, it uses this for the image tag and the `org.opencontainers.image.version` field in the manifest metadata. This means that the image that we just pushed, `quay.io/myuser/mychart:v1.2.3`, is discarded. title: get-helm-N installs inconsistent versions due to CDN caching
body: ## Summary  [get_helm-3](https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/main/scripts/get-helm-3) queries `https://get.helm.sh/helm3-latest-version` to determine the latest version, but the request has no cache-control headers or cache-busting query string. CDN edge servers can serve stale cached responses for hours after a new Helm release. This means `get_helm-3` running on different machines at the same time can install different versions depending on which CDN edge server they reach.  ## Context  We discovered this while debugging a flaky integration test in minikube: [kubernetes/minikube#23323](https://github.com/kubernetes/minikube/issues/23323)  Helm v3.21.3 was released on Jul 9, 2026 ~22:00 UTC. About 19 hours later, our CI ran `get_helm.sh` on multiple machines: - Some machines installed v3.21.3 (hit updated CDN edge nodes) - Some machines installed v3.21.2 (hit stale CDN edge nodes) - One machine installed v3.21.2 on the first run and v3.21.3 on the second run minutes later  ## Impact  After a new Helm release, `get_helm-3` becomes non-deterministic. Running it on different machines (or even the same machine at different times) can install different versions. This makes it an "install random version from {current-1, current}" tool rather than a reliable "install latest" tool.  This affects: - CI/CD pipelines that run `get_helm.sh` on multiple nodes and expect consistent versions - Multi-machine deployments where all machines should have the same Helm version - Any automation that compares the installed version to an expected "latest"  ## Current cache behavior  The version file is served from Azure Blob Storage behind Azure Front Door CDN. The origin sets **no `Cache-Control` header**:  ``` $ curl -sI 'https://get.helm.sh/helm3-latest-version' HTTP/2 200  date: Fri, 10 Jul 2026 18:45:44 GMT content-type: application/octet-stream content-length: 8 content-md5: CsRKs3WCs5c4CaZod7y6XQ== last-modified: Thu, 09 Jul 2026 21:12:31 GMT etag: 0x8DEDDFECA26742A x-ms-request-id:

title: CI: govulncheck-action pinned to untagged master SHA is not Dependabot-trackable (follow-up to #32299)
body: ## Problem  PR #32299 re-pins the `govulncheck` step in `.github/workflows/govulncheck.yml` from the released `golang/govulncheck-action@v1.0.4` (`b625fbe0`, tagged **2024-10-01**) to an **untagged `master`-HEAD commit** (`032d45514ae346b1db93c04b0c90b841c370344f`, 2026-07-07) with the comment:  ```yaml uses: golang/govulncheck-action@032d45514ae346b1db93c04b0c90b841c370344f # pin@032d455 (from main 2026-07-06) ```  That change is legitimate and needed — `v1.0.4` internally uses `actions/checkout@v4` / `actions/setup-go@v5` (Node 20, now deprecated), and there is **no newer release** carrying the Node 24 fix. But it introduces a maintainability problem worth tracking separately.  ## Why this is a problem  `golang/govulncheck-action` has not cut a release since **v1.0.4 (Oct 2024)**, despite active commits on `master`. To get the fix, we had to pin ahead of the latest tag. As a result, Dependabot can no longer track this step reliably:  - Helm runs Dependabot on the `github-actions` ecosystem (`.github/dependabot.yml`, `target-branch: main`, daily). It cleanly bumps other steps *by semver* because they are pinned as `<sha> # pin@v7.0.0` — Dependabot reads the version from the comment and matches it to a release tag. - This new pin has **no tag on the SHA** and a **non-semver comment**, so Dependabot cannot establish a "current version" for the entry. Likely outcomes:   1. **Blind spot** — the entry is silently skipped, so a future `v1.0.5` produces no bump PR; or   2. **Proposed downgrade** — Dependabot anchors to the highest known tag (`v1.0.4`) and opens a PR to revert the pin to `b625fbe0`, silently reintroducing the Node 20 deprecation this fix removes.  Either way, it will not behave like the clean `actions/checkout` / `actions/setup-go` bumps.  ## Suggested resolution  - **Preferred:** ask the `golang/govulncheck-action` maintainers to cut a tagged release (e.g. `v1.0.5`) that includes the Node 24 fix, then re-pin to that tag with a `# pin@v1.0.5` comment — thi

Github docs: https://docs.github.com/en/repositories/configuring-branches-and-merges-in-your-repository/configuring-pull-request-merges/managing-suggestions-to-update-pull-request-branches  The advantage of the functionality is that is cheaply allows maintainers (strictly: anyone with repository write access) to update a contributor PRs with new commits from `main` (or the target branch), re-running CI on the PR with the new contribution to `main`, ensuring `main` compatibility. Notably, when Github updates a PR via the "Update branch" workflow, it doesn't invalidate reviews (if I have remembered correctly), and maintainers/reviewers can rely on the fact that PR update only contains changes from `main` (or the target branch).  Compared to today, where the PR author would update the PR against main/target branch (via merge or rebase). Which frequently doesn't happen, and invalidates any review if it does. And also forces any PR reviewer to ensure the "manually" updated PR doesn't  contain any additional extra changes.

title: Helm Files.Lines panic on empty file causes deterministic render failure
body: ### What happened?  reported via email on 26 May 2026 - no response.  ### What did you expect to happen?  The `Files.Lines` template helper in pkg/engine/files.go panics with "index out of range [-1]" when the referenced file is empty. The engine recovers the panic and surfaces it as a render error, but every helm template / install / upgrade / lint and every SDK Engine.Render call that hits the template fails non-zero.  Affected: [helm.sh/helm/v3](http://helm.sh/helm/v3) from 3.13.0 onward, [helm.sh/helm/v4](http://helm.sh/helm/v4) all releases including v4.2.0, confirmed against the main branch.  Root cause: the function checks `f[path] == nil` but not `len(f[path]) == 0`. An empty file inside a chart is stored as a non-nil zero-length byte slice. `s := string(f[path])` is empty, then `s[len(s)-1]` panics.    ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  Proof of concept: a chart containing an empty file in files/ and a single `{{ range .Files.Lines "files/empty.txt" }}` block fails every render:  Build helm from the affected commit (or use any release from v3.13.0 onward, including v3.21.0 and v4.2.0):  ```bash mkdir -p panicchart/templates panicchart/files cat > panicchart/Chart.yaml <<'EOF' apiVersion: v2 name: panicchart version: 0.1.0 EOF touch panicchart/files/empty.txt cat > panicchart/templates/cm.yaml <<'EOF' apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:   name: panic-test data:   lines: | {{- range .Files.Lines "files/empty.txt" }}     {{ . }} {{- end }} EOF  helm template ./panicchart ```  Observed:  ``` Error: template: panicchart/templates/cm.yaml:7:16: executing "panicchart/templates/cm.yaml" at <.Files.Lines>: error calling Lines: runtime error: index out of range [-1] Use --debug flag to render out invalid YAML ```  `helm install --dry-run mytest ./panicchart` produces the same error and exits non-zero.  Suggested fix: guard with `len(f[path]) == 0` and use `strings.TrimSuffix(s, "\n")` instead of subscripting.  ### Helm version

title: fix: `TestStatusWaitForDelete` flakes due to `WaitForDelete` informer initialization race
body: ### What happened?  During informer sync, resources briefly report as `Unknown`. Causing the observer to cancel the watch early, causing intermittent test flakes.  `statusObserver` skips `Unknown` resources when `desired == NotFoundStatus`, so if all resources happen to be in that transient state the filtered list (rss) is empty. `aggregator.AggregateStatus` on an empty slice returns the desired status, causing cancel() to fire immediately — before any real status event is delivered. The watch exits without hitting the deadline, so `ctx.Err()` returns nil, and the test assertion for "context deadline exceeded" fails.  PR attempted to fix, but https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/32081 caused https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/32214 (https://github.com/helm/helm/pull/32081  was then reverted)    ### What did you expect to happen?  `WaitForDelete` needs to handle transient informer initialization behavior, and not assume `Unknown` resources can be skipped.  The fix must include some sort of testing to show that object which are expected to be deleted e.g. hook objects which utilize `helm.sh/hook-delete-policy: before-hook-creation` are successfully "waited" (ie. skipped).  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  Repeated runs of `TestStatusWaitForDelete`  ### Helm version  <details>  ```console $ helm version version.BuildInfo{Version:"v4.2.2", GitCommit:"b05881cf967a5a09e19866799d0edfd40675803a", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.26.4", KubeClientVersion:"v1.36"} ``` </details>   ### Kubernetes version  N/A

title: [Feature] Allow users to disable ServerSideApply for pre-delete hooks during helm uninstall
body: ### What would you like to be added?  In Helm v4, all pre-delete hooks hardcode serverSideApply = true with no configurable switch. We request adding CLI flag / API option to let users disable server-side apply and fall back to client-side apply for uninstall hooks.    ### Why is this needed?  **Cross-tool managedFields ownership conflict** Many clusters use multi-tool management stacks (Flux, ArgoCD, custom operators) that write separate managedFields owners. SSA triggers persistent field ownership conflicts on pre-delete hook resources, causing uninstall failures even with --force-conflicts. Client-side apply avoids this managedFields lock conflict entirely. **Compatibility with legacy Kubernetes clusters & custom webhooks** Some on-prem / restricted clusters have custom admission webhooks that block ServerSideApply requests; pre-delete hooks cannot run without client-side apply fallback. **Breaking change from Helm v3 behavior** Helm v3 executed all hooks with client-side apply. After upgrading to v4, existing charts relying on pre-delete hooks started failing unexpectedly, with no official toggle to revert to old behavior. Users are forced to either: Use --no-hooks (lose pre-delete logic entirely) Maintain custom patched Helm binaries (high maintenance cost) Extract hook logic into external scripts (extra pipeline complexity) **No alignment with existing --server-side flag design** The global --server-side flag controls install/upgrade hook apply mode, but it is ignored for pre-delete hooks. This inconsistent behavior confuses users and breaks expected configuration parity.

title: [Helm v4.2.1] pre-install hook Jobs not created, release stuck in pending-install
body: ### What happened?  Helm v4.2.1 fails to create pre-install hook resources (Jobs) when installing charts that use `helm.sh/hook: pre-install` annotations. The release gets stuck in `pending-install` status with no resources created — including the hook Jobs themselves. This worked correctly in v4.2.0. title: Helm ignores ownership during upgrade
body: ### What happened?  When a resource is transferred from one release to another using `--take-ownership`, and then the original release is upgraded to a version that no longer includes that resource, helm deletes the resource from the cluster — even though it is now owned by a different release.  This was recently fixed for the **uninstall** case in PR #31584 (which resolved #31333), where `verifyOwnershipBeforeDelete` now correctly skips resources not owned by the release being uninstalled. However, the **upgrade** path has no equivalent ownership check.  When helm computes the diff between old and new manifests during upgrade, it deletes orphaned resources based solely on whether `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` is present — it does not check `meta.helm.sh/release-name` or `meta.helm.sh/release-namespace`.  The deletion happens in `pkg/kube/client.go` in the `update()` function (around line 647):  ```go for _, info := range originals.Difference(targets) {     // ...     if annotations != nil && annotations[ResourcePolicyAnno] == KeepPolicy {         continue     }     if err := deleteResource(info, metav1.DeletePropagationBackground); err != nil { ```  This checks `helm.sh/resource-policy: keep` but does not check `meta.helm.sh/release-name`. Adding an ownership check here (similar to `verifyOwnershipBeforeDelete` in the uninstall path) would complete the feature.  ### What did you expect to happen?  When upgrading release-a to a version that no longer includes a resource, helm should check the live ownership annotations before deleting. If `meta.helm.sh/release-name` on the resource points to a different release (e.g. release-b), it should skip deletion — the same way `helm uninstall` now does after PR #31584.  ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  ```bash # Create two simple charts: # chart-a-v1: contains ConfigMap "shared-config" + ConfigMap "chart-a-own" # chart-a-v2: contains only ConfigMap "chart-a-own" (shared-config removed)

body: ### What happened?  I use Helm as a Go package (`helm.sh/helm/v4` v4.2.0), not the CLI. `kube.(*Client).IsReachable()` panics with a nil pointer dereference when it is called a second time on a `Client` whose Kubernetes client could not be created on the first call.  The root cause is in `getKubeClient`:  ```go func (c *Client) getKubeClient() (kubernetes.Interface, error) { 	var err error 	if c.kubeClient == nil { 		c.kubeClient, err = c.Factory.KubernetesClientSet() 	} 	return c.kubeClient, err } ```  `KubernetesClientSet()` returns `(*kubernetes.Clientset, error)`. When `ToRESTConfig()` fails (for example, the selected context does not exist, or the config is empty), it returns `(nil, err)`. The `nil` concrete pointer is then stored into the `c.kubeClient` field, which is an interface (`kubernetes.Interface`). A typed nil stored in an interface makes the interface itself non-nil.  Because of this:  1. First call to `getKubeClient`: `c.kubeClient` is nil, so it calls the factory. The factory returns `(nil, err)`. The field now holds a typed nil, and the error is returned. `IsReachable` sees the error and returns a clean "kubernetes cluster unreachable" error. This part is fine. 2. Second call to `getKubeClient`: `c.kubeClient == nil` is now false (the interface is non-nil), so the factory is not called again. It returns the typed-nil client and `err == nil`. 3. Back in `IsReachable`, both error checks pass because the error is nil. title: Optimize index.yaml loading to only process required chart entries
body: ## Problem  When resolving dependencies (`helm dependency update` / `helm dependency build`), Helm loads the **entire** `index.yaml` for every configured repository into memory — deserializing, validating, and sorting all chart entries — even though only a small subset of entries (the declared dependencies) are actually needed.  For large repository indexes (e.g., Bitnami with 1000+ charts), this causes: - **Unnecessary memory consumption** — all chart versions for all charts are held in memory - **Wasted CPU cycles** — every chart version is validated (`Validate()`) and sorted, even if never accessed - **Repeated full loads** — the same index is loaded fully multiple times during a single operation (once in the resolver, once in `downloadAll`)  ### Example scenario  A chart with 3 dependencies from a repository with 1,200 charts: - Current: loads + validates all 1,200 charts × N versions each (multiple times) - Proposed: loads only 3 charts × their versions, skips validation for the other 1,197  ## Proposed Solution  Add a new public function `LoadIndexFileForEntries` that accepts a set of chart names to retain:  ```go // LoadIndexFileForEntries loads an index file but only validates and retains // entries matching the provided chart names. Unmatched entries are discarded // after unmarshal without validation, reducing memory and CPU overhead. // If entries is nil, all entries are loaded (equivalent to LoadIndexFile). func LoadIndexFileForEntries(path string, entries map[string]struct{}) (*IndexFile, error) ```  ## Impact  - Reduced memory usage proportional to (needed entries / total entries) - Faster `helm dependency update` on systems with large repo indexes - No breaking changes to CLI behavior or public Go API  ## Benchmark Results  Tested with a real-world index.yaml (79 MB, 71 chart entries, 92,807 total versions) on Apple M3 Pro, filtering to 3 entries:  ### Retained Heap (live objects after GC)  | Metric | Full Load | Filtered (3 entries) | Savings | |----

title: Make version optional for OCI charts for promotion workflows
body: ### What would you like to be added?  By using OCI images, versions are generally expressed by tags. The actual image content doesn't need to have version information contained. This allows images to be promoted by retagging.  The author of an helm chart should be able **not specifing** `version:` in `Chart.yaml`. title: ci: add check to prevent invisible Unicode characters (ZWSP/bidi) in source
body: ## Summary  PR #32134 removed three U+200B (zero-width space) characters from a comment in `internal/plugin/plugin.go`. The characters were invisible, had no effect on behavior, but caused Renovate to emit a repo-wide warning for every project that vendors `helm.sh/helm/v4`:  > ⚠️ WARN: Hidden Unicode characters have been discovered in file(s) in your repository...  ## Proposal  Add a CI step that fails if any invisible/dangerous Unicode codepoints are found in the source tree. A one-liner like:  ```bash grep -rP '[\x{200B}-\x{200D}\x{FEFF}\x{202A}-\x{202E}\x{2066}-\x{2069}]' --include='*.go' . && echo 'FAIL: invisible Unicode found' && exit 1 || true ```  This covers: - U+200B–U+200D: zero-width spaces - U+FEFF: BOM / zero-width no-break space - U+202A–U+202E: bidirectional text controls - U+2066–U+2069: bidirectional isolates (the "trojan source" class)  Alternatively, a `golangci-lint` plugin or a standalone tool such as [`bidichk`](https://github.com/breml/bidichk) could be wired into the existing lint pipeline.  ## Motivation  - Prevents the same class of issue from silently reappearing. - Protects downstream `vendor/` consumers from noisy Renovate warnings that can't be suppressed per-path. - Guards against "trojan source" style attacks (bidi overrides in code comments/strings).

title: toYamlPretty renders integer values as floats

title: `null` overrides in parent values.yaml ignored for always-enabled subcharts
body: ### What happened?  When a parent chart sets a subchart value to `null` to erase the subchart's default (e.g. `runAsUser: null` to suppress `runAsUser: 65534`), the override is silently ignored and the subchart's integer default leaks into the rendered output.  This only affects subcharts whose `enabled: true` is set in the parent's `values.yaml`. Subcharts that are condition-gated and activated via `--set` (or `-f`) are **not affected** — their null overrides work correctly. Both subcharts have a `condition` in `Chart.yaml`.  This appears to be related to #32093 (same root cause: `merge=true` path skips `cleanNilValues`), but the trigger scenario is different: here the parent is explicitly setting `null` to erase a subchart default, rather than subchart-default nils leaking into parent scope.  ### What did you expect to happen?  A `null` value set by the parent chart under a subchart namespace should erase the corresponding subchart default during coalescing, regardless of whether the subchart is always-enabled or condition-gated.   ### How can we reproduce it (as minimally and precisely as possible)?  Create the reproducer chart:  ```bash mkdir -p reproducer/charts/always-on/templates reproducer/charts/gated/templates  cat > reproducer/Chart.yaml << 'EOF' apiVersion: v2 name: reproducer version: 0.1.0 dependencies:   - name: always-on     version: 0.1.0     condition: always-on.enabled   - name: gated     version: 0.1.0     condition: gated.enabled EOF  cat > reproducer/values.yaml << 'EOF' always-on:   enabled: true   securityContext:     runAsUser: null     runAsGroup: null gated:   enabled: false   securityContext:     runAsUser: null     runAsGroup: null EOF  cat > reproducer/charts/always-on/Chart.yaml << 'EOF' apiVersion: v2 name: always-on version: 0.1.0 EOF  cat > reproducer/charts/always-on/values.yaml << 'EOF' securityContext:   runAsUser: 65534   runAsGroup: 65534   runAsNonRoot: true EOF  cat > reproducer/charts/always-on/templates/pod.yaml << 'EOF' {{

title: Add some sort of warning (at least to debug level logging) if the lookup function returns nil
body: ### What would you like to be added?  Some sort of warning (at the debug logging level of `helm template`) that would warn if `lookup` failed/returned nil, even if such an occurrence is handled with a `default`  ### Why is this needed?  Here is a logging example from a very simple chart that creates a configmap from a lookup, with a default as fallback:  ``` (samuzad) lookup-test-chart (feat/lookup-warnings)$ helm template . --debug -v 10  I0505 15:44:49.027664   90018 loader.go:405] Config loaded from file:  /Users/samuzad/.kube/config level=DEBUG msg="Original chart version" version="" level=DEBUG msg="Chart path" path=/Users/samuzad/fork/argo-cd/hack/lookup-test-chart I0505 15:44:49.028425   90018 loader.go:405] Config loaded from file:  /Users/samuzad/.kube/config I0505 15:44:49.029754   90018 loader.go:405] Config loaded from file:  /Users/samuzad/.kube/config level=DEBUG msg="number of dependencies in the chart" chart=lookup-test dependencies=0 --- # Source: lookup-test/templates/01-test.yaml apiVersion: v1 kind: ConfigMap metadata:   name: test data:   token: "fallback-test" ```  This is expected behaviour - I added a default and I did not have `--dry-run=server`. The problem is that nothing in the logs indicates that the lookup failed/returned nil. You can imagine a situation where, for instance, you think you're setting the admin password of your instance with a lookup of an existing secret. However, this silently fails and the admin password falls back to `password`   The reason this is a problem is because ArgoCD does not currently support `lookups`. And in order to warn people that there are lookups, a some sort of indication that `I tried using lookup but returned with nothing` during `helm template` would be very useful.   Would there be any openness to adding this in to `helm`? I'd be very happy to open a PR for this, but am wondering if there is any reason not to  A reference for the discussion on the ArgoCD side: - https://github.com/argoproj/argo-c

title: CVE-2025-53547: writeLock missing symlink-target check on `release-3.16`
body: Upstream commit `4b8e61093d` (CVE-2025-53547) hardens `pkg/downloader/manager.go::writeLock` so that a pre-existing `Chart.lock` / `requirements.lock` symlink is detected before the dependency-resolver writes through it. Without the guard, a malicious chart can plant a symlink pointing into `~/.kube/config` (or any other path) and trigger an arbitrary file overwrite the next time `helm dependency update` runs.  On `release-3.16` `pkg/downloader/manager.go::writeLock` (around line 844-855) is still the pre-fix shape — straight `yaml.Marshal` then `os.WriteFile(dest, data, 0644)`, no `os.Lstat` / `os.ModeSymlink` / `os.Readlink` to bail out. The upstream change is ~14 lines on a single function and applies cleanly.  Reported via port-credit-hunting.

title: pkg/chart/common/util/jsonschema: structured log outputs byte array instead of string
body: ## Bug Description  In [`pkg/chart/common/util/jsonschema.go` line 137](https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/4bd9e90aa0ef29a1a7b4dfbd5234be785e846204/pkg/chart/common/util/jsonschema.go#L137), the structured log call passes `schemaJSON` (a `[]byte`) directly as a log attribute value:  ```go slog.Debug("unmarshalled JSON schema", "schema", schemaJSON) ```  `schemaJSON` is a `[]byte`, so `log/slog` logs it as a base64-encoded string rather than the actual JSON content.
