title: Question: potential collision in package cache?
body: We are seeing a strange problem where 2 simultaneous helm install invocations and one of the invocations using the chart of the other invocations. This only happens if the 2 invocations are simultaneous.  By using strace on a single invocation we found the following:  - we invoke `/helm install myrelname http://xxx:7004/foo/bar/baz/ae3625db-fddd-49f5-9804-4355e8211910?path=//Artifacts/Images/onechart.tgz`. So the difference between 2 different chart URLs would be only in the part after `?path=`  - Strace shows that helm is fetching the chart an storing it in the repository. The name of the file in the cache is like the last component in the URI "plus some extra characters":     - `openat(AT_FDCWD, "/root/.cache/helm/repository/ae3625db-fddd-49f5-9804-4355e82119101085157973", O_RDWR|O_CREAT|O_EXCL|O_CLOEXEC, 0600 <unfinished ...>`  - A little bit later, the file is renamed to a new name that is just the last component:     - `2736520 renameat(AT_FDCWD, "/root/.cache/helm/repository/ae3625db-fddd-49f5-9804-4355e82119101085157973", AT_FDCWD, "/root/.cache/helm/repository/ae3625db-fddd-49f5-9804-4355e8211910" <unfinished ...>`  - So two concurrent invocations that use different charts but whose URL only differ in the part after `?path=` in the URL would end up fighting for the same file in the repository cache.  - This collision could very well explain the strange race condition behaviour that we are experiencing.  Could anyone please confirm the reasoning above?  Thanks in advance  cc: @abhishek-kumar0409  Edit: This has been seen with helm version: ``` version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.14.2", GitCommit:"c309b6f0ff63856811846ce18f3bdc93d2b4d54b", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.21.7"} ```  And also with: ``` version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.15.1", GitCommit:"e211f2aa62992bd72586b395de50979e31231829", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.22.3"} ```

title: Helm lint exlusion list
body: Hello, my name is Danilo Patrucco, and I am part of the Big Bang team working on the Platform 1 project.   I am proposing an enhancement to the helm lint command to include an exclusion capability. This feature would involve the introduction of a .helmlintignore file, which would list files and specific errors found within those files. If an error occurs during linting and it matches a pattern specified in the .helmlintignore file, that error will not be displayed.  Additionally, we plan to introduce a --lint-ignore-file flag. This flag will allow users to specify a single .helmlintignore file when working with sub-repositories, enabling more precise and efficient lint management across complex projects.  Here below a draft for a HIP :   --- hip: 9999 title: "Add Exclude File Option to Helm Lint Command" authors: Danilo Patrucco created: "2024-06-18" type: "feature" status: "draft" ---  ## Abstract  This proposal suggests enhancing the `helm lint` command to exclude specific files or patterns from linting through a `.helmlintignore` file, similar to `.gitignore` or `.helmignore`. Additionally, a `--lint-ignore-file` flag will be introduced to specify alternative locations for the `.helmlintignore` file, facilitating its use in projects with multiple sub-charts.  ## Motivation  In large Helm charts, certain files or configurations may deviate from standard linting rules but are accepted by the maintainers. Currently, `helm lint` evaluates all files within a chart, leading to irrelevant warnings or errors. An exclusion option and the ability to specify ignore file locations would allow developers to better manage lint results.  ## Rationale  This proposal aims to give developers and integrators greater control over the linting process by allowing exclusions for:  - Files imported or managed by third parties that are not directly editable.  - Files that may not conform to static linting rules.  - Files containing intentional deviations from standard practices due to sp

title: Custom burst limit settings don't apply to discovery
body: Helm currently has the `--burst-limit`/`$HELM_BURST_LIMIT` options, which allows users to give Helm more headroom when making bursty API requests. I've seen it said that setting `--burst-limit` will help with rate limiting issues on clusters with large numbers of CRDs, since the number of requests required for discovery goes up as the number of CRDs increases.  Unfortunately, this is not the case: https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/a2a324e51165388448be8caaf8737b7fd2f1a19a/pkg/cli/environment.go#L127  Here, Helm sets `k8s.io/client-go/rest.Config.Burst`. When `genericclioptions` instantiates a discovery client, it overrides `Config.Burst` with `ConfigFlags.discoveryBurst`: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/3f9b79fc119d064d00939f91567b48d9ada7dc43/staging/src/k8s.io/cli-runtime/pkg/genericclioptions/config_flags.go#L281  This means that no matter what `--burst-limit` is set to, `generricclioptions` (and by extension, Helm) will only allow a burst limit of 300 for discovery. I found this because I was helping someone deal with client-side throttling on a large cluster.  There are two ways this issue could be addressed: 1. Add a separate `--discovery-burst-limit`/`$HELM_DISCOVERY_BURST_LIMIT` flag that would independently set `generricclioptions.ConfigFlags.discoveryBurst` 2. Set `generricclioptions.ConfigFlags.discoveryBurst` to the value of `--burst-limit`  The benefit to the first approach is flexibility. However, I don't know if we even need that flexibility (there's talk of removing client-side throttling now that APF is a thing). The second approach is nice because it's a very small change and makes the `--burst-limit` flag meet people's expectations. To me, the second approach seems to be more inline with the principle of least astonishment. Here's the diff: ```diff diff --git a/pkg/cli/environment.go b/pkg/cli/environment.go index ba103252..d5101c68 100644 --- a/pkg/cli/environment.go +++ b/pkg/cli/environment.go @@ -112,7 +112,7 @@ func New() *EnvSet

title: RFE: Support for multi-document values files
body: Helm support providing multiple values files. Unfortunately, only first YAML document of each file is taken into consideration.  As many values files (i.e. document) are supported, there's no functional reason to not support one values file with many documents. Documents in a single values file should be considered if they were split into many files and just passed in order.  To be more precise giving:  * `A.yaml`  ```yaml --- # A-1.yaml --- # A-2.yaml ````  * `B.yaml`  ```yaml --- # B-1.yaml --- # B-2.yaml ````  implies these two equivalent:  * `helm template my-release my-chart -f A.yaml -f B.yaml` * `helm template my-release my-chart -f A-1.yaml -f A-2.yaml -f B-1.yaml -f B-2.yaml`

title: Enhancement: Allow deep overriding of Values in a list using `-f values.yaml` the way it works with `--set`
body: There's a strange asymmetry since Helm 2.5.0: one can override individual values that are part of `Values` inside lists with the syntax `--set servers[0].port=8080` but one cannot do the equivalent override using `-f override_values.yaml` overrides, i.e. the following does not work:  ``` # values.yaml servers: - protocol: tcp   port: 80 ```  ``` # override_values.yaml servers[0]:   port: 8080 ```  It's unintuitive that one can do deep overrides in lists using indexes via `--set` syntax but not with `-f` overrides.  In fact, based on this [StackOverflow Q&A with 5k views](https://stackoverflow.com/questions/63833877/override-value-in-list-with-helm-override-file), indexed `-f` override seemed to work at some point in the past, maybe with v2, but it doesn't seem to work anymore.  My questions are: - Is this intended behaviour, that one cannot use `-f` for deep overrides, the way one can do it with `--set`? - When was the behaviour changed? Per StackOverflow Q&A it used to be possible (albeit with +/- 1 differences in index) - Would it be possible to symmetrise `--set` and `-f`, by adding the deep override capability to `-f` overrides?  I looked carefully through previous issues, but couldn't find a recent one that was quite as explicit - there may well have been bugs/changes over time so I'm not sure old issues apply one-to-one.  Here are a few I looked at: - https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/5711 - https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/11734

title: Update backward compatibility promise in CONTRIBUTING.md to reflect HIP 0004

The section should point to HIP-0004  ### HIP-0004 > programs using the Helm Go API will continue to compile - Should this also include changing functionality? If a public function/method should probably not change overall internal functionality e.g if a change removes previous functionality and makes the function a no-op, perhaps this should not be allowed.

title: helm mixes namespaces from kubeconfig file and actionConfig.Init funtion
body: I'm developing a Golang application that uses Helm as a library. And I noticed the behavior that Helm ignores the client settings and uses the namespace that is specified in kubeconfig. Here is my function code: ```go func (vc *HelmConn) DeleteHelmRelease(name, ns string) error { 	actionConfig := new(action.Configuration)  	if err := actionConfig.Init(vc.HelmConfig.RESTClientGetter(), ns, "", log.Printf); err != nil { 		return err 	}  	client := action.NewUninstall(actionConfig) 	client.Timeout = helmDeleteTimeout 	client.DeletionPropagation = "background" 	client.Wait = true  	_, err := client.Run(name) 	if err != nil { 		return err 	}  	return nil } ```  at the same time, even the namespace from kubeconfig is not fully used. Let's say namespace test1 is set in kubeconfig, and I pass namespace test2 to the function, the result will be:  * helm release (metadata) will be removed from namespace **test2** * k8s resources will be removed from namespace **test1** * post-install hooks will run in namespace **test1** , but `{{ .Release.Namespace }}` in hooks template will be **test2**.  Also in command line utility I managed to reproduce the same behavior.  1. Set namespace test1 in kubeconfig 2. run helm uninstall release_name 3. immediately change the namespace in kubeconfig to test2.  The result will be the same as described above. title: `--set-literal` does not allow backslash escaping in NAME
body: ### Problem  Helm option `--set-literal` does not perform backslash escaping for value _names_.  Example: `--set-literal 'a.b\.b\.b.c=x,\[]{}x'` has the same effect as using the following values file:  ```yaml a:   b\\:     b\\:       b:         c: 'x,\[]{}x' ```  This does not make any sense, because it prevents setting values with special characters in the name.  ### Expected Behavior  `--set-literal` should allow to set values whose name contains characters with special meanings in a path (e.g. `.` or `[`) using the same backslash escaping rules as used for other -`--set*` options. title: Helm's ports merging logic differs from Kubernetes
body: <!-- If you need help or think you have found a bug, please help us with your issue by entering the following information (otherwise you can delete this text): -->  ## Problem statement  In Helm, ports are merged via their port `name` while in Kubernetes ports are merged via their `port` number. This difference in logic can lead to state inconsistencies in Helm releases (see `Example` section) and the only way to "repair" Helm's broken state is to use the `--force` flag of `helm upgrade`.  Related to closed issue https://github.com/helm/helm/issues/7957.  ## Example  Given 2 ports with names `first-port` and `second-port` and respective values `8080` and `9090`:  ``` spec:   template:     spec:       containers:         - ports:             - name: first-port               containerPort: 8080               protocol: TCP             - name: second-port               containerPort: 9090               protocol: TCP  ```  If the value of `second-port` is changed from `9090` to `8080`, Helm will retain both ports with the same port number (`8080`), while Kubernetes will have in fact merged both ports into `first-port` with port number `8080`. Our current method involves adding a list of all (helm) registries we use and then trying to find a helm release name in one. We can likely do something similar for OCI registries, but this method has several issues:  - naming conflicts happen occasionally between registries, causing the check to return the wrong items  - it is quite slow and uses a lot of cpu, even for helm registries with all information locally stored after a `helm repo update`. title: Template warning function
body: I've been thinking through what it means to provide guarantees around the `values.yaml` between versions of our chart, and one thing I'd really like to see is the ability to issue warnings. Why? Because for most `values.yaml` structure changes, we can implicitly migrate the user's old values, but similar to how [`kube-apiserver` warns about deprecated APIs](https://github.com/kubernetes/enhancements/blob/master/keps/sig-api-machinery/1693-warnings/README.md), we could issue warnings in helm and then remove the implicit migration later.  Right now there is a [`fail`](https://masterminds.github.io/sprig/flow_control.html) function, but that's a hard stop. What I'd like is something like a `warn` function, or even just a printf that made it to stderr.  Barring that I may just make sure any migrations we do fail brightly during the upgrade horizon, I.e. if `foo.bar` moved to a new place in `values.yaml` we'd still accept the value and fail with something like `foo.bar has moved to foo.controller.bar, please update your deployment` so the user knows what to change.

title: OCI image annotation org.opencontainers.image.created should use timestamp of pushed TGZ instead of current time
body: ``` helm create mychart helm package mychart  # initial push [ok] helm push mychart*tgz oci://registry:5000 --plain-http  # now, following should be a noop, but it pushes new manifest with different digest helm push mychart*tgz oci://registry:5000 --plain-http ```  subsequent helm push calls always pushes new manifest with different digest because of change in `org.opencontainers.image.created`  There is no change in config (same digest), no change in layers (same digest). And only change in manifest is `org.opencontainers.image.created` annotation.  This, for example, complicates detection of actual change in mutable tags, and produces useless objects in registry.  At this point, helm push operation should be idempotent, it should even skip push if there are no changes to be pushed.  Helm 3.14.3

title: Proposal: New omitted function to set a default value if value omitted
body: ## Motivation  The current function `default` doesn't behave the way it's logically expected or even explained [in the manual](https://helm.sh/docs/chart_template_guide/functions_and_pipelines/#using-the-default-function): > This function allows you to specify a default value inside of the template, in case the value is omitted  ## Proposal  So I propose creating a function that does the work that is expected out of `default` by most people. Creating a function which sets a value when such value has never been defined (AKA, doesn't exist, AKA omitted).  The concept of omitted in Go doesn't exist, however, go templates in helm are largely done on top of go `map` (equivalent to sprig `dict`) and when getting an element from the map that doesn't exist, it returns `Nil`.  Given such, I propose an alternative to `default` which has the same API as `default` but only tests for `Nil`, considering all non-Nil values as defined values and not omissions.  ## Implementation example  ``` func omitted(a, b interface{}) interface{} { 	if b == nil { 		return a 	} 	return b } ```  ## Documentation changes  #### https://helm.sh/docs/chart_template_guide/functions_and_pipelines/#using-the-default-function  Either:  1. Change to mention `omitted` instead of `default` 2. Create a copy for `omitted` and make a warning about pitfalls of `default`.   #### https://helm.sh/docs/chart_template_guide/function_list/#default  Mention that, in most cases, the function the user wants to use is `omitted` available since [version]  #### https://helm.sh/docs/chart_template_guide/function_list/  Explain the `omitted` function  ## See also  #12781

body: <!-- If you need help or think you have found a bug, please help us with your issue by entering the following information (otherwise you can delete this text): -->  Helm does a permission check on the kubeconfig and displays a warning if the file is readable beyond the user. But, there are 2 situations where this displays a warning improperly.  1. If the kubeconfig file is on Windows and is passed through to WSL. The permissions on Windows don't map nicely to Linux so this creates a situation where the permissions are more permissive. Helm in Linux will see this and display both warnings. 2. If you place a kubeconfig file in a container running in Kubernetes and mount it using a secret. Then you run the container as a non-root user. Mounting a kubeconfig via a secret is an appropriate way to pass that in. Running commands in the container as non-root is good for security. This setup will cause a message to be generated.  The warning message are handled by the `checkPerms()` function.  This addition was after a security audit from a 3rd party (report [here](https://github.com/helm/community/blob/main/security-audit/Helm%20Final%20Report%202020.pdf)). It is finding 1.  This warning should be removed. Beyond the above 2 issues, here are the reasons to remove it:  * kubectl does not provide such a message. The Kubernetes project is in more of a position to make and set permissions policies for this configuration file. It does not provide direction here and does not do any checks. * The kubeconfig file is owned by the Kubernetes project more than Helm. title: Helm has the potential to prefer requirements.lock
body: I recently had a helm chart that had been working fine, just suddenly stop working with the following error:  ``` Error: the lock file (Chart.lock) is out of sync with the dependencies file (Chart.yaml). Please update the dependencies ```  I immediately ran `helm dependency update` and the resulting `Chart.lock` digest was the same. So I tried `helm dependency build` and I get the same error.  I tried removing `Chart.lock` and I still get the same error.  I tried commenting out the dependency section of `Chart.yaml` or setting `dependencies:` to `[]`. It still gives me the same error.  Eventually after putting in some debug statements into `manager.go` I can clearly see that `lock.Digest` is not the same thing that is in Chart.lock.  After spending some more time digging in, I eventually found out that for some reason the way that helm is walking the helm chart directory, it started finding `requirements.lock` after `Chart.lock` which caused helm to just overwrite the Helm `chart.Lock` struct with `requirements.lock` instead of `Chart.lock`.  You can see from this section of code that depending on the order of the `files` slice it will just overwrite `c.Lock` with whatever it happens to find most recently: https://github.com/helm/helm/blob/main/pkg/chart/loader/load.go#L100-L140  When it finds `requirements.yaml` it will output a warning, but no such warning will be output if `requirements.lock` is used instead of `Chart.lock`. I feel like this violates the principle of least surprise.  In my case, `Chart.lock` and `requirements.lock` had coexisted for more than a year and I've never run into issues today. I just I got lucky with the slice ordering?  Output of `helm version`:   ``` version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.14.2", GitCommit:"c309b6f0ff63856811846ce18f3bdc93d2b4d54b", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.21.7"} ```

But when I query the status of this CR just after send the update request to k8s, the status is still `done`(the operator is not fast enough to change it to `updating` before this), so the program will consider it already updated, but in fact, it wasn't. title: Key unsetting should occur before schema validation
body: Suppose that I have a chart that expects an optional integer value for key `foo`, and the chart provides a JSON schema to that effect: ``` {   "$schema": "http://json-schema.org/schema#",   "type": "object",   "properties": {     "foo": {type": "integer"},   } } ``` The chart provides a default values file ``` foo: 1 ``` but a user overrides that to unset `foo`: ``` foo: null ``` Helm promises to remove that key altogether; and having done so, this should pass validation, since the key is optional. But instead we see validation errors of the form ``` - foo: Invalid type. Expected: integer, given: null ``` indicating that helm has not removed the key prior to validation. This is extremely counter-intuitive, and IMO is a bug.  The only workaround I am aware of is to type `foo` as ```     "foo": {type": ["integer", "null"]}, ```  Output of `helm version`: ``` version.BuildInfo{Version:"v3.14.2", GitCommit:"c309b6f0ff63856811846ce18f3bdc93d2b4d54b", GitTreeState:"clean", GoVersion:"go1.21.7"} ```

title: No way to check if template exists
body: It would be very helpful when writing library charts to support some mechanism to detect if a template is defined or not. Defining 'block' templates is ok, but you can not programmatically define a block so it limits how you can use the library chart. If it were possible to write an if statement that checks if a template is defined then it could be skipped or default yaml could be output instead. For example:  {{- if hasTemplate (printf "%s.section" $name) }} {{- include (printf "%s.section" $name) . }} {{- else }} ...default yaml {{- end }}  That could then be included multiple times with different names allowing a library chart to define deployments and other resources that may not be singletons and still allow customization by the application chart.

body: ### Describe the bug  When a PostgreSQL `DOMAIN` type is copied (via `DOMAIN.copy()`, `Table.to_metadata()`, `Column._copy()`, or when used on a declarative mixin), the copy silently drops `default`, `not_null`, `check`, `constraint_name`, `collation`, and `collation_schema`.  In `lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/named_types.py`: `DOMAIN.__init__` accepts these parameters as keyword-only arguments after `*`: ```python     def __init__(         self,         name: str,         data_type: _TypeEngineArgument[Any],         *,         collation: Optional[str] = None,         collation_schema: Optional[str] = None,         default: Optional[str] = None,         constraint_name: Optional[str] = None,         not_null: Optional[bool] = None,         check: Optional[str] = None,         ... ```  `DOMAIN.copy()` delegates to `TypeEngine.adapt()`, which invokes `util.constructor_copy(self, cls, **kw)`. title: MutableDict |= and MutableList *= do not emit change events; changes are not persisted
body: ### Describe the bug  When modifying a `MutableDict` using the in-place union operator (`|=`) or a `MutableList` using in-place multiplication (`*=`), change events are not emitted. The underlying instance is not marked as modified (`session.is_modified(instance) == False`), and subsequent `session.commit()` or `session.flush()` silently skips persisting the changes to the database.  `MutableDict` does not implement `__ior__` (introduced for Python dictionaries in PEP 584 / Python 3.9), and `MutableList` does not implement `__imul__`. As a result, the built-in `dict.__ior__` and `list.__imul__` run without calling `self.changed()`.  In ticket #3853, upstream added `__ior__`, `__iand__`, `__ixor__`, and `__isub__` to `MutableSet`, and `__iadd__` (`+=`) to `MutableList` for the exact same reason. `dict |=` and `list *=` appear to have been overlooked.  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import JSON, create_engine, select from sqlalchemy.ext.mutable import MutableDict, MutableList from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Document(Base):     __tablename__ = "doc"     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     payload: Mapped[dict] = mapped_column(MutableDict.as_mutable(JSON))     tags: Mapped[list] = mapped_column(MutableList.as_mutable(JSON))   engine = create_engine("sqlite://") Base.metadata.create_all(engine)  with Session(engine) as session:     session.add(Document(id=1, payload={"a": 1}, tags=[1, 2]))     session.commit()      doc = session.get(Document, 1)     # In-place mutations     doc.payload |= {"b": 2}     doc.tags *= 2      print("In memory:", doc.payload, doc.tags)     print("session.is_modified(doc):", session.is_modified(doc))  # False!      session.commit()  with Session(engine) as session:     reloaded = session.execute(select(Document.payload, Document.tags)).one()     print("In DB after commit:      ", reloaded)  # ({'a': 1}, [1, 2]) -> changes sil

title: str(select(func.aggregate_strings(...))) raises TypeError in default SQLCompiler (regression in 2.1)
body: ### Describe the bug  In 2.1, calling `str()` or `compile()` on a statement containing `func.aggregate_strings()` without specifying a dialect (or using `DefaultDialect`) fails with: ``` TypeError: SQLCompiler.visit_aggregate_strings_func() missing 1 required keyword-only argument: 'use_function_name' ```  In `lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py:3136`: ```python     def visit_aggregate_strings_func(self, fn, *, use_function_name, **kw): ``` The method requires a keyword-only argument `use_function_name`. When `compile()` is called without a specific dialect, generic `visit_function()` resolves this compiler method via `getattr` and invokes it without `use_function_name`, resulting in a `TypeError`. title: DDL and special transaction SQL lost "autoclose" since 1.4
body: ### Describe the bug  With the MSSQL dialect, the DBAPI cursors used for the savepoint statements issued by `begin_nested()` (`SAVE TRANSACTION <name>` and `ROLLBACK TRANSACTION <name>`) are never closed. They are released only when the cursor object is garbage collected. Other statements in the same transaction, including the `IF @@TRANCOUNT = 0 BEGIN TRANSACTION` emitted by `MSDialect.do_savepoint`, are closed normally.  This looks like a small leftover from #12798. Since 2.0.44, `mssql+aioodbc` closes result cursors through aioodbc's awaitable close, but the savepoint cursors still fall through to GC. Under asyncio that free (pyodbc `SQLFreeHandle`) then runs on the event-loop thread. The synchronous `mssql+pyodbc` dialect shows the same unclosed cursors.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.44, 2.0.54, 2.1.3 (all identical)  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  aioodbc 0.5.0 over pyodbc 5.2.0 (also plain pyodbc 5.2.0)  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  Microsoft SQL Server (reproducer uses a fake pyodbc connection; no server needed)  ### Python Version  3.11.9  ### Operating system  Windows 10 and Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python import asyncio import gc  import aioodbc import sqlalchemy from sqlalchemy import text from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import AsyncSession, create_async_engine from sqlalchemy.pool import NullPool  UNCLOSED = [] CLOSED = []   class FakeCursor:     """Stands in for a pyodbc cursor; records whether close() was called."""      def __init__(self):         self.closed = False         self.sql = None         self.description = None         self.rowcount = -1         self.arraysize = 1      def execute(self, sql, *params):         self.sql = sql         self.rowcount = 1         return self      def fetchall(self):         return []      def nextset(self):         return False      def setinputsizes(self, *sizes):         pass

In 2.0.52 they are freed by refcount as soon as the loop ends. Is this intended?  `_iterator_getter` is a `HasMemoized_ro_memoized_attribute`, so the `iterrows` closure it returns is stored on the Result, and the closure calls `self._fetchiter_impl()`. The Result holds the closure and the closure holds the Result. `.all()`, `.first()` and `.partitions()` don't go through `_iterator_getter`, so they don't create the cycle.  In 2.0 the closure didn't capture the Result: `iterrows` took `self: Result[Any]` as a parameter and `_iter_impl` called `self._iterator_getter(self)`. That part may well be the connector's problem, but the cycle is new in 2.1 and it is what moves cursor cleanup off the owning thread.  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.1.0 and 2.1.3 (the same closure is on `main`). title: column order from MappedAsDataclass mixin no longer follows declaration order in 2.1
body: Reported in discussion #13632 by @ovidiu-eremia.  When a mapped class receives its columns from an unmapped `MappedAsDataclass` mixin, the resulting `Table` columns no longer follow declaration order in 2.1. Columns that have no dataclass default (e.g. a primary key with no `default=`, or a field using `default_factory`) are moved after the columns that do have a default. 2.0 kept declaration order.  ```python import dataclasses from typing import Optional  from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped from sqlalchemy.orm import MappedAsDataclass from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Mixin(MappedAsDataclass):     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     name: Mapped[Optional[str]] = mapped_column(default=None)     description: Mapped[Optional[str]] = mapped_column(default=None)   class ViaMixin(Base, Mixin):     __tablename__ = "via_mixin"   print([f.name for f in dataclasses.fields(ViaMixin)]) # ['id', 'name', 'description']  print(ViaMixin.__table__.columns.keys()) # 2.0: ['id', 'name', 'description'] # 2.1: ['name', 'description', 'id'] ```  Cause: since #12854 an unmapped `MappedAsDataclass` class is turned into a dataclass at class creation time, using `dataclasses.Field` objects placed on the class. `dataclasses` deletes the class attribute for any field without a plain default; SQLAlchemy then restores the `mapped_column()` objects, which re-appends those attributes at the end of the class `__dict__`. The mapped subclass scan then sees the mixin's attributes in that altered order.  Workaround: `mapped_column(sort_order=...)` on the mixin columns.

title: `ExceptionContext.__slots__ = ()` makes the documented `context.is_disconnect = True` fail mypy's slots check
body: ### Ensure stubs packages are not installed  - [x] No sqlalchemy stub packages is installed (both `sqlalchemy-stubs` and `sqlalchemy2-stubs` are not compatible with v2)  ### Verify if the api is typed  - [x] The api is not in a module listed in [#6810](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/6810) so it should pass type checking  ### Describe the typing issue  The `handle_error` event is typed as handle_error(exception_context: ExceptionContext), and the documentation of `ExceptionContext.is_disconnect` says that "by assigning to this flag, a 'disconnect' event which then results in a connection and pool invalidation can be invoked or prevented".  However, `ExceptionContext declares __slots__ = ()` and only annotates `is_disconnect: bool` without a value. mypy therefore rejects the documented assignment as writing to an attribute that is not in `__slots__`. The same applies to invalidate_pool_on_disconnect, which the docs also describe as assignable.  The concrete class passed at runtime, `sqlalchemy.engine.base.ExceptionContextImpl`, lists both names in its `__slots__`, so annotating the handler with `ExceptionContextImpl` type-checks, but that class is not part of the documented API.  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine, event from sqlalchemy.engine.interfaces import ExceptionContext  engine = create_engine("sqlite://")   @event.listens_for(engine, "handle_error") def mark_disconnect(context: ExceptionContext) -> None:     context.is_disconnect = True ```  ### Error ``` repro.py:9: error: Trying to assign name "is_disconnect" that is not in "__slots__" of type "sqlalchemy.engine.interfaces.ExceptionContext"  [misc] Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file) ```  ### Versions  - OS: macOS - Python: 3.13.7 - SQLAlchemy: 2.0.52 (the ExceptionContext declaration on main is unchanged) - Type checker: mypy 1.10.0 (reproduces with and without --strict)  ### Additional context  Docs referenced: - https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/

title: regression in 2.1: selectinload ignores extra primaryjoin criteria on many-to-many relationships
body: ### Describe the bug  In 2.1.x, using `selectinload` on a many-to-many relationship whose `primaryjoin` includes an extra condition beyond the key (e.g. like a `deleted` column used for soft-deletes) loads rows that should have been excluded by the condition. The default lazy load respects the condition.  In 2.0.x, both the `selectinload` and lazy load agreed; tracing for this regression points to PR #13278, specifically the `omit_join` optimization for the `many-to-many` relationship. The optimized query uses the key column pairs + `secondaryjoin`, which means anything else in the `primaryjoin` doesn't reach the SQL; the function `_JoinCondition.secondary_covers_parent_primary_key` only checks the `synchronize_pairs`.  Looking at the original PR, a `secondaryjoin` with a filter were tested but not a `primaryjoin` with a filter. The safety flag above was added following review, but only checked against primary-key coverage and not any extra criteria.     ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.1.1  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  Reproduced using pysqlite, first found using psycopg3  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  SQLite (reproduction), PostgreSQL  ### Python Version  3.12  ### Operating system  OSX  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import Boolean from sqlalchemy import Column from sqlalchemy import create_engine from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey from sqlalchemy import Integer from sqlalchemy import select from sqlalchemy import Table from sqlalchemy import and_ from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload from sqlalchemy.orm import Session   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   a_b = Table(     "a_b",     Base.metadata,     Column("a_id", ForeignKey("a.id")),     Column("b_id", Forei

title: sqlalchemy 2.1: str(select(...)) with an Enum column leads to a memory leak
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13624
Originally posted by **uriyyo** September 30, 2026 Hi, I might have found a potential memory leak. I noticed that my app crashes because of OOM every N hours, after some debugging I have found that there are a lot of enum SQLAlchemy schema objects sitting in memory. Minimal code to reproduce this issue: ```py import enum import sqlalchemy as sa class Color(enum.Enum): red = "red" metadata = sa.MetaData() table = sa.Table("t", metadata, sa.Column("color", sa.Enum(Color))) for _ in range(3): str(sa.select(table)) print(len(metadata.get_schema_objects(sa.Enum))) ``` This is a regression, this issue is not present in the latest 2.0 version. From a quick look it looks like str(stmt) is creating a new enum type object on every call and adding it to the table's MetaData, where it never gets deleted, so it just accumulates and causes OOM.

body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13620  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **cooper-oai** September 30, 2026</sup> ### Describe the bug  Cancelling an `engine.connect()` task twice while it recycles an existing asyncpg connection can permanently consume a pool slot. title: 2.1: TypeError "Expected tuple, got Row" when DBAPI returns tuple subclasses (e.g. databricks-sql-connector)
body: ### Describe the bug  Starting in 2.1, fetching rows fails with `TypeError: Expected tuple, got Row` when the DBAPI cursor returns rows that are a **subclass** of `tuple` rather than a plain `tuple`. The Databricks SQL connector (`databricks-sql-connector`) does this: its `databricks.sql.types.Row` subclasses `tuple`, so every query through `databricks-sqlalchemy` fails on SQLAlchemy 2.1.x. It works on 2.0.x.  It looks like this comes from 95ab6ed79c7956bcf6ad7e18ad6241f0c9c90f23 ("perf tuning of `BaseRow`"), which changed the row construction from  ```python data_tuple: Tuple[Any, ...] = (     _apply_processors(processors, data)     if processors is not None     else tuple(data) ) ```  to  ```python self._set_attrs(     parent,     key_to_index,     (         _apply_processors(processors, data)         if processors is not None         else data if isinstance(data, tuple) else tuple(data)     ), ) ```  A tuple subclass passes `isinstance(data, tuple)`, so it is passed through as-is, but the compiled `BaseRow` then requires an exact `tuple` and raises. title: TypeDecorator.comparator_factory creates a new class with type() on every access
body: ### Describe the bug  `TypeDecorator.comparator_factory` is a property that calls `TypeDecorator._create_td_comparator_type()` on every access, and that function builds a brand new `TDComparator` class with `type()` each time. Nothing is cached, so every new column expression against a `TypeDecorator` type pays for creating a class (about 7.5 us here), and each of those classes can only be freed by the cyclic GC.  This looks like it has been this way since the 2013 `sqlalchemy.sql` refactor. The only thing I found that depends on the closure over `impl` is the pickling support added in fa5682157 (#12002).  ### To Reproduce  ```python import timeit  import sqlalchemy from sqlalchemy import Integer from sqlalchemy import column from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column from sqlalchemy.types import TypeDecorator   class Cents(TypeDecorator):     impl = Integer     cache_ok = True   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Item(Base):     __tablename__ = "item"      id = mapped_column(Integer, primary_key=True)     price = mapped_column(Cents)   def best(fn, number):     return min(timeit.repeat(fn, number=number, repeat=7)) / number * 1e6   cents = Cents() print(sqlalchemy.__version__, sqlalchemy.__file__) print(     "same class on repeated access:",     cents.comparator_factory is cents.comparator_factory, ) print(f"cents.comparator_factory     {best(lambda: cents.comparator_factory, 20000):7.2f} us") print(f"column('x', Cents()) * 2     {best(lambda: column('x', Cents()) * 2, 5000):7.2f} us") print(f"Item.price * 2               {best(lambda: Item.price * 2, 5000):7.2f} us") print(f"Item.price == 5              {best(lambda: Item.price == 5, 5000):7.2f} us") ```  ### Results  main at 749086adb, CPython 3.14.7, Linux x86_64, no database involved. "pure" means `DISABLE_SQLALCHEMY_CEXT_RUNTIME=1`; I used it for the before/after comparison because my patched checkout has no compiled extensions.  ```

title: tstring() string portions should not parse :param bind names or \: escapes
body: The literal string portions of a `tstring()` template are each turned into a `TextClause`, so all of the `text()` parsing rules apply to them: `:name` is taken to be a bound parameter, and `\:` is the escape for a literal colon. None of this is documented or tested for `tstring()`, and it doesn't fit how t-strings work:  ```python from sqlalchemy import tstring, create_engine  x = 5 e = create_engine("sqlite://") with e.connect() as conn:     # colon inside a quoted SQL literal is parsed as a bound parameter     # renders: SELECT ?, 'time is ?'     # raises: A value is required for bind parameter 'now'     conn.execute(tstring(t"SELECT {x}, 'time is :now'"))      # works, but is undocumented; the parameter can't be typed since     # TString.bindparams() is not supported     conn.execute(tstring(t"SELECT {x}, :p"), {"p": 10})      # the escape is an invalid Python escape sequence in a non-raw     # t-string: SyntaxWarning on Python 3.14     conn.execute(tstring(t"SELECT {x}, '\:p'")) ```  In a t-string, parameters come from interpolation, so everything outside `{}` should be rendered as-is. The string portions will therefore no longer be scanned for `:name` parameters and will have no escaping rules. The only processing will be what the dialect needs, such as doubling `%` for the `pyformat` and `format` paramstyles. A named parameter can still be used explicitly with `{bindparam("p")}`, or `text()` semantics can be applied to a fragment with `{text(":p")}`.  This is a behavioral change to 2.1.0 / 2.1.1 and is targeted for 2.1.2.

title: PostgreSQL reflection drops columns from composite primary keys when a constraint and a commented object share an OID
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13614  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **Elaskinok** September 28, 2026</sup> ## Describe the bug  On PostgreSQL, `_constraint_query`, `_foreing_key_query` and `_check_constraint_query` outer-join `pg_description` on `objoid = pg_constraint.oid` alone. OIDs are only unique within one catalog, so a comment on another object with the same OID as a constraint joins too, and the constraint's rows are repeated once per matching comment. #11961 fixed this for `_comment_query` only.  Since 2.0.41 (#10665), `_reflect_constraint` takes the first `indnkeyatts` entries of the aggregated column list as the key and the rest as INCLUDE columns. title: mssql+pyodbc DATETIMEOFFSET: years before 1000 are formatted without zero padding on Linux, year 1 is stored as 2001
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13608  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **yuansuentw** September 26, 2026</sup> Opening this as a discussion per the bug report guidelines; happy to turn it into an issue if it's confirmed.  ### Describe the bug  The mssql+pyodbc `DATETIMEOFFSET` bind processor (also used for `DateTime(timezone=True)`) formats values with `strftime("%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S.%f %z")`:  https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/rel_2_1_1/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/mssql/pyodbc.py#L493  `%Y` zero-padding is platform dependent, and on Linux (glibc) years before 1000 are not padded. So `datetime(1, 1, 1, tzinfo=utc)` is sent as `'1-01-01 00:00:00.000000 +00:00'`. SQL Server reads the one-digit year using its two-digit-year cutoff and **silently stores 2001-01-01**. Years 100–999 produce `'999-01-01 ...'`, which the server rejects.  `0001-01-01 00:00:00 +00:00` is a realistic value: it is .NET's `DateTimeOffset.MinValue`, commonly stored as an "unset" sentinel.  Formatting with `value.isoformat(sep=" ")` instead gives `'0001-01-01 00:00:00+00:00'`, which is zero-padded and already has the colon in the offset, so the `re.sub` would no longer be needed. I checked that SQL Server accepts these strings (including year 1, year 999 with microseconds and a `+08:00` offset) via pyodbc `execute` and `executemany`, with `fast_executemany` both on and off, and the stored values are exact.  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.1.1 (the same code is on main)  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  pyodbc 5.3.0, ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server 18.7.1.1  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  SQL Server 2022 (16.0.4210.1)  ### Python Version  3.13.2  ### Operating system  Linux (Ubuntu 24.04)  ### To Reproduce  ```python import datetime  from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, MetaData, Table, create_engine, insert, select from sqlalchemy.dialects import mssql  utc = datetime.timezone.utc  # 1. title: literal_binds: a string literal containing %(name)s is rendered as '?' (qmark) or '%%s' (format) in 2.x
body: ### Describe the bug  When a statement is compiled with `literal_binds=True` for a dialect whose paramstyle is `qmark` or `format`, a string literal whose text contains `%(name)s` is rewritten: `'%(k)s'` becomes `'?'` (qmark, e.g. SQLite) or `'%%s'` (format, e.g. MySQL). The rendered SQL then compares against a different value and silently returns the wrong rows. `pyformat` (PostgreSQL) is not affected, and SQLAlchemy 1.4.54 renders all three correctly.  It looks like `SQLCompiler._process_positional` applies `_positional_pattern` to the whole compiled string, including the text of string literals rendered inline.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.52 and 2.1.1 (1.4.54 is not affected)  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  sqlite3 (stdlib)  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  SQLite 3.50.4  ### Python Version  3.11  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python import sqlalchemy as sa from sqlalchemy.dialects import mysql, postgresql  engine = sa.create_engine("sqlite://") t = sa.Table("t", sa.MetaData(), sa.Column("x", sa.String)) t.create(engine) with engine.begin() as c:     c.execute(t.insert(), [{"x": "%(k)s"}, {"x": "?"}])  stmt = sa.select(t.c.x).where(t.c.x == "%(k)s") sql = str(stmt.compile(engine, compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})) print(sql) with engine.connect() as c:     print(c.exec_driver_sql(sql).fetchall()) for d in (mysql.dialect(), postgresql.dialect()):     print(stmt.compile(dialect=d, compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})) ```  ### Error  No exception. title: Fix duplicate normalized extra in the 2.1.0 source distribution
body: ## Describe the bug  The SQLAlchemy 2.1.0 source distribution cannot be installed with uv because its `pyproject.toml` declares two optional extras that normalize to `mssql-pymssql`. The 2.1.0 wheel installs, but source-only installation fails before the build starts.  ## Versions and environment  - SQLAlchemy: 2.1.0 - Python: CPython 3.14.4 - OS: macOS arm64 (the failing Kitaru CI jobs ran on Linux) - DBAPI and database: not applicable; installation fails before import  ## To reproduce  ```bash UV_CACHE_DIR=/tmp/sqlalchemy-210-sdist-repro uv run --no-config --no-project --no-binary-package sqlalchemy --with sqlalchemy==2.1.0 python -c 'import sqlalchemy; print(sqlalchemy.__version__)' ```  ## Error  ```text Building sqlalchemy==2.1.0 × Failed to download and build `sqlalchemy==2.1.0` ├─▶ Failed to parse: .../sqlalchemy/2.1.0/.../src/pyproject.toml ╰─▶ TOML parse error at line 45, column 1        |     45 | [project.optional-dependencies]        | ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^     duplicate normalized extra name `mssql-pymssql` ```  Three Kitaru plugin artifact CI shards hit this when 2.1.0 was published, before its wheels were available. A fresh source-only reproduction still fails. Kitaru temporarily capped its server extra at `<2.1` in [PR #1197](https://github.com/zenml-io/kitaru/pull/1197).

title: named_dollar paramstyle
body: ### Describe the use case  asyncpg uses the `numeric_dollar` paramstyle, but [SQLite](https://sqlite.org/lang_expr.html#parameters) has an affordance for a `named_dollar` style as well.  There is precedent for this naming, in [SQL Params](https://python-sql-parameters.readthedocs.io/en/latest/sqlparams.html#:~:text=named_dollar).  It would be nice to be able to add this style to SQLAlchemy for completeness.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  SQLite.  Also, maybe, one day, PostgreSQL? While client parameters are still exclusively numbered, [named SQL function parameters](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/18/xfunc-sql.html#XFUNC-SQL-FUNCTION-ARGUMENTS) were added to PostgreSQL 9.2, which suggests maybe such a thing could be added to the driver interface eventually?   ### Example Use  N/A  ### Additional context  I'm trying to define a type-safe "paramstyle" parameter in DBXS while supporting this paramstyle for completeness, and SQLAlchemy support means I can't actually include it in the published type without triggering potential type errors.  I don't really *need* it but it would be nice to get it added in advance of any driver deciding this is a good way to do things, so this should be considered low-priority if at all.

title: `_extract_mapped_subtype` seems to be broken in Python 3.14 without `from __future__ import annotations`
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13601  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **Daverball** September 22, 2026</sup> Currently `_extract_mapped_subtype` seems to make the mistaken assumption that the only way a `NameError` occurs in `de_stringify_annotation` is if the outside of the annotation is a string. But this is no longer the case with Python 3.14+ without `from __future__ import annotations`, it could very easily be a `ForwardRef` too.  This means [this line](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/6e870776cbf298b541877af9b6caf73bc86b379e/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py#L2459), which is supposed to ignore errors on annotations that are not wrapped in `Mapped`, will now error on any annotation that results in a `NameError` when trying to de-stringify it.  This line needs to take into account whether `raw_annotation` is a string, if it's a `ForwardRef` it should check `__forward_arg__` instead and if it's not its `typing.get_origin` should match `Mapped`. title: test_from_linter.py: assert start == start is always true after the loop variable is reassigned
body: Three tests in `test/sql/test_from_linter.py` reuse the loop variable as the tuple-unpack target, so the assertion that's supposed to check the returned value ends up comparing the same freshly-assigned object to itself:  ```python def test_disconnect_between_ab_cd(self):     ...     for start in self.a, self.b:         froms, start = find_unmatching_froms(query, start)         assert start == start         assert froms == {self.c, self.d} ```  By the time `assert start == start` runs, `start` has already been overwritten by the tuple unpack on the line above, so both sides of `==` are the same object. The assertion passes no matter what `find_unmatching_froms` returns as its second element, so it isn't actually checking anything.  The same file shows what this was clearly meant to look like, in the non-loop calls right after each of these loops:  ```python froms, start = find_unmatching_froms(query, self.c) assert start == self.c ```  Here the comparison is against the value that was passed in, which is a real check. The loop versions lost that because the loop variable and the unpack target share the same name.  Minimal illustration of why this always passes, independent of SQLAlchemy:  ```python def demo(start):     froms, start = ("whatever", "anything, does not matter at all")     assert start == start  # always true, start was just reassigned above     return froms  demo("self.a")  # passes no matter what demo() returns as its 2nd element ```  Affected spots (current main): - `test_disconnect_between_ab_cd`, both loops (lines ~278-284) - `test_c_and_d_both_disconnected`, the loop (line ~294-296) - `test_right_nested_join_with_an_issue`, the loop (line ~401-403)  I checked with a quick mutation test: if I make `find_unmatching_froms` return `None` for the second tuple element instead of the real `start`, `test_disconnect_between_ab_cd` still passes -- its two loops give zero coverage of that return value. The other two tests happen to also make a non-loop call

title: 2.0.x free-threaded wheels re-enable the GIL on import; Cython extensions lack freethreading_compatible
body: ### Describe the bug  The free-threaded (`cp313t` / `cp314t`) wheels published for SQLAlchemy 2.0.x re-enable the GIL as soon as SQLAlchemy is imported. The Cython extensions in `sqlalchemy.cyextension` are compiled without the `freethreading_compatible` directive, so they don't declare `Py_mod_gil`, and CPython turns the GIL back on when the first of them loads:  ``` <frozen importlib._bootstrap>:491: RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load module 'sqlalchemy.cyextension.collections', which has not declared that it can run safely without the GIL. To override this behavior and keep the GIL disabled (at your own risk), run with PYTHON_GIL=0 or -Xgil=0. ```  As a result, any application importing SQLAlchemy 2.0.x on a free-threaded interpreter is silently running with the GIL enabled.  The 2.1 series is not affected: `setup.py` on `main` sets `cython_directives["freethreading_compatible"] = True` for Python 3.13 and above. That change was never backported to `rel_2_0`.  The same warning is visible in the cp314t wheel build logs for 2.0.53, e.g. https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/actions/runs/34894069738/job/104143548730  ### To Reproduce  On a free-threaded CPython 3.14 (confirmed on 3.14.3t and 3.14.6t using the `manylinux_2_28` images used by cibuildwheel):  ``` python3.14t -m venv venv venv/bin/pip install --only-binary :all: "sqlalchemy==2.0.51" venv/bin/python -c "import sys, sqlalchemy.orm; print(sys._is_gil_enabled())" ```  ### Error  ``` RuntimeWarning: The global interpreter lock (GIL) has been enabled to load module 'sqlalchemy.cyextension.collections', ... title: mssql+mssqlpython raises arithmetic overflow for Decimal values with mssql-python 1.15
body: mssql-python 1.15.0 (released 2026-09-11) changed how it binds Python `Decimal` values ([microsoft/mssql-python#742](https://github.com/microsoft/mssql-python/pull/742)). It now sends every `Decimal` as `SQL_NUMERIC`. Before, values within MONEY range were sent as `VARCHAR`. The `mssql+mssqlpython` dialect in SQLAlchemy 2.1 doesn't work correctly with this version.  The dialect still turns very large and very small `Decimal` values into strings before binding, a workaround inherited from the pyodbc dialect. With 1.14 and earlier this was harmless, since most `Decimal` values reached SQL Server as varchar anyway. With 1.15 those strings sit alongside real numeric parameters, and SQL Server converts them to the narrower numeric type. Statements such as a multi-row INSERT then fail:  ```python import decimal  from sqlalchemy import Column from sqlalchemy import create_engine from sqlalchemy import Integer from sqlalchemy import MetaData from sqlalchemy import Numeric from sqlalchemy import Table  e = create_engine("mssql+mssqlpython://scott:tiger@host/test?Encrypt=No")  m = MetaData() t = Table(     "t",     m,     Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),     Column("x", Numeric(38, 12)), )  with e.begin() as conn:     m.drop_all(conn)     m.create_all(conn)     conn.execute(         t.insert(),         [             {"x": decimal.Decimal("31943874831932418390.01")},             {"x": decimal.Decimal("87673.594069654243")},         ],     ) ```  With mssql-python 1.15.0:  ``` sqlalchemy.exc.DataError: (mssql_python.exceptions.DataError) Driver Error: Numeric value out of range; DDBC Error: [Microsoft][SQL Server]Arithmetic overflow error converting varchar to data type numeric. [SQL: INSERT INTO t (x) VALUES (%(x__0)s), (%(x__1)s)] [parameters: {'x__0': '31943874831932418390.01', 'x__1': Decimal('87673.594069654243')}] ```  The same script succeeds with mssql-python 1.14.0. title: aliased() of a with_polymorphic() entity discards its polymorphic selectable and mappers
body: Sub-issue of #13581. The original plan was to deprecate this behavior in 2.1 (#13582, now closed) and change it in 2.2. It is instead fixed directly in 2.0.x and 2.1, in the same change as #13583.  ### Current behavior  Calling `aliased()` with no explicit selectable against a `with_polymorphic()` entity produces a plain alias of the **base** entity. The polymorphic selectable, the additional mappers, `innerjoin` and `name` are all discarded:  ```py wp = with_polymorphic(Person, [Engineer, Manager]) ap = aliased(wp)  select(ap) # SELECT people_1.id, people_1.name, people_1.type FROM people AS people_1  select(ap.name).where(ap.Engineer.lang == "py") # SELECT people_1.name FROM people AS people_1, engineers # WHERE engineers.lang = :lang_1        <- cartesian product, all rows ```  Consequences:  * with `innerjoin=True` or a custom `selectable=`, rows the   `with_polymorphic()` excludes are returned * criteria against `aliased(wp).Engineer.<attr>` render against the   unaliased subclass table. In WHERE they have no effect and produce a   Cartesian product; in an ON clause the statement fails. * subclass columns are not loaded up front, so they lazy-load per object * `name=` is ignored for `aliased=True` entities  ### Fix  `aliased()` with no explicit selectable, called against a `with_polymorphic()` entity, produces a new `with_polymorphic()` entity. It re-aliases the entity's own selectable and carries along `with_polymorphic_mappers`, the discriminator, `represents_outer_join` (that is, `innerjoin`) and `name`.  Rendered SQL changes for these constructs. The default `flat=False` renders a subquery around the polymorphic join, and `flat=True` renders individually aliased joined tables. For the outer-join forms the rows returned are unchanged, with fewer lazy loads. For `innerjoin=True` and custom selectables, only the rows the `with_polymorphic()` selects are returned.  ### Steps  Applies to Gerrit 6964 (main) and 6965 (rel_2_0).  1. title: aliased() of an aliased CTE / aliased subquery entity drops the selectable; CTE.alias() of an alias renders undefined name (2.0.x / 2.1 fix)
body: Sub-issue of #13581, covering the part of that issue that can be fixed in 2.0.x and 2.1 without changing behavior for existing correct usage. See #13581 for the full report, reproduction and analysis.  ### Scope  **ORM**: `aliased()` with no explicit selectable, called against an existing `aliased()` entity, aliases that entity's own selectable instead of the mapped table when the selectable is anything other than plain aliases of the mapped table:  * a CTE, or an alias of a CTE * an alias of a subquery, i.e. `aliased()` applied a second time * a lateral subquery * a table sample  In addition:  * `name=` is applied when the existing selectable is a subquery (currently ignored) * the `adapt_on_names` setting of the existing entity is carried along  Entities that are only aliases of the mapped table, including flat aliases of joined inheritance, keep their current code path, so rendered SQL and anonymous alias names are unchanged.  **Core**:  * `cte.alias("a1").alias("a2")` renders `c AS a2` against the original CTE, rather than `a1 AS a2`, which refers to a name not present in the WITH clause * `Join._anonymous_fromclause(name=..., flat=True)` against a join of anonymously named aliases no longer embeds the anonymous label within a literal name, which failed with `KeyError` at execution  ### Related  `aliased()` against a `with_polymorphic()` entity, which currently discards the polymorphic selectable, is fixed in the same change under #13584.

Entities produced by `with_polymorphic()` were deliberately left with their existing behavior so that the fix can be backported to 2.0 without changing results for them. title: PostgreSQL get_indexes reports an invalid index (failed CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY) as a normal index
body: ### Describe the bug  A `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` that fails (unique violation, cancel, crash) leaves the index in `pg_index` with `indisvalid = false`. Postgres ignores it for planning, but reflection returns it exactly like a healthy index.  The PG index query selects `indisunique`, `indoption`, `indpred`, `indnkeyatts`, `indnullsnotdistinct` and filters on `indisprimary` only; `indisvalid` and `indisready` are never read (`lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/base.py`, `_index_query`: 2.0.52 lines 4885-4917, 2.1.0rc2 lines 5269-5301). The columns are already declared on `pg_catalog.pg_index` (`pg_catalog.py` lines 183 and 185).  Consequence: Inspector callers and Alembic autogenerate compare the reflected dict to metadata, find it equal, and emit nothing, so the broken index is never rebuilt.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/21/dialects/postgresql.html#postgresql-index-reflection  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.52 and 2.1.0rc2  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg 3.3  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 15  ### Python Version  3.12  ### Operating system  macOS  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine, inspect, text  e = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg://...") with e.connect().execution_options(isolation_level="AUTOCOMMIT") as c:     c.execute(text("CREATE TABLE t (id int primary key, x int)"))     c.execute(text("INSERT INTO t VALUES (1, 1), (2, 1)"))     try:         c.execute(text("CREATE UNIQUE INDEX CONCURRENTLY ix_t_x ON t (x)"))     except Exception as err:         print("build failed as intended:", type(err).__name__)     print(c.execute(text("SELECT indisvalid FROM pg_index WHERE indexrelid = 'ix_t_x'::regclass")).scalar())     print(inspect(c).get_indexes("t")) ```  ### Error  ``` build failed as intended: IntegrityError False [{'name': 'ix_t_x', 'unique': True, 'column_names': ['x']}] ```  Same result wh

title: False SAWarning on second pickle round-trip of an ORM instance with a per-instance lazy loader
body: Reported by @BlastyCZ in discussion https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13573; confirmed against main.  `_LoadLazyAttribute.__getstate__()` warns whenever `self.extra_criteria is not None`, but the state it emits sets `extra_criteria` to `()` rather than `None`:  ```python     def __getstate__(self):         if self.extra_criteria is not None:             util.warn(                 "Can't reliably serialize a lazyload() option that "                 "contains additional criteria; please use eager loading "                 "for this case"             )         return {             "key": self.key,             "strategy_key": self.strategy_key,             "loadopt": self.loadopt,             "extra_criteria": (),         } ```  The instance-level callable is created with `extra_criteria=None` when no criteria are present (`strategies.py`, `_LazyLoader.create_row_processor`), so the first pickle is silent. title: we dont close on GC connections that were detached (and weren't closed).  should we?
body: ### Describe the bug  A connection that has been detached from its pool with `Connection.detach()` / `PoolProxiedConnection.detach()` and is then garbage collected without being explicitly closed never has its DBAPI connection closed.  The connection is leaked until the DBAPI itself reclaims it, if it ever does.  Detaching hands ownership of the DBAPI connection to the fairy, and the explicit close path handles this correctly: `_ConnectionFairy._checkin()` calls `_finalize_fairy()` with `connection_record=None`, which takes the `detach = connection_record is None` branch and calls `pool._close_connection()`.  The garbage collection path never reaches that branch.  The finalizer established for the fairy at checkout closes over the *record*, and `_ConnectionFairy.detach()` clears `_ConnectionRecord.fairy_ref`, so when the fairy is later collected the cleanup is skipped entirely.  The connection is not closed, and for asyncio dialects the "garbage collector is trying to clean up non-checked-in connection" warning that a non-detached abandoned connection would produce is not emitted either. title: Fresh parent row silently dropped from flush when co-flushed with multiple fresh FK-dependent child rows (Postgres, both asyncpg and psycopg2)
body: # Title  Fresh parent row silently dropped from flush when co-flushed with multiple fresh FK-dependent child rows (Postgres, both asyncpg and psycopg2)  # Body  ### Describe the bug  When a session has a freshly-added parent row and two freshly-added child rows (each with a FK to the parent) pending in the same flush, the parent's `INSERT` is sometimes never emitted at all — only the children's `INSERT` runs, which then fails a FK constraint because the parent row was never written. `sqlalchemy.inspect()` on the parent object confirms it is correctly `pending`/`db.new` right up to the point of `commit()`; the dependency-ordering/topological-sort step that decides what to flush and in what order appears to drop it rather than ordering it first.  Confirmed on Postgres 15 with **both** `psycopg2` (sync) and `asyncpg` (async) — not driver- or async-specific. **Does not reproduce on SQLite** (`aiosqlite`) with the identical model/session code, so it appears specific to how the unit-of-work handles this shape against the Postgres dialect.  Also confirmed **not** related to `insertmanyvalues` batching — forcing `insertmanyvalues_page_size=1` (one INSERT per row, no multi-row VALUES) still reproduces it.  ### To Reproduce  ```python import os  from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, String, create_engine from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, Session, mapped_column   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Parent(Base):     __tablename__ = "repro_parent"     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50))   class Child(Base):     __tablename__ = "repro_child"     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     parent_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("repro_parent.id"))     name: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(50))   engine = create_engine(os.environ["PG_URL"], echo=True)  with engine.begin() as conn:     Base.metadata.drop_all(conn)     Base.metadata.create_all(conn)  with Session(engine)

title: DBAPI connection is stranded when the connect event raises
body: ### Summary  When the pool creates a new DBAPI connection, `_ConnectionRecord.__connect()` assigns it to `self.dbapi_connection` and *then* fires the `first_connect` / `connect` events. If anything raised by those events escapes, the exception propagates out of `_ConnectionRecord.__init__()` with a live connection attached to a record that nothing owns. `Pool._close_connection()` is never called for it — not `do_close`, not `do_terminate`. The connection is stranded.  (The pool slot itself is fine: `QueuePool._do_get()` calls `_dec_overflow()` when `_create_connection()` raises, so capacity is returned. The pool does not starve.)  The `connect` event is where `dialect.initialize()` runs, so this is the window a great deal of per-connection setup lives in.  This affects **every async dialect we ship**: asyncpg, psycopg, aiosqlite, aiomysql, asyncmy, oracledb async and aioodbc.  It is not specific to cancellation, and not specific to asyncio — any exception from a `connect` event handler does it. On a sync driver the damage is hidden, because dropping the last reference to the DBAPI object closes the socket. Some async drivers happen to do the same; others do not, and the consequences differ sharply between them (see Impact).  Reported as connection "corruption" under `asyncio.Task` cancellation in discussion #13542. The connection is not corrupt; it is leaked, and what the reporter saw was psycopg's `ResourceWarning` at collection time.  ### MCVE  Any exception from a `connect` handler reproduces it, so the repro does not need asyncio cancellation at all:  ```python import asyncio import gc import sys  from sqlalchemy import event from sqlalchemy import select from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine  URL = sys.argv[1]  created, closed = set(), set()   def instrument(engine):     """count the DBAPI connections the pool creates, and the ones it closes"""     pool = engine.pool     real_create, real_close = pool._invoke_creator, pool._close_connection

title: SQLite reflection drops STRICT and WITHOUT ROWID; Table.kwargs is empty after autoload
body: ### Describe the bug  Reflecting a SQLite table created with `STRICT` and/or `WITHOUT ROWID` produces a `Table` whose `.kwargs` does not carry `sqlite_strict`/`sqlite_with_rowid` at all -- nothing in reflection surfaces either modifier back onto the `Table` object, even though the dialect can render both (`SQLiteDDLCompiler` appends `"WITHOUT ROWID"` / `"STRICT"` to `table_options` when compiling `CREATE TABLE`) and even *parses past* them during column reflection.  `Dialect.get_table_options()` exists for exactly this ("Return a dictionary of options specified when the table of the given name was created"), but SQLite's dialect doesn't implement it, so it falls through to the base `Dialect.get_table_options` and raises `NotImplementedError`.  Separately, `SQLiteDialect.get_columns()` already parses the raw `CREATE TABLE` text from `sqlite_master` for generated-column handling, and its own regex explicitly matches (and discards) the trailing modifier:  https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/main/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/sqlite/base.py#L2417-L2426  ```python match = re.match(     (         r"create table .*?\((.*)\)"         r"(?:\s*,?\s*(?:WITHOUT\s+ROWID|STRICT))*$"     ),     tablesql.strip(),     re.DOTALL | re.IGNORECASE, ) assert match, f"create table not found in {tablesql}" tablesql = match.group(1).strip() ```  Only `match.group(1)` (the column list) is kept; whether `WITHOUT ROWID`/`STRICT` was actually present is never captured or returned to the caller. title: IdentifierPreparer.quote() raises IndexError on an empty identifier, reachable through reflection
body: ### Describe the bug  `IdentifierPreparer.quote("")` raises `IndexError: string index out of range` from `_requires_quotes`, which reads `value[0]` without checking for an empty string:  ```python def _requires_quotes(self, value: str) -> bool:     lc_value = value.lower()     return (         lc_value in self.reserved_words         or value[0] in self.illegal_initial_characters   # <-- IndexError when value == ""         ... ```  The reason this is worth reporting rather than dismissing as "don't use an empty name" is that **reflection can hand you one**. SQLite accepts `CREATE TABLE "" (...)`, `MetaData.reflect()` reflects it happily, and only when the reflected table is *used* does the compiler raise a bare `IndexError` with no indication of what was wrong.  It also looks like the same failure that was reported in #5919, where a naming convention produced a blank constraint name. That was fixed on the producing side; the preparer still raises `IndexError` for any other route to a blank identifier.  `Column("")` is already rejected with a clear message — *"Column must be constructed with a non-blank name or assign a non-blank .name"* — so blank identifiers are handled deliberately in at least one place. `Table("")` is accepted and then fails on use.  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import MetaData, create_engine, pool, select  e = create_engine("sqlite://", poolclass=pool.StaticPool) with e.begin() as c:     c.exec_driver_sql('CREATE TABLE "" (c INTEGER)')  md = MetaData() md.reflect(bind=e)          # succeeds, table is reflected under the name "" print(sorted(md.tables))    # ['']  select(md.tables[""]).compile(e) ```  Direct routes to the same line:  ```python e.dialect.identifier_preparer.quote("")                 # IndexError Table("", MetaData(), Column("c", Integer)).create(e)   # IndexError ```  ### Error  ```   File "lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py", line 8096, in _requires_quotes     or value[0] in self.illegal_initial_characters        ~~~~~^

title: Bind parameter name escaping is not injective; distinct params can silently collide
body: Reported by @alonfaraj in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/13533.  `SQLCompiler.bindname_escape_characters` maps several distinct characters - `.`, `[`, `]` and space - all onto `_`.  The mapping is therefore not injective, and two logically distinct bind parameters can escape to the same rendered parameter name.  The collision is silent: one value simply overwrites the other, so the statement executes with the wrong data.  ### Repro  ```python from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, MetaData, Table, select from sqlalchemy.engine.default import DefaultDialect  d = DefaultDialect(paramstyle="named")  t = Table(     "t",     MetaData(),     Column("a.b", Integer),     Column("a_b", Integer), )  stmt = select(t).where(t.c["a.b"] == 111).where(t.c["a_b"] == 222)  comp = stmt.compile(dialect=d) print(" ".join(str(comp).split())) print(comp.construct_params()) ```  Output:  ``` SELECT t."a.b", t.a_b FROM t WHERE t."a.b" = :a_b_1 AND t.a_b = :a_b_1 {'a_b_1': 222} ```  Both the escaped name `a.b_1 -> a_b_1` and the naturally occurring name `a_b_1` render as the same placeholder, and only one value survives.  Two names that both require escaping collide the same way - e.g. columns `"a.b"` and `"a b"` both produce `a_b_1`:  ``` SELECT t2."a.b", t2."a b" FROM t2 WHERE t2."a.b" = :a_b_1 AND t2."a b" = :a_b_1 {'a_b_1': 222} ```  With a positional paramstyle the damage shows up in `positiontup`, where the same key is emitted for both positions:  ``` SELECT t3."a.b", t3.a_b FROM t3 WHERE t3."a.b" = ? AND t3.a_b = ? params: {'a_b_1': 222}   positiontup: ['a.b_1', 'a.b_1'] ```  so the DBAPI receives one value twice.  This affects reads (a row that should match does not) and writes (a value can be stored in the wrong column).  ### Root cause  The disambiguating counter that SQLAlchemy applies to generated bind names already runs against a pre-escaped name, precisely so that names which would otherwise collide get distinct `_1` / `_2` suffixes - see `_anonymous_lab

title: catastrophic backtracking in sqlite foreign key reflection regex
body: while reflecting foreign keys on sqlite, `get_foreign_keys` scans the stored `CREATE TABLE` text (taken verbatim from `sqlite_master.sql`) with `FK_PATTERN` to recover constraint names and options. the referred-columns part of that pattern is `((?:(?:"[^"]+"|[a-z0-9_]+)\s*(?:,\s*)?)+)`, which repeats a bare column token `[a-z0-9_]+` while the separator `(?:,\s*)?` between iterations is optional. that is a nested quantifier of the `(a+)+` shape, so a run of word characters that is not eventually followed by a closing `)` can be split across the iterations in exponentially many ways, and the engine tries them all before giving up.  sqlite keeps the original text of a `CREATE TABLE` statement in `sqlite_master`, and the pattern is applied with `re.finditer` over the whole statement, so the run does not need to be an actual foreign key. any account that can create a table can leave such a run inside e.g. a column `DEFAULT` string literal, and later reflection of that ordinary table hangs.  a small reproduction:  ```python import time from sqlalchemy import create_engine, inspect, pool  e = create_engine("sqlite://", poolclass=pool.StaticPool) with e.begin() as c:     c.exec_driver_sql(         "CREATE TABLE t (id INTEGER, note TEXT DEFAULT "         "'FOREIGN KEY (a) REFERENCES b(" + ("a" * 26) + "')"     )  start = time.perf_counter() inspect(e).get_foreign_keys("t") print("get_foreign_keys took %.2fs" % (time.perf_counter() - start)) ```  timings scale exponentially with the length of the run (measured here): `n=18` 0.04s, `n=22` 0.56s, `n=26` 9.0s, and a couple more characters make it effectively hang.  the run can be made unambiguous by requiring a non-empty separator (a comma clause or whitespace) between column tokens, so a single word run only parses one way; valid foreign key clauses reflect exactly as before. happy to send a PR with a regression test if that's useful.

title: SQLite reflection loses constraint names when CONSTRAINT <name> is on its own line
body: The SQLite dialect recovers constraint names by regexp-parsing the stored `CREATE TABLE` text, since the `PRAGMA` calls don't report them. The patterns for PRIMARY KEY, UNIQUE and FOREIGN KEY in `dialects/sqlite/base.py` require `CONSTRAINT`, the name, and the following keyword to be separated by literal spaces only:  ```python PK_PATTERN = r'CONSTRAINT +(?:"(.+?)"|(\w+)) +PRIMARY KEY'  r'(?:CONSTRAINT +(?:"(.+?)"|(\w+)) +)?UNIQUE *\((.+?)\)'  FK_PATTERN = (     r'(?:CONSTRAINT +(?:"(.+?)"|(\w+)) +)?'     r"FOREIGN KEY *\( *(.+?) *\) +"     ... ) ```  `+` following a literal space matches more spaces but not a newline. SQLite stores DDL exactly as it was typed, so a table created with the constraint name on its own line reflects with `name: None`, silently.  The CHECK constraint pattern in the same module already uses `\s+` and is not affected.  **Repro**  ```python import sqlalchemy as sa  e = sa.create_engine("sqlite://") with e.begin() as c:     c.exec_driver_sql("CREATE TABLE a (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, x INTEGER)")     c.exec_driver_sql("""CREATE TABLE t (     id INTEGER NOT NULL,     x INTEGER,     CONSTRAINT my_pk         PRIMARY KEY (id),     CONSTRAINT my_uq         UNIQUE (x),     CONSTRAINT my_ck         CHECK (x > 0),     CONSTRAINT my_fk         FOREIGN KEY (x) REFERENCES a (x) )""")      insp = sa.inspect(c)     print("pk    :", insp.get_pk_constraint("t")["name"])     print("unique:", [u["name"] for u in insp.get_unique_constraints("t")])     print("check :", [u["name"] for u in insp.get_check_constraints("t")])     print("fk    :", [u["name"] for u in insp.get_foreign_keys("t")]) ```  Output:  ``` pk    : None unique: [None] check : ['my_ck'] fk    : [None] ```  Expected `my_pk`, `my_uq`, `my_ck`, `my_fk` throughout.
