title: Rendering of dialect options in postgres primary key constraint / factor out constraint rendering into components
body: ### Describe the bug  When creating a table in postgres, creating a `PrimaryKeyConstraint` with both `postgresql_include` and `deferrable` leads to generating wrong DDL, since sqlalchemy at the moment always adds the dialect options after the standard DDL generated, but postgres requires the `DEFERRED` options after the include (see https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html).  Probably the problem is [here](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/8bb8c1a6d6439380f682a57b92e3d1b0092250eb/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/base.py#L2360) since the include is always appended after the rendered DDL.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.43  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 16  ### Python Version  3.12  ### Operating system  any  ### To Reproduce  ```python m = sa.MetaData()  T = sa.Table(     "foo",     m,     sa.Column("id", sa.Integer, nullable=False),     sa.Column("col", sa.String, nullable=True),     # INDEXES     sa.PrimaryKeyConstraint(         "id",         postgresql_include=["col"],         deferrable=True,     ), )  engine = ...  # a postgresql engine m.create_all(engine) ```  ### Error  ``` Traceback (most recent call last):   File "/home/canton/source/mamba/source/server/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/base.py", line 1967, in _exec_single_context     self.dialect.do_execute(   File "/home/canton/source/mamba/source/server/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/sqlalchemy/engine/default.py", line 951, in do_execute     cursor.execute(statement, parameters)   File "/home/canton/source/mamba/source/server/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/psycopg/cursor.py", line 97, in execute     raise ex.with_traceback(None) psycopg.errors.SyntaxError: syntax error at or near "INCLUDE" LINE 5:  CONSTRAINT foo_pk PRIMARY KEY (id) DEFERRABLE INCLUDE (col) ```

title: sqlite reflection function `get_columns` has regex for generated column that does not match when table uses WITHOUT ROWID and/or STRICT
body: ### Describe the bug  When running reflection on SQLite tables, for generated columns it uses a regex match (https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/13f569fd615485c50e07f211e37e45d749ccc40d/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/sqlite/base.py#L2379). However, this match doesn't anticipate the possibility of WITHOUT ROWID and STRICT after the final parenthesis. Hence, the match fails. Consequences include that if you try to autogenerate an Alembic migration on an SQLite table that contains generated columns in a table that is strict and/or doesn't have rowid, an error will be trigerred. title: add some way to have unmapped dataclasses when making hierarchies with the decorator approach
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/12733  patch is at https://gerrit.sqlalchemy.org/c/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/+/6013  when using `@mapped_as_dataclass` we want to be able to have superclasses that are not mapped, but are dataclasses.    There's no built-in way to do this right now, as the example at #12733 at the top shows using the `MappedAsDataclass` superclass does not interact well with the class decorator (it can't really since metaclasses / `__init_subclass__()` runs much earlier than `@mapped_as_dataclass`, and our means of "mapping as a dataclass" requires that the "dataclass" step is run **in the middle** of the declarative process).   new decorator works as:  ```py  from sqlalchemy import Integer from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column from sqlalchemy.orm import registry from sqlalchemy.orm import unmapped_dataclass  @unmapped_dataclass(kw_only=True) class DataModel:     pass   @unmapped_dataclass(kw_only=True) class RelationshipsModel(DataModel):     __tablename__ = "relationships"      entity_id1: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     entity_id2: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)   some_target_tables_registry = registry()   @some_target_tables_registry.mapped_as_dataclass class Relationships(RelationshipsModel):     im_going_to_be_mapped = True     level: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(Integer)   Relationships(     entity_id1=1,     entity_id2=2,     level=1  )  ```

title: PostgreSQL: JSONB subscription syntax missing parentheses for JSONB-returning functions
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/12777  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **noirbee** August  1, 2025</sup> Following https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/10927 and https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/commit/2ac0c459669d0200a4d15162ffc0a8765c60cb07 , upgrading to sqlalchemy 2.0.42 now triggers syntax errors on PostgreSQL's side when using JSONB-returning functions, e.g. `jsonb_array_elements()`.  This is due to a quirk in PostgreSQL's own syntax, where the `["key"]`-style JSONB subscription cannot be used as readily as the `->` / `->>` one.  A good example is worth a thousand words:  ``` postgres=# SELECT jsonb_array_elements('[{"key": "value1"}, {"key": "value2"}]'::jsonb) -> 'key';  -- good old "->" syntax, no parentheses needed  ?column?  ----------  "value1"  "value2" (2 rows)  postgres=# SELECT jsonb_array_elements('[{"key": "value1"}, {"key": "value2"}]'::jsonb) ['key']; -- no parentheses around jsonb_array_elements(), fail ERROR:  syntax error at or near "[" LINE 1: ...ts('[{"key": "value1"}, {"key": "value2"}]'::jsonb) ['key'];                                                                ^ postgres=# SELECT (jsonb_array_elements('[{"key": "value1"}, {"key": "value2"}]'::jsonb)) ['key']; -- parentheses around jsonb_array_elements(), OK  jsonb_array_elements  ----------------------  "value1"  "value2" (2 rows) ```  Since 2ac0c459669d0200a4d15162ffc0a8765c60cb07, sqlalchemy now uses the `['key']` syntax everywhere; in most cases (i.e. JSONB column subscription) this pauses no problem, but when using functions with an explicit `type_=JSONB` it now always generates statement using the new syntax, which may fail.   ```python # sqla_postgresql_jsonb_subscript.py from sqlalchemy import __version__, func from sqlalchemy.dialects import postgresql from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Hello(Base):     __tablename_

This behavior occurs **only with PostgreSQL** and does **not** affect SQLite. The issue disappears when the Enum class is renamed to something that doesn't contain `"Interval"` (e.g., `IntrvalUnit`).    **Expected behavior** No changes should be detected in the second migration if the database schema and models remain unchanged.  **To Reproduce**  ```py # main.py from enum import StrEnum from sqlmodel import Field, SQLModel  class IntervalUnit(StrEnum):  # This triggers the issue     DAY = "day"     WEEK = "week"     MONTH = "month"     YEAR = "year"  class Task(SQLModel, table=True):     id: int = Field(default=None, nullable=False, primary_key=True)     interval_unit: IntervalUnit ```  ```bash # 1. Generate initial migration alembic revision --autogenerate -m "create simple table with 'Interval' enum"  # 2. Apply migration alembic upgrade head  # 3. Generate second migration (no changes made to code) alembic revision --autogenerate -m "second autogenerate without changes" ```  **Error**  The second autogenerated migration falsely detects a type change: ``` op.alter_column(     'task',     'interval_unit',     existing_type=postgresql.INTERVAL(),  # ???     type_=sa.Enum('DAY', 'WEEK', 'MONTH', 'YEAR', name='intervalunit'),     existing_nullable=False ) ```  **Versions.**  - OS: macOS 15.4.1 (24E263)  - Python: Python 3.13.5 (main, Jun 11 2025, 15:36:57) [Clang 17.0.0 (clang-1700.0.13.3)] on darwin  - Alembic: 1.16.4  **Additional context** The issue appears to be caused by Alembic or SQLAlchemy interpreting the Enum name IntervalUnit as PostgreSQL's native INTERVAL type.  This does not happen with SQLite.

title: Revisit inherit_schema implementation
body: After more talk around the https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/10594 and #12642 we came to the conclusion that the cleanest option is to go in another direction.  The main change is the following: Schema object are defined as belonging to a particular "parent", with a behaviour that matches that of sql. This means that tables have schema as parent, columns have tables as parent, etc.  What changes here is how Enum, Domain (and other eventual pg named types), Sequences etc behave. These all have the schema as parent, not the table why happen to be used in. This behavior is consistent with that of Table  In SQLAlchemy there isn't an object that maps 1 to 1 with a schema in sql, but the metadata comes close and we can think of as a "main" schema with optional references to extra schema. The main schema is the one passed to the `schema` kw arg.  In practice what this means is: - deprecated inherit_schema  - Enum, Doman, etc will attache themselves to a metadata automatically. - The schema of Enum, Domain, etc will be the same as the main schema of the metadata, unless specified differently. - The schema of the table they happen to be used in it's no longer relevant  TBD - metadata has a list of such objects and maybe we could have a method `get_schema_objects(type...)` to get collections of them

One instance of this is in the the module-level `__getattr__` definition here: https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/10ff201db40e069e8f90bb0883a916ba3d9cc96e/lib/sqlalchemy/__init__.py#L284-L292  When encountering this issue previously, the solution I found was to put the `def` inside an `if not TYPE_CHECKING:` block, which is ugly but seems to work.  ### To Reproduce  ```python from typing import TYPE_CHECKING  if TYPE_CHECKING:     from sqlalchemy import does_not_exist ```  ### Error  Running `mypy 1.10.0` over this file:-  Expected ``` error: Module "sqlalchemy" has no attribute "does_not_exist"  [attr-defined] ```   Actual ``` Success: no issues found in 1 source file ```  ### Versions  - Python: 3.12.2 - SQLAlchemy: 2.0.25 - mypy: 1.10.0   ### Additional context  The actual example we encountered was `from sqlalchemy import Session` (which should instead be `from sqlalchemy.orm [...]`)  `Session` was only used for type annotations in this particular file, hence in an `if TYPE_CHECKING:` block ([Ruff: typing-only-third-party-import (TC002)](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/rules/typing-only-third-party-import/#typing-only-third-party-import-tc002)) however this also prevented other linters (`ruff` and `pylint`) from spotting this issue.

title: No Public API Expose for Schema CRUD
body: ### Describe the use case  Recently, I was working with SQLAlchemy on a task that involved performing CRUD operations on schemas and creating tables within specific schemas. While exploring the public APIs exposed by both the `sqlalchemy.orm` and `sqlalchemy.sql` modules, I was unable to find any direct or intuitive classes/methods related to schema-level CRUD operations.  Eventually, I had to rely on internal components from the `sqlalchemy.schema` module (e.g., `CreateSchema`, `DropSchema`) to get the job done. However, these utilities are not prominently exposed or documented in the main public-facing API, which made the process a bit opaque.  Additionally, I noticed that there is **no support for altering schemas** (`AlterSchema` or equivalent doesn't exist), which makes schema-level management feel incomplete from a developer's perspective.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  - **PostgreSQL**   - **Driver**: `psycopg2`  ### Example Use  ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine, MetaData, Table, Column, Integer, String from sqlalchemy.schema import CreateSchema  engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg2://user:pass@localhost/dbname")  # Create a new schema with engine.connect() as conn:     conn.execute(CreateSchema("test_schema"))  # Create a table in that schema metadata = MetaData(schema="test_schema") test_table = Table(     "users", metadata,     Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),     Column("name", String), ) metadata.create_all(engine) ```  In this example, schema creation works via `CreateSchema`, but it's not discoverable unless one digs into `sqlalchemy.schema`. For other schema operations like **checking existence**, **renaming**, or **modifying**, there's no built-in or obvious path.  ### Additional context  The lack of an ``AlterSchema`` and the fragmented exposure of schema-level tools across internal APIs make this area of ``SQLAlchemy`` feel less polished than the rest. title: Invalid SQL emitted using aliased() and two tables with the same name in different schemas
body: ### Describe the bug  If two tables exist with the same name, one in the default database schema and the other in a custom schema, a `SELECT` statement querying both and using `aliased()` on one of them can sometimes cause SQLAlchemy 2.x to emit two `AS ...` clauses in a row, which is not valid SQL syntax.  MCVE:  ```python from sqlalchemy import select from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, aliased, mapped_column, Mapped  class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass  class Foo(Base):     __tablename__ = "foo"      a: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)  class OtherFoo(Base):     __tablename__ = "foo"     __table_args__ = {"schema": "other"}      b: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)  stmt = select(OtherFoo, aliased(Foo)) print(stmt.compile()) ```  Output:  ```sql SELECT other.foo.b, foo_1.a FROM other.foo, foo AS foo_2 AS foo_1 ```  Some notes:  - Reproducible in 2.0.0 through 2.0.39 - Not easily reproductible in 1.4.x - Inverting tables order in `select` has no impact ❌ - Using `flat` or `adapt_on_names` options in `aliased` has no impact ❌ - If one of the tables appear later in the query (eg. `select(aliased(Foo)).join(OtherFoo, true())`), the same bug occurs ❌ - If not using aliased tables (`select(Foo, OtherFoo)`), it works as expected ✅ - If the non-public table is the one aliased (`select(Foo, aliased(OtherFoo))`), it works as expected ✅ - If both tables are aliased (`select(aliased(Foo), aliased(OtherFoo))`), it works as expected ✅ - If explicitly specifying `__table_args__ = {"schema": "public"}` in `Foo`, it works as expected ✅ _(emits `public.foo` instead of `foo`)_  Thanks!  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/queryguide/api.html#sqlalchemy.orm.aliased  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.39  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  N/A  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  N/A  ### Python Version  3.12.2  ### Operating system  OSX  ### To

title: Support for GROUPS Frame Specification in Window Functions
body: Hello team,  ### Summary   Starting a new discussion ahead of PR (this would be my first to the project, so please bear with me). I would like to propose adding support for the **GROUPS** frame specification in SQLAlchemy’s window functions. Currently, SQLAlchemy supports only **RANGE** and **ROWS** as frame-spec clauses, but both **PostgreSQL** and **SQLite** (my main work drivers) have supported **GROUPS** for a good number of years.   https://www.sqlite.org/windowfunctions.html https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/functions-window.html    I wanted to integrate this functionality into SQLAlchemy, so I studied how **RANGE** and **ROWS** were implemented. It was fairly straightforward to extrapolate from these how **GROUPS** should be implemented as GROUPS can be used interchangeably with RANGE and ROWS.   ### Approach On my local copy of SQLAlchemy, I amended the following files to implement **GROUPS**:   - lib/sqlalchemy/sql/compiler.py – to render the **GROUPS** frame spec.   - lib/sqlalchemy/sql/functions.py – to extend the `FunctionElement.over` method to include `groups` as an option for window functions.   - lib/sqlalchemy/sql/elements.py – to extend the `Over` class to include `groups` as an option for window functions.   - lib/sqlalchemy/sql/_elements_constructors.py – linked to the above  I have written passing tests for: - test/sql/test_functions.py - test/sql/test_compiler.py  ### Next Steps   If you support the integration of the GROUPS frame-spec to Window functions, I will proceed with a pull request implementing the changes, including tests. Please share thoughts and comments.  _Originally posted by @Kaan191 in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/12444_

title: handle cast of postgresql empty ARRAY using specified type

Proposal: ```python >>> str(postgresql.array([], type_=sqlalchemy.CHAR).compile()) 'ARRAY[]::CHAR[]' ```  ### Additional context  I've been hacking on this in https://github.com/dlax/sqlalchemy/commit/1dc325cc8687ee6f1d22b13dd327df4628510b0c, so if this is okay, I can open a PR.

title: Will it be a good idea to implement `bulk_upsert_mappings` on Session?
body: ### Describe the use case  I have to do the following when dealing with bulk operations to insert or update data.  ```python # Bulk Insert or Update if inserts:     logger.info(f"Inserting {len(inserts)} records into {table_model.__name__}")     db.bulk_insert_mappings(table_model, inserts)  if updates:     logger.info(f"Updating {len(inserts)} records into {table_model.__name__}")     db.bulk_update_mappings(table_model, updates) ```  The problem with this approach is that on scale. Assume that I had around 3 Billion records which I am processing in batches of 10k. For each batch it will call the DB twice. Once for inserts and once for updates.  In total : 3B/10k = 300k calls  So basically it will run 300k * 2 = 600k queries.   If we allow bulk upserting method on the `Session` class, It will reduce queries by half.  I am also happy to contribute in case if required and this sounds like a good idea.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  DB : RDS-PGSQL  ### Example Use  ```python # Bulk Upsert if data     db.bulk_upsert_mappings(table_model, data) ```  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: Improve `eager_default=True` behavior in insert / updates
body: ## update Currently `eager_default=True` in case of an update of multiple rows does the following: - when the driver supports returning, runs single updates with returning, one for each row. Results in n queries - when the driver does not support returning, runs execute many updates and one select for each rows. Results in n + num-update queries. In the good cases it may just be n+1 if all the updates are in the same update-many   both of these options are not great.  A better behavior in both cases could be the to always do the update-many without returning then use a single select with in, basically what selectin does, to load the eager defaults. This would result in a best case of 2 queries.  it may be interesting to reuse completely the logic in selectin here, since the operation is exactly the same  ## insert Currently `eager_default=True` in case of an insert of multiple rows does the following: - when the driver supports returning, runs insert many with returning. Results in usually 1 query - when the driver does not support returning, runs an insert many and one select for each rows. Results in n + 1 queries.   The case with returning is fine, no changes there. The case without it's not.  A better behavior in the second case is do as what's suggested above: do the insert-many then use a single select with in, basically what selectin does, to load the eager defaults. This would result in a best case of 2 queries.

title: `SmallInteger` is compiled to `SERIAL` instead of `SMALLSERIAL` on table creation when `asyncpg` driver is used.
body: ### Describe the bug  If you are trying to create a table with a primary column of `SmallInteger` and the asyncpg driver is used, it will be compiled to `SERIAL` rather than `SMALLSERIAL`. This is because this type is not implemented as a column spec and `AsyncpgInteger` is used instead, and a check for `SmallInteger` in the code below will return `False`, this should be fixed in #12171. https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/860ca0b9d21874d9827f7f37cd0c330436baefb4/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/base.py#L2202-L2207  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.36  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  asyncpg  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 16  ### Python Version  3.12.7  ### Operating system  Windows  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import SmallInteger, create_engine from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, declarative_base, mapped_column from sqlalchemy.schema import CreateTable  ASYNCPG_SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL = "postgresql+asyncpg://postgres:postgres@localhost/postgres" PSYCOPG_SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL = "postgresql+psycopg2://postgres:postgres@localhost/postgres" asyncpg_engine = create_async_engine(ASYNCPG_SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL) psycopg_engine = create_engine(PSYCOPG_SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URL)  Base = declarative_base()   class TestTable(Base):     __tablename__ = "test_table"      id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(SmallInteger(), primary_key=True, autoincrement=True)   def main():     print(CreateTable(TestTable.__table__).compile(psycopg_engine))     print(CreateTable(TestTable.__table__).compile(asyncpg_engine))   if __name__ == "__main__":     main() ```   ### Error  ``` CREATE TABLE test_table (         id SMALLSERIAL NOT NULL,         PRIMARY KEY (id) )  CREATE TABLE test_table (         id SERIAL NOT NULL,         PRIMARY KEY (id) ) ```   ### Additional context  _N

title: fix CLOB->NVARCHAR output handler
body: > Hi Mike, >  > While looking into this issue (https://github.com/oracle/python-oracledb/issues/424) I discovered that SQLAlchemy is using an output type handler for CLOB to return NVARCHAR data. This is wrong! CLOB should use VARCHAR and NCLOB should use NVARCHAR. If you use CLOB with NVARCHAR you will end up performing two conversions instead of one. If one of those conversions fails you may get invalid data. >  > So this code in lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/oracle/cx_oracle.py: >  >>             elif dialect.auto_convert_lobs and default_type in ( >>                 cx_Oracle.CLOB, >>                 cx_Oracle.NCLOB, >>             ): >>                 return cursor.var( >>                     cx_Oracle.DB_TYPE_NVARCHAR, >>                     _CX_ORACLE_MAGIC_LOB_SIZE, >>                     cursor.arraysize, >>                     **dialect._cursor_var_unicode_kwargs, >>                 ) > should be: >  >>             elif dialect.auto_convert_lobs and default_type in ( >>                 cx_Oracle.CLOB, >>                 cx_Oracle.NCLOB, >>             ): >>                  typ = cx_Oracle.DB_TYPE_VARCHAR if default_type is cx_Oracle.CLOB else cx_Oracle.DB_TYPE_NVARCHAR >>                  return cursor.var( >>                     typ, >>                     _CX_ORACLE_MAGIC_LOB_SIZE, >>                     cursor.arraysize, >>                     **dialect._cursor_var_unicode_kwargs, >>                 )

title: Upgrade `adbc_ingest` parameter `temporary` to `prefixes`
body: ### Describe the use case  Currently `adbc_ingest` supports a parameter `temporary` to execute `CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE` statements. `sqlalchemy` supports this in a more abstract way, by accepting a list of table [`prefixes`](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/metadata.html#sqlalchemy.schema.Table.params.prefixes). I suggest to upgrade the API by implementing a `prefixes` parameter like `sqlalchemy.Table`.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  Some DBMS, e.g. `ibm db2`, support the use of [`CREATE GLOBAL TEMPORARY TABLE`](https://www.ibm.com/docs/en/db2/11.5?topic=statements-create-global-temporary-table) and therefore need multiple table prefixes.  ### Example Use  Create a global temporary table from some data.  ```python with con.cursor() as cur:     total_inserted = cur.adbc_ingest(         table_name="TEST",         data=some_data,         mode="create",         db_schema_name="SESSION",         temporary=["GLOBAL", "TEMPORARY"],     )  con.commit() ``` User can then use this "empty shell" to insert and further process data within their respective session.  ### Additional context  I'm currently working on adding a `prefixes` parameter to `pandas to_sql()` method, see https://github.com/pandas-dev/pandas/pull/60409 for reference. Since `to_sql()` supports both `sqalchmy` and `adbc` it would be beneficial for the ecosystem to have feature parity. The current state of progress:  - I fully implemented `prefixes` for `sqlalchemy` drivers - I implemented a way to only use the `TEMPORARY` keyword from `prefixes` for `adbc` drivers

title: Invalid OID Handling in SQLAlchemy with asyncpg and autoload_with Causes DataError
body: ### Describe the bug  I encountered an issue when using SQLAlchemy with asyncpg and the autoload_with option while trying to load table metadata. The problem occurs because PostgreSQL's oid type is treated as a signed 32-bit integer (int32) by asyncpg, which leads to a DataError when the OID value exceeds the maximum range of int32 (2,147,483,647).  ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Create a PostgreSQL table with an OID that exceeds the int32 range. For example, an OID like 3195477613. 2. Use SQLAlchemy to define the table with autoload_with to load metadata:  ```python from sqlalchemy import Table, MetaData  metadata = MetaData() table = Table("master_product_view", metadata, autoload_with=conn) ```  3. Execute the code.  ### Observed Behavior The following exception is raised during metadata loading:  ```python sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError: (sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.asyncpg.Error) <class 'asyncpg.exceptions.DataError'>: invalid input for query argument $1: 3195477613 (value out of int32 range) ```  ### Expected Behavior The autoload_with option should correctly handle OID values, even if they exceed the int32 range.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  1.4.54  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  asyncpg  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 14  ### Python Version  3.13  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import Table, MetaData  metadata = MetaData() table = Table("master_product_view", metadata, autoload_with=conn) ```   ### Error  The following exception is raised during metadata loading:  ```python sqlalchemy.exc.DBAPIError: (sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.asyncpg.Error) <class 'asyncpg.exceptions.DataError'>: invalid input for query argument $1: 3195477613 (value out of int32 range) ```  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: TypeVar bound by declarative base type "`has no attribute "__mapper__"`"
body: ### Describe the typing issue  The SQLAlchemy `mypy` plugin [tells `mypy` about the `__mapper__` attribute on subclasses of declarative bases](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/1b40521f5fb1628dfc6beec73fddda6855f6c77f/lib/sqlalchemy/ext/mypy/apply.py#L299-L301).  Unfortunately this information does not get conveyed to `mypy` when using a generic `TypeVar` which is `bound` by the declarative base. `mypy` just complains that the base class `has no attribute "__mapper__"`.  For now I'm working around this by just adding a `# type: ignore` comment when I access `__mapper__` on the generic argument. But am filing this issue to explain the `# type: ignore` comment itself. 🙂  ### To Reproduce  ```python # file: test.py from typing import Any, Iterable, Tuple, Type, TypeVar  from sqlalchemy import Column, Text from sqlalchemy.orm import as_declarative from sqlalchemy.orm.mapper import Mapper   @as_declarative() class Base:     __abstract__ = True   MY_METADATA_KEY = object() "Key used for setting my special metadata on columns"   class MyModel(Base):     __tablename__ = "my_model"     id = Column(Text, primary_key=True)     col1 = Column(Text, info={MY_METADATA_KEY: "foo"})   MyModel.__mapper__  # type checks ✅   M = TypeVar("M", bound=Base)   def column_metadata(model_type: Type[M]) -> Iterable[Tuple[str, Any]]:     mapper: Mapper = model_type.__mapper__  # does NOT type check ❌     for column in mapper.columns.values():         if MY_METADATA_KEY in column.info:             yield (column.name, column.info[MY_METADATA_KEY])   print(dict(column_metadata(MyModel))) ```   ### Error  ``` test.py: note: In function "column_metadata": test.py:31:22: error: "type[M]" has no attribute "__mapper__"  [attr-defined]         mapper: Mapper = model_type.__mapper__  # does NOT type check ❌                          ^~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~ Found 1 error in 1 file (checked 1 source file) ```  Note that running the file directly succeeds: ```console $ python test.py {'col1': 'foo'

title: Better support of locking clauses (FOR UPDATE/SHARE) when supported
body: ### Describe the use case  The [Postgres docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/17/sql-select.html) specifically say that you should be able to have both a FOR UPDATE and a FOR SHARE in the same query:  > Multiple locking clauses can be written if it is necessary to specify different locking behavior for different tables  which is often useful with join queries. In a common scenario, I'd want to take an exclusive lock on the primary row(s) being queried, and a SHARE lock on any rows that are brought in via relationships, since they're going to be read-only for the current transaction.  As far as I can tell, though, it's not actually possible to construct that in the SqlAlchemy ORM. That's because `Query` only supports a single `ForUpdateArg`, which is overwritten by `with_for_update()` as opposed to appending to a list. On supported platforms - or maybe attempt on all platforms and leave a user-beware dragon - we should be able to have _multiple_ for-update clauses (see example).  I do recognize that the [SqlAlchemy docs](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/orm/query.html#sqlalchemy.orm.Query.with_for_update) have a dragon warning for this whole area:  > Using with_for_update in the context of eager loading relationships is not officially supported or recommended by SQLAlchemy and may not work with certain queries on various database backends. When with_for_update is successfully used with a query that involves [joinedload()](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/14/orm/loading_relationships.html#sqlalchemy.orm.joinedload), SQLAlchemy will attempt to emit SQL that locks all involved tables.  That seems overly pessimistic, though, at least when using `joinedload()` (it's clearly more problematic with `selectinload()`, where we'd need to set the right lock clauses on the right individual selects). This feels along the lines of https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/5583 - is it possible to have more tailored warnings (both in code and in docs) when there are scenarios

title: Task cancellation with SA connection pool + asyncpg + direct_tls can lead to connection leak
body: ### Describe the bug  Hi, while tracking down #12076  / #12077 we found that we were hitting another connection leak under similar circumstances.  The setup is as follows: - SA connection pool + asyncpg with a `direct_tls=true` connection. - an asyncio task takes a session from the pool, starts a transaction and locks some rows with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`, then does some async work, while holding the lock + transaction - the asyncio task is cancelled.  At this point, it is possible that the connection holding the lock will leak (and still hold the lock).  The `direct_tls` stuff is what is used to connect to GCP CloudSQL instances with the [gcp cloud sql python connector](https://github.com/GoogleCloudPlatform/cloud-sql-python-connector), where we were having the issue in the first place.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.36  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  asyncpg  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  postgresql 16  ### Python Version  3.12  ### Operating system  linux  ### To Reproduce The setup is a little bit involved, so I created a repo with a docker compose config to make it easier to reproduce:  https://github.com/brittlesoft/repro-starlette-sa-conn-leak  The idea is to: - install the deps - docker compose up to start postgres + nginx (ssl connection termination) - run direct_tls_leak.py - watch the number of connections grow beyond the configured pool size. title: Comment reflection confused by pg_description entries with overlapping oid values
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/11958  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **gordthompson** October  6, 2024</sup> I uncovered this behaviour while testing sqlalchemy-cockroachdb, but I'm not sure if this would also affect PostgreSQL itself if [extensions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/catalog-pg-extension.html) were installed.  CockroachDB includes support for geography and geometry columns. That support appears to be registered as a "pg_extension". Those objects use oid values that overlap with those assigned to user tables.  ``` root@localhost:26257/defaultdb> select d.objoid, d.classoid, c.relname, d.objsubid, d.description                              -> from pg_catalog.pg_description d inner join pg_catalog.pg_class c                              ->   on c.oid = d.classoid                              -> where d.objoid = 128;   objoid |  classoid  | relname  | objsubid |                                        description ---------+------------+----------+----------+--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------      128 | 4294967053 | pg_proc  |        0 | Calculates slope of the least-squares-fit linear equation determined by the (X, Y) pairs. (1 row) ```  If we create a table with no comment, `.get_table_comment()` returns the pg_extension text  ```python import sqlalchemy as sa  engine = sa.create_engine(     "cockroachdb+psycopg2://root@localhost:26257/defaultdb" )  acct = sa.Table("account", sa.MetaData(), sa.Column("id", sa.Integer)) acct.drop(engine, checkfirst=True) acct.create(engine)  with engine.connect() as conn:     print(         conn.exec_driver_sql(             "SELECT oid FROM pg_catalog.pg_class WHERE relname='account'"         ).scalar()     )     # 128  insp = sa.inspect(engine) print(insp.get_table_comment("account")) # {'text': 'Calculates slope of the least-squares-fit linear equation determined by the (X, Y) pairs.'} ```

title: the ORM does not expire server_onupdate columns during a bulk UPDATE (new style)
body: This was discussed in #11911  The `server_onupdate` columns do not get expired by the orm following an update, requiring populate-existing to fetch the new values. This impact mainly computed columns.  Reproducer: ```py from sqlalchemy import orm import sqlalchemy as sa  class Base(orm.DeclarativeBase):     pass  class T(Base):     __tablename__ = "t"     id: orm.Mapped[int] = orm.mapped_column(primary_key=True)     value: orm.Mapped[int]     cc: orm.Mapped[int] = orm.mapped_column(sa.Computed("value + 42"))  e = sa.create_engine("sqlite:///", echo=True) Base.metadata.create_all(e) with orm.Session(e) as s:     s.add(T(value=10))     s.flush()     s.commit() with orm.Session(e) as s:     assert (v := s.get_one(T, 1)).cc == 52      s.execute(sa.update(T).values(id=1, value=2))      assert (v := s.get_one(T, 1)).cc != 44  # should be 44 with orm.Session(e) as s:     assert (v := s.get_one(T, 1)).cc == 52      r = s.execute(sa.update(T).values(value=2).returning(T))     assert (v := r.scalar_one()).cc != 44  # should be 44     assert (v := s.get_one(T, 1)).cc != 44  # should be 44 with orm.Session(e) as s:     r = s.execute(sa.insert(T).values(value=9).returning(T))     assert (v := r.scalar_one()).cc == 51      r = s.execute(sa.update(T).values(value=2).filter_by(id=2).returning(T))     assert (v := r.scalar_one()).cc != 44  # should be 44     r = s.execute(sa.select(T).filter_by(id=2))     assert (v := r.scalar_one()).cc != 44  # should be 44 ```

title: mariadbconnector doesn't pass along query parameters in the url as arguments to connect method as mysqldb does
body: While trying to ensure our codebase works with both connectors the first issue was that appending, in our case, `?unix_socket=/path/to/socket` wasn't having any effect while using mariadbconnector while mysqldb passes it as args to the connect method.  Both drivers are very similar and supports the same argument in almost all cases so I assume it would work fine just doing the same call in both drivers (or if that is not a desired usage deprecate passing it as url_params and document that it's prefered to pass it as explicit options to create_engine).  We can work around it either way but it feels like an unnecesary inconsistency.  I havn't checked the behavior of other dialects in this regard but the difference between these to is simply the call to `opts.update(url.query)` at  https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/29c2c15902094965f9dca66efae33305f09c3878/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/mysql/mysqldb.py#L208  which has no corresponding call in mariadbconnector. Just adding it here https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/29c2c15902094965f9dca66efae33305f09c3878/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/mysql/mariadbconnector.py#L169  works reasonably in my preliminary testing.  _Originally posted by @tapetersen in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/11868_

The ORM model becomes "corrupted" by construction of a different specific select, selecting the column returned by `hybrid_property.expression`. title: Support Oracle with_statement_hint
body: ### Describe the use case  Today, the `with_statement_hint` [is not supported](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/11702#issuecomment-2273825974) for Oracle.  The only way to use hints in Oracle is to use table hints via `with_hint`, however this requires a selectable which is not always relevant.  In Oracle there are multi-table hints such as:  ``` LEADING(first second) ```  And there are no-table hints such as:  ``` /*+ ORDERED */  /*+ CACHE */  /*+ RESULT_CACHE */  /*+ FIRST_ROWS */  /*+ ALL_ROWS */ ```  Using with_hint today can be confusing in these cases because it requires specifying a selectable.  I think it would be better to have with_statement_hint support Oracle.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  Oracle  cx_Oracle or oracledb  ### Example Use  ``` from sqlalchemy import table, column, select from sqlalchemy.dialects import oracle  first = table('first', column('a')) second = table('second', column('a'))  sel = select(first, second).select_from(first.join(second, first.c.a == second.c.a))  print(     sel.with_statement_hint(         'ORDERED'     ).compile(         dialect=oracle.dialect()     ) )  print(     sel.with_statement_hint(         'LEADING(first second)     ).compile(         dialect=oracle.dialect()     ) ) ```  ### Additional context  _No response_

body: ### Describe the bug  The with_hint function takes a selectable as well as the hint.  ``` with_hint(selectable: '_FromClauseArgument', text: 'str', dialect_name: 'str' = '*') ```  In Oracle, the `selectable` is not relevant, because all hints must be placed after the SELECT keyword:  ``` SELECT /*+ USE_NL(second) */ ```  If I pass in `None` for the selectable, SQLAlchemy will not compile the hint correctly with the Oracle style.  ``` from sqlalchemy import table, column, select from sqlalchemy.dialects import oracle  first = table('first', column('a')) second = table('second', column('a'))  sel = select(first, second).select_from(first.join(second, first.c.a == second.c.a))  print(     sel.with_hint(         None, 'USE_NL(second)'     ).compile(         dialect=oracle.dialect()     ) ) ``` This outputs the following which is wrong for Oracle:  ``` SELECT first.a, second.a AS a_1 FROM first JOIN second ON first.a = second.a USE_NL(second) ```  The solution to this is to just put any random selectable instead of `None`:  ``` print(sel.with_hint(first, 'USE_NL(second)').compile(dialect=oracle.dialect())) # or  print(sel.with_hint(second, 'USE_NL(second)').compile(dialect=oracle.dialect())) # or  print(sel.with_hint(table('totally_irrelevant'), 'USE_NL(second)').compile(dialect=oracle.dialect())) ```  which outputs the correct:  ``` SELECT /*+ USE_NL(second) */ first.a, second.a AS a_1 FROM first JOIN second ON first.a = second.a ```  However, I believe this is a bug because the `selectable` is meaningless for Oracle. I think it is confusing to have to put in a random selectable here. It would be better to allow `None`.   ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.32  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  N/A  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  Oracle  ### Python Version  3.12.4  ### Operating system  Linux and Windows  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy

title: Reflection caching is not handling quoted_name instances correctly
body: ### Describe the bug  I have already prepared a pull request for it, but the pull request template says I should create an issue first...and here we are...  I have noticed this issue when playing around with some toy examples in context of the SAP HANA dialect (https://github.com/SAP/sqlalchemy-hana), but technically it affects all dialects which require name normalization (i.e. also the built-in Oracle dialect).  When names (schema, tables, ...) are returned by the reflection methods of a dialect which requires name normalization the names are typically normalized in a way that for example uppercase names in the database are represented in lowercase in SQLAlchemy. When using these names again in a query the names have to be denormalized again. To distinguish between normalized lowercase names (i.e. names which appear in uppercase in the database) and non-normalized lowercase names (i.e. names which appear in lowercase in the database) during denormalization the quoted_name class resp. an instance of the class is used for the non-normalized names. title: add frame exclusion support
body: ### Describe the use case  frame exclusion reference: https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-expressions.html#:~:text=The%20frame_exclusion%20option%20allows%20rows,ordering%20peers%20from%20the%20frame.  I had a hard time trying to figure out how to implement PostgreSQL's frame exclusion when using window function, without resorting to building raw sql string. This is roughly what I've been working with (In our use case,  core SQL builder constructs like `column` and `text` are used to build fragments of a larger query):   ```python import sqlalchemy as sa  def demo(db):     window_args = {"partition_by": text("group_id"), "order_by": text("created_at"), "range_": (None, 0)}     query = sa.select(         sa.func.sum(sa.column("price")).over(**window_args),         # this translates to -> SUM(price) PARTITION BY group_id ORDER BY created_at RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW         # but I want it to be   .....RANGE UNBOUNDED PRECEDING EXCLUDE CURRENT ROW"         sa.column("other_column"),         ...     ).select_from(sa.table("some_table"))      for row in db.execute(query):         print(row)  ``` Currently,  it looks like the parameters in `over()` does not support frame exclusion.  What would be a reliable workaround for this ?  Patching `SQLCompiler._format_frame_clause` may work, but I want to seek out other "safer" options first.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  Postgres 11 or higher  ### Example Use  If it will be supported in future release, it may look something like this: ```python column("foo").over(exclude="CURRENT ROW") # other values:  GROUP, TIES ```  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: Expand Default Value Constraint Support
body: ### Describe the use case  SQL allows the creation of default value constraints during column creation via the syntax[^1] ```SQL CREATE TABLE Person (     ID int NOT NULL,     LastName varchar(255) NOT NULL,     FirstName varchar(255),     Age int,     City varchar(255) DEFAULT 'Sandnes' );  ``` which is currently well supported within SQLalchemy.  Several flavors of SQL also allow for the adding of a default value constraint outside of column creation via the syntax[^1] ```SQL ALTER TABLE Person ALTER City SET DEFAULT 'Sandnes';  ``` which is not currently supported within SQLalchemy.  SQL Server in particular also supports the ability to name default constraints via the syntax[^1] ```SQL ALTER TABLE Person ADD CONSTRAINT df_City DEFAULT 'Sandnes' FOR City;  ``` which is not currently supported within SQLalchemy.  I propose to add support for both creating default value constraints separate from creating a column (for dialects which support it) as well as allowing for naming default value constraints (in SQL Server). title: Support Oracle 23ai BOOLEAN datatype
body: ### Describe the bug  The latest Oracle DB release as of 7/22/24 - DB23AI - Supports native "BOOLEAN" types, whereas the type used to be captured by a SMALLINT. As a result, the documentation and behavior around CamelCase type "Boolean" is now out of date for Oracle DB:  https://support.oracle.com/knowledge/Oracle%20Database%20Products/3002488_1.html """ Unlike [String](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/type_basics.html#sqlalchemy.types.String), which represents a string datatype that all databases have, not every backend has a real “boolean” datatype; some make use of integers or BIT values 0 and 1, some have boolean literal constants true and false while others dont. For this datatype, [Boolean](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/type_basics.html#sqlalchemy.types.Boolean) may render BOOLEAN on a backend such as PostgreSQL, BIT on the MySQL backend and _SMALLINT on Oracle_ """  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.31  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  cx_oracle  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  OracleDB 23  ### Python Version  3.10  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python # create table w/ sqlalchemy op.create_table('test', sa.Column('col1', sa.Boolean())  # query table in oracle select col1 from test;  COL1 ----    0  # create table using Boolean in oracle just fine create table test2 (col2 boolean); insert into test values (TRUE);  Col2 ---- TRUE ```   ### Error  The result of the behavior mismatch is we get some nasty error when trying to run queries using the .is_ flag - the .is_(False) feature works just fine on Postgres, and then fails when using Oracle. The fix, for now, I believe is to use BOOLEAN instead of Boolean type.  ### Additional context  Oracle 23 only just came out recently, so I don't expect this to be done right away. See also: https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/10375

title: Connection object released back to the pool after commit()
body: ### Describe the bug  I am using sqlalchemy to manage an sql server database from fastapi. For each endpoint execution, I need to set up a context variable to the session with `session.execute("sys.sp_set_session_context 'context_var', 'value'")`  which will be used for row-level security.  I found out that when I execute multiple commits within an endpoint function, there is a chance that when executing session.commit(), the connection object is released to the Pool and a new one is acquired which will be used in the following commits. This forces me to reset the context variable every time after each `session.commit()` to maintain the correct row-level security. The closest case related to my issue I could find is https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/4925, but in my case I don't think I am deleting any strong reference as mentioned in: >  when you create a connection pool, then acquire some connections, and then you delete all strong references to those connections, the connection pool uses a weakref callback that still contains a strong reference to pool's internal record of this connection as well as the DBAPI connection itself, so that it can be brought back into the pool as though it were explicitly returned  Is there a way to keep the same connection object consistently until the `session.close()`?. Is there a better way to manage this? I would also like to avoid solutions such as using a `NullPool` to prevent jumping from one connection to another. title: Inconsistent SQLAlchemy logging with hidden timestamp type coercion
body: ### Describe the bug  Datetime is automatically coerced into `::timestamp` when passed to `func.timezone`, which causes unexpected behavior. This is not shown through SQLAlchemy logs and this coercion is completely hidden until actually viewing database logs.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/engines.html#configuring-logging  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.30  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg2  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 13.14  ### Python Version  3.10.11  ### Operating system  Windows  ### To Reproduce  ```python >> current_dt = func.timezone('US/Eastern', start_date) >> current_time = func.cast(current_dt, TIME) >> sel = select(current_time) >> res = session.execute(sel)  >> print(res.fetchall()) [(datetime.time(19, 44),)]  # Engine logs SELECT CAST(timezone(%(timezone_2)s, %(timezone_3)s) AS TIME WITHOUT TIME ZONE) AS timezone_1 [generated in 0.00014s] {'timezone_2': 'US/Eastern', 'timezone_3': datetime.datetime(2024, 6, 24, 15, 44)}  # Expected result based on engine logs 11:44:00  # Actual query to run SELECT CAST(timezone('US/Eastern', '2024-06-24T15:44:00'::timestamp) AS TIME WITHOUT TIME ZONE) AS timezone_1 ```   As shown above, logging actually shows a different query than the one that runs on the database. In this specific use case, this causes timezone to incorrectly add time when converting UTC -> US/Eastern instead of subtracting time, while the coercion happens silently and is not implied anywhere throughout sqlalchemy logs.  I imagine this is a base use-case for the timezone functionality and being able to properly parse in & display how datetimes are interacted with is a significant part of it.   ### Error  N/A  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: pool_pre_ping fails to reconnect on psycopg2 "SSL SYSCALL error: Success"
body: ### Describe the bug  When a psycopg2 SSL connection to Postgres terminates abnormally, the error message returned by libpq will be sometimes be `SSL SYSCALL error: Success`.  This is a [known issue with OpenSSL 1](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man1.1.1/man3/SSL_get_error.html#BUGS), and anecdotally we still see it with recent versions of OpenSSL 3 on Linux when misbehaving network equipment causes the connection to terminate unexpectedly.  [According to the OpenSSL documentation](https://www.openssl.org/docs/man3.3/man3/SSL_get_error.html#SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL), any SSL_ERROR_SYSCALL is non-recoverable.  We are using `pool_pre_ping` to verify connections prior to check-out.  However, when a connection has failed with this error, no reconnect is attempted because this error is not [in the list of exceptions that are considered a "disconnect" event.](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/2607262110bdc5c5dc96fc19ddca895a15a58e4e/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/psycopg2.py#L865).  We are attempting to use `pool_pre_ping` to work around an issue where a firewall between our service and the database will silently drop connections that have been idle for some time, so the desired behavior would be for it to re-connect when the ping fails, instead of throwing an exception.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.25  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg2  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  Postgres 13  ### Python Version  3.12  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python uri = "postgresql://..." engine = sqlalchemy.engine.create_engine(uri, pool_pre_ping=True) with engine.connect() as connection:     connection.execute(...)  # Wait around for a while until misbehaving network equipment # abnormally terminates the idle connection...  with engine.connect() as connection: # exception raised when pinging connection here     ... ```   ### E

title: Microsoft SQL Server miscompilation for ROWS PRECEDING/FOLLOWING
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/11513
Originally posted by **suhas-dc** June 19, 2024 On Microsoft SQL Server running a query with an OVER clause containing a row range fails. For example, ``` query = sa.select(sa.func.avg(col_one).over(order_by=[col_two], rows=(-5,1))) connection.execute(query) ``` fails with `ProgrammingError: ('42000', "[42000] [Microsoft][ODBC Driver 18 for SQL Server][SQL Server]Incorrect syntax near '@P1'. (102) (SQLExecDirectW)")`. The sqlalchemy query object is compiled into some thing similar to ``` SELECT avg(anon_1.[col_one]) OVER (ORDER BY anon_1.[col_two] ASC ROWS BETWEEN ? PRECEDING AND ? FOLLOWING) FROM dbo.table AS anon_1''' ``` And, pyodbc does not seem to support bind parameters for PRECEDING and FOLLOWING since running the above query as textual SQL will also fail with the same error. Compiling the query with `literal_binds` `True` substitutes the bind parameters giving a query pyodbc will run. EDIT: I faced this issues on sqlalchemy 1.4 but it seems to me that the issue may also exist on sqlalchemy 2.0 after looking through the `visit_over` definition.

title: Add Built-in Soft Delete Functionality
body: ### Describe the use case  I propose adding built-in support for soft deletes in SQLAlchemy. This feature would allow users to mark records as deleted without physically removing them from the database.  For example, in a customer management system, you might want to "delete" a customer who has requested account closure. However, for audit purposes and potential future recovery, you don't want to remove their data completely from the database. Instead, you mark the customer as deleted, which prevents the data from appearing in regular queries but keeps it available for administrators or recovery operations.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  - **Databases**: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, and any other database that supports Boolean fields. - **Drivers**: All drivers supported by SQLAlchemy (e.g., psycopg2 for PostgreSQL, pymysql for MySQL).  ### Example Use  **SQL Example** Here's what the SQL might look like for a soft delete operation: ``` -- Mark a record as deleted UPDATE some_model SET deleted = TRUE WHERE id = 1;  -- Query non-deleted records SELECT * FROM some_model WHERE deleted = FALSE; ``` **DBAPI Example** Using SQLAlchemy to perform a soft delete and query non-deleted records: ``` from sqlalchemy.ext.declarative import declared_attr from sqlalchemy import Boolean, Column, Integer, String, create_engine, inspect from sqlalchemy.orm import sessionmaker, scoped_session, declarative_base  Base = declarative_base()  class SoftDeleteMixin:     @declared_attr     def deleted_column(cls):         return 'deleted'      @declared_attr     def deleted(cls):         return Column(Boolean, default=False)      def soft_delete(self):         if not hasattr(self, self.deleted_column):             raise AttributeError(f"This record does not have '{self.deleted_column}' column to support soft delete.")          setattr(self, self.deleted_column, True)  # Example Model using the SoftDeleteMixin with an alias class SomeModel(Base, SoftDeleteMixin):     __tablename__

While the serializer extension in considered legacy, we are (unfortunately) still using it in our RPC scenario with untrusted user inputs. Any tips on how to patch `over` on the user side or any alternatives to `sqlalchemy.ext.serializer` are much appreciated)    ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/serializer.html  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  1.4.52, 2.0.30  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  -  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  -  ### Python Version  3.12  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python import sqlalchemy as sa from sqlalchemy.ext.serializer import dumps as sa_dumps, loads as sa_loads   stmt = sa.func.SUM().over(range_=(None, 0)) dumped_query = sa_dumps(stmt) loaded_query = sa_loads(dumped_query) ```   ### Error  Expected result (the same as for the original statement): ``` >>> str(stmt.compile(compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})) 'sum() OVER (RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)' ```  Actual result for `SQLAlchemy-2.0.30`: ``` >> str(loaded_query.compile(compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})) 'sum() OVER (RANGE BETWEEN CURRENT ROW AND 1 FOLLOWING)' ```   Actual result for `SQLAlchemy-1.4.52`: ``` >>> str(loaded_query.compile(compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})) 'sum() OVER (RANGE BETWEEN 2152484616254935939 FOLLOWING AND 2545834031883131234 FOLLOWING)' ```  with exact numbers varying per run.  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: Add additional information to the `ReflectedColumn`

title: Use of `raise NotImplementedError` instead of `NotImplemented`
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10645  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **fazledyn-or** November 16, 2023</sup> I am here to discuss about an issue that we came across while triaging your project.  ## Background  While traiging your project, our bug fixing tool generated the following message(s)-  In file: [associationproxy.py](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/main/lib/sqlalchemy/ext/associationproxy.py#L1980), class: _AssociationSet, there is a special method `__ixor__` that raises a NotImplementedError. If a special method supporting a binary operation is not implemented it should return [NotImplemented](https://docs.python.org/3/library/constants.html#NotImplemented). On the other hand, [NotImplementedError](https://docs.python.org/3/library/exceptions.html#NotImplementedError) should be raised from abstract methods inside user defined base classes to indicate that derived classes should override those methods. iCR suggested that the special method `__ixor__` should return NotImplemented instead of raising an exception. An example of how NotImplemented helps the interpreter support a binary operation is [here](https://docs.python.org/3/library/numbers.html#implementing-the-arithmetic-operations).  The same message is generated for `__imul__`, `__iand__`, `__isub__`, `__ior__` methods too.   ## Details The reason behind suggesting this fix is that developers often confuse `NotImplemented` and `NotImplementedError` equivalent, which is wrong. Using `NotImplemented` allows the Python interpreter to take over and try performing that operation. If it fails to do so, the interpreter throws a `TypeError`.   ## Suggested Changes It is suggested that `raise NotImplementedError` be replaced with `return NotImplemented`. If you're willing, I can create a fix and submit a PR.   ## Previously Found & Fixed - https://www.github.com/SciTools/iris/pull/5544 - https://www.github.com/cupy/cupy/pull/7900

title: URL corrupted if '@' character present in password
body: ### Describe the bug  # Description  When using a `@` character in the password of a connection URL string, the password is truncated at the `@` and the URL becomes mangled, causing connection issues. The expected behavior is for the password to be correctly parsed, even when it contains special characters like '@'.  # Example  ```python import sqlalchemy  url = "mysql+pymysql://username:p@ssword@mydb.com" engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine(url) with engine.connect() as connection:     pass ```  Raises:  ```bash sqlalchemy.exc.OperationalError: (pymysql.err.OperationalError) (2003, "Can't connect to MySQL server on 'ssword@mydb.com' ([Errno -2] Name or service not known)") ```  As you can see, the client attempts to connect to `ssword@mydb.com` instead of `mydb.com`.  # Solution  I believe this is because the regex defined in the `_parse_url()` function (`lib/sqlalchemy/engine/url.py`) ignores any `@` present in the password, thus assuming the password ends at the first `@` encountered:  > url.py, line 855  > ```python > (?::(?P<password>[^@]*))? > ```  Instead, the regex could capture any characters greedily using `.*`:  > url.py, line 855  > ```python > (?::(?P<password>.*))? > ```  This fix should work correctly, as demonstrated here: <https://regex101.com/r/0b8SUr/1>  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.29  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  pymysql  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  MySQL  ### Python Version  3.10.12  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python import sqlalchemy  url = "mysql+pymysql://username:p@ssword@mydb.com" engine = sqlalchemy.create_engine(url) with engine.connect() as connection:     pass ```   ### Error  ``` Traceback (most recent call last):   File "/home/jchouinard/Work/Lighting/Tools/doo-firmware-upgrade-multi/.venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/pymysql/connections.py", line 644, in connect     sock = socket.create_connection(   File "/nix/store/pzf6dnxg8gf04xazzjdwarm7s03cbrgz-python3-3.10.12/lib/python3.10/socket

title: Exists.select() annotated as returning Select[Any] instead of Select[bool]
body: ### Ensure stubs packages are not installed  - [X] No sqlalchemy stub packages is installed (both `sqlalchemy-stubs` and `sqlalchemy2-stubs` are not compatible with v2)  ### Verify if the api is typed  - [X] The api is not in a module listed in [#6810](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/6810) so it should pass type checking  ### Describe the typing issue  tl;dr: `Exists.select()` claims to return `Any`, while in reality its' a query returning a boolean:  ``` python class Exists(UnaryExpression[bool]):     def select(self) -> Select[Any]: ```  this causes type checkers to complain about `Any` for no good reason.  some background to clarify. a query of the form  ``` sql SELECT EXISTS (     SELECT 1     FROM ...     WHERE ... ) ```  … returns a scalar boolean value indicating the existence of data matching a condition.  there are multiple ways to build these in sqlalchemy, e.g. fully nested, which results in a lot of indentation and wasted space when formatted over multiple lines:  ``` python sa.select(sa.exists(sa.select(...).where(...))) ```  or via `Select.exists()` which returns `Exists`, with similar indentation ugliness:  ``` python sa.select(sa.select(...).where(...).exists()) ```  alternatively, via `Select.exists()` and `Exists.select()` chaining, which looks very clean:  ``` python statement = (     sqlalchemy.select(...)     .where(...)     .exists()     .select() ) ```  all of these result in the same query, b/c:  - `Select.exists()` is a convenience helper to turn `SELECT ...` into `EXISTS (SELECT ...)` - `Exists.select()` is a convenience helper to turn `EXISTS (...)` into `SELECT EXISTS (...)`    ### To Reproduce  ``` python def f() -> bool:     statement = (         sqlalchemy.select(1)         .select_from(Thing)         .where(Thing.col == "foo")         .exists()         .select()     )     return session.scalars(statement).one() ```   ### Error  Returning Any from function declared to return "bool"  [no-any-return] (python-mypy)   ### V

title: Delete Propagation to Parent Table for Joined Table Inheritance
body: ### Describe the use case  When a polymorphic table is created via joined table inheritance, I would expect that deleting a row in the subclass table would also delete the row in the parent table. I've found that when the subclass row is explicitly deleted, the delete propgates to the parent table as I would expect. However when the subclass row is deleted via cascading delete, that deletion doesn't propagate to the parent table. This leaves us in an undesirable state with several orphaned rows in the parent table. The only clear way of handling this I've found is to use event listeners in place of a proper cascading delete but ideally there should be a way to handle this so that cascading deletes are properly carried through to the parent table.   ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  Postgresql / psycopg  ### Example Use  To give an example, imagine there are three tables:  ``` Company ------- id  Employee ------ id  Engineer(Employee) ------ id company_id = Column(ForeignKey("company.id", ondelete="CASCADE")) ```  When a row in the engineer table is explicitly deleted, the related row in the Employee table is deleted successfully  ``` session.delete(engineer) # This deletes the related Employee row without issue ```  When a row in the company table is deleted, the related row in the Engineer table is deleted but that deletion doesn't propagate to the Employee table and this is what I would like to be addressed  ``` session.delete(company) # This deletes the related Engineer row but the Employee row remains ```  ### Additional context  We're using sqlalchemy version 1.4.31

title: feat: support kwargs to Select.where(), similar to .filter_by()
body: ### Describe the use case  in sqlalchemy 2.x, the `Select` construct is the spiritual successor to the 1.x style `Query` construct.  `Select.where()` already existed, and the 1.x style `Query.filter()` and `.filter_by()` methods got added as `Select.filter()` (an alias to `Select.where()`) and `Select.filter_by()`.  this means there are 3 ways to produce `WHERE` clauses, two of which are identical (`.where()` and `.filter()`), and one of which takes `**kwargs` (`.filter_by()`)  if `Select.where()` would also take keyword arguments (currently it only takes `*conditions` varargs), it could supplant the features offered by `.filter_by()`, and become the the canonical way to add `WHERE` clauses, which is a clean and unsurprising API.  (i wouldn't be surprised if others had the same idea, but i couldn't find any prior discussion about this after a quick search)  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  all  ### Example Use  ``` python sqlalchemy.select(...).filter_by(name='example') ```  … currently works, but  ``` python sqlalchemy.select(...).where(name='example') ```  … currently does _not_ work. it would be great if it it did 🙃  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: document the "as_string" / "as_int" etc JSON methods not as "CAST" methods, since this is not accurate as to their purpose
body: ### Describe the bug  When using the SQLite driver, calling `.as_string()` on a JSON column in a query does not cast the result to a string. For example, if a have a table `Table` with a JSON column `json`, I may write a query such as `select(Table.data['foo'].as_string())`. If a row has the value `{"foo": 1}`, the result should be `'1'`, a string. Instead, SQLAlchemy returns `1`, an int.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/type_basics.html#sqlalchemy.types.JSON.Comparator.as_string  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.27  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  pysqlite  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  3.45.1  ### Python Version  3.10.13  ### Operating system  OSX  ### To Reproduce  ```python import sqlalchemy as sa  engine = sa.create_engine('sqlite://') meta = sa.MetaData() table = sa.Table(     'example',     meta,     sa.Column('json', sa.JSON), )  cxn = engine.connect() meta.create_all(cxn) cxn.execute(sa.insert(table).values(json={'foo': 1})) res = cxn.execute(sa.select(table.c.json['foo'].as_string())) row = res.first() assert row print(row[0], type(row[0])) # Expected: 1 <class 'str'> # Got: 1 <class 'int'> ```   ### Error  n/a  ### Additional context  I don't believe this is relevant to the *current* SQLite driver implementation, but SQLite's JSON access operators are not compatible with postgresql. In postgres, `->` returns JSON while `->>` returns text. In SQLite, `->` returns text while `->>` may return NULL, INT, REAL, or JSON.

title: deprecate noload() option
body: this option was added as kind of a one-off about 18 years ago to suit an example case for custom loading of relationships which I'd never recommend today.   because the option turns off the related attribute entirely, it has all kinds of not easily predictable behaviors, it returns essentially incorrect results (e.g. None when there would normally be a collection there) and we continue to get complaints about other features not working when it's used e.g. #11040.  The one place people use this is when they have some kind of serializer that touches every attribute and they dont want an attribute to load.    I think that's a bad use case.  They should do one of 1. dont have that relationship there if it isnt part of the object's state 2. get a serializer that can select for which attributes you want to serialize and which you dont 3. eagerly load the collection there.    it's no different from an object with a relationship that has a huge list of related objects already loaded and you don't want to serialize that either.  so let's just deprecate it and we dont have to deal with complaints anymore, people will write better programs.

title: [postgresql] Support the `USING <method>` option for `CREATE TABLE`
body: ### Describe the use case  The Postgre `CREATE TABLE` supports a `USING ...` option:  > This optional clause specifies the table access method to use to store the contents for the new table; the method needs be an access method of type TABLE. See [Chapter 63](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/tableam.html) for more information. If this option is not specified, the default table access method is chosen for the new table. See [default_table_access_method](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-client.html#GUC-DEFAULT-TABLE-ACCESS-METHOD) for more information.  Some variants of Postgres use this to allow creating tables with different access methods, e.g. `columnar`.  https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-createtable.html#SQL-CREATETABLE-METHOD   ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  PostgreSQL  ### Example Use  ```python Table("my_columnar_table", metadata, ..., postgresql_using="columnar") ```  Which would translate to  ```sql CREATE TABLE my_columnar_table (...) USING columnar; ```  ### Additional context  The overall purpose is to support [Hydra databases](https://docs.hydra.so/concepts/using-hydra-columnar), so I may need to create a new dialect anyway but this still would be nice to have for the builtin postgres dialect.  Is this as easy as updating https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/b455b1fc03e25fc6a53cac74f3cee515c3efbf8a/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/base.py#L2381  and  https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/b455b1fc03e25fc6a53cac74f3cee515c3efbf8a/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/postgresql/base.py#L3001-L3010  ?

title: OrderingList typing incorrect / incomplete and implementation doesn't accept non-int indices
body: ### Describe the bug  There are a number of issues with the sqlalchemy.ext.orderinglist:OrderingList type hints and implementation:  1. The ordering function is documented as being allowed to return any type of object, and the tests demonstrate this by returning strings. The type annotation requires it to return integers, only, however. 2. The `OrderingList` signature marks the `ordering_attr` as optional, but accepting `None` here would lead to a type error when `getattr(entity, self.ordering_attr)` is called.  3. List objects accept any `SupportsIndex` type object, one that implements the [`.__index__()` method](https://docs.python.org/3/reference/datamodel.html#object.__index__). The codebase assumes it is always an integer (`count_from_1()` and `count_from_n_factory()` use addition with the value, which `SupportsIndex` objects don't need to support). It's probably best to use `operator.index()` on the value before passing it to the ordering function. 4. The `ordering_list()` ignores the `_T` type variable in the `OrderingFunc` and `OrderingList` signatures 5. The `OrderingFunc.ordering_func` annotation ignores the `_T` type variable in the `OrderingFunc` signature 6. List objects accept setting values via a slice and any iterable, e.g. `listobj[start:stop] = values_generator()`, but `OrderingList.__setitem__` with a slice object assumes the value is a sequence (supporting indexing), where a list accepts any iterable, plus it doesn't adjust the list length when the slice is being assigned fewer or more elements or handle slices with stride other than 1. Flushing the whole session instead of just the two objects fixes the problem, but since it worked up to 2.0.18 it might be an unintended regression.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.24  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg2  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 14  ### Python Version  3.11  ### Operating system  Windows  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import Column, Integer, Table, ForeignKey, create_engine, select from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship from sqlalchemy.orm import Session from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base  Base = declarative_base()  roles_users = Table(     "roles_users",     Base.metadata,     Column("user_id", Integer, ForeignKey("users.id"), primary_key=True),     Column("role_id", Integer, ForeignKey("roles.id"), primary_key=True), )   class User(Base):     __tablename__ = "users"     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     roles: Mapped[list["Role"]] = relationship(         "Role", secondary=roles_users, back_populates="users"     )   class Role(Base):     __tablename__ = "roles"     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     users: Mapped[list["User"]] = relationship(         "User", secondary=roles_users, back_populates="roles"     )  engine = create_engine("postgresql+psycopg2://localhost/bugtest", echo=True) Base.metadata.create_all(engine)  with Session(engine) as session:     role = Role(id=1)     session.add(role)     session.flush([role])      user = User

title: uselist not inferred correctly for relationship when a non-string type annotation is used in Mapped
body: ### Describe the bug  It seems that the [one-to-one](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/basic_relationships.html#one-to-one) example for a relationship does not infer correctly the `uselist` value if the mapped argument is not a string annotation.  The difference is in the value inferred for uselist in the `Parent.child` relationship, that is correctly inferred to `False` in the example, while it is inferred to `True` if the type annotation for `child` is changed to `Mapped[Child]`.  In the docs of the uselist parameter (https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/relationship_api.html#sqlalchemy.orm.relationship.params.uselist) it is stated that uselist may be derived from whether the mapped argument is a collection or not, but in this case `Mapped[Child]` is not a collection, so I would expect uselist set to `False`.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/relationship_api.html#sqlalchemy.orm.relationship.params.uselist  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.24  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg2  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 13  ### Python Version  3.10  ### Operating system  Windows  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped, mapped_column, relationship, DeclarativeBase   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Child(Base):     __tablename__ = "child"      id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     parent_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("parent.id"))     parent: Mapped["Parent"] = relationship(back_populates="child")   class Parent(Base):     __tablename__ = "parent"      id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     # this relationship has uselist=True     child: Mapped[Child] = relationship(back_populates="parent")     # this relationship has uselist=False     # child: Mapped["Child"] = relationship(back_populates="parent") ```   ### Error  ``` # Cop

title: Support jsonpath-like column select syntax in the expression language
body: ### Describe the use case  Redshift provides a `SUPER` data type that is intended to hold unstructured data. This is similar to the `JSON` type in postgres, except that it's a more generic approach. For instance, while a common way to create a `SUPER` value is to use Redshift's built-in `json_parse` function, there's nothing stopping users from defining functions to parse other serialization formats into `SUPER`.  Traversing a `SUPER` value uses a SQL-level syntax (i.e. not within a string) that is very similar to a jsonpath. I've provided a toy example further down to show off how it works.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  Redshift has had this syntax for its new `SUPER` type since 2022. I don't know enough about other backends to know if other dialects also have similar syntax.  Regardless, there would be no reason to make an implementation for this dialect-specific. Imo it would make more sense to provide this as a method on the `Column` class (or an appropriate ancestor).  ### Example Use  ```SQL SELECT     sub.data[0].name::varchar AS first_dog_name,     sub.data[0].age::int AS first_dog_age,     sub.data[0].breed.name::varchar AS first_dog_breed,     sub.data[1].name::varchar AS second_dog_name,     sub.data[1].age::int AS second_dog_age FROM (     SELECT         json_parse('[{"name": "Luna", "age": 2, "breed": {"name": "Golden Retriever"}}, {"name": "Cooper", "age": 5}]') as data ) as sub; ```  ![image](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/assets/37582022/f6353c7b-d528-4ef7-904c-fb1d36d9ce9c)    ### Additional context  Implementing this should be relatively straightforward using python's `__getattr__` and `__getitem__` dunders. In a way it's very similar to what the `func` accessor does, where it just keeps on giving proxy objects that 'remember' the full dotted path that's been traversed so far. title: `RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration` raised in clsregistry _MultipleClassMarker.add_item
body: ### Describe the bug  We have several tests that use flask and sqlalchemy, they create & destroy the database multiple times for each test case in a single test invocation. They use automap_base to generate mapped classes.  We saw the tests can fail with a `RuntimeError: Set changed size during iteration` raised here: https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/6e089c3dbf7e7348da84dfc62cc1c6100a257fd4/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/clsregistry.py#L245  Upon investigation, when running the list comprehension `[ref() for ref in self.contents]`, the `self.contents` set itself could be modified during a GC cycle when `_remove_item` is called.
