I hope this is understandable since the bug is triggered by a Python GC cycle, and I also hope the fix should be clear.  ### Error  ```   File "sqlalchemy/ext/automap.py", line 891, in prepare     mapped_cls = type(                  ^^^^^   File "sqlalchemy/orm/decl_api.py", line 72, in __init__     _as_declarative(reg, cls, dict_)   File "sqlalchemy/orm/decl_base.py", line 126, in _as_declarativ

title: Rowcount isn't returned for INSERTs without RETURNING when using psycopg3
body: ### Describe the bug  The `CursorResult.rowcount` property returns `-1` instead of the actual cursor's rowcount value when using psycopg3 when performing an INSERT without a RETURNING clause. With psycopg2, it works as expected.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.23  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  psycopg  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  PostgreSQL 14  ### Python Version  3.11  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python import uuid  from sqlalchemy import UUID, Column, MetaData, Table, create_engine, insert  metadata = MetaData()  engine = create_engine('postgresql+psycopg://')  t1 = Table(     "data",     metadata,     Column("id", UUID, primary_key=True), )  with engine.begin() as conn:     metadata.create_all(conn)     stmt = insert(t1).values({'id': uuid.uuid4()})     result = conn.execute(stmt)     assert result.rowcount == 1 ```   ### Error  N/A  ### Additional context  I dug into it a bit and it seems that with psycopg2, the `rowcount` property of a cursor remains unchanged after the cursor is closed, but with psycopg3, it turns to `-1` at that point. The memoized property `CursorResult.rowcount` isn't accessed before the cursor is closed [here](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/44771ab0c32730d1ecefac21af13f113b1b19726/lib/sqlalchemy/engine/default.py#L1933), so the rowcount information is lost by the time the execute call returns.  I can't say if the psycopg behavior change is intentional or not, but it would seem to me that it would be prudent to grab the value before the cursor is closed in any case.

title: SQLAlchemy does not respect ancestor loggers' handlers
body: ### Describe the bug  SQLAlchemy installs default logging handler when there are existing ancestor loggers' handlers. This causes the main program with its own logging setup to have unexpected logging activity.  In general, you should not need to attach a handler to more than one logger - if you just attach it to the appropriate logger which is highest in the logger hierarchy, then it will see all events logged by all descendant loggers, provided that their propagate setting is left set to True. title: BUG: `INSERT ... ON CONFLICT` breaks on magic cookie 'updated value' for column types that cannot convert the string
body: ### Describe the bug  The [docs](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/dialects/postgresql.html#insert-on-conflict-upsert) for `INSERT…ON CONFLICT` provide an example for the most commonly desired upsert behaviour: if the constraint matches, use the incoming values. This is especially important for batch operations.  The example uses `set_=dict(data='updated value')` to update a single column called `data`, and while the docs don't go into much detail about the magic cookie `'updated value'`, it's clear from the generated SQL query that this is not taken as a literal, but rather causes a `SET data = %(param_1)s`.  Trying to adapt this to my example, I tried to set `'updated value'` basically for all columns of my table. Unfortunately, this failed. After some debugging, it appears to be primarily a problem for column types that cannot convert from the string `'updated value'`, i.e. probably there is a layering mismatch between when the types are checked and when the magic cookie gets utilized as "use the incoming values".  In my case, the generated query looked as follows (linebreaks added for legibility):  <details> <summary>generated query</summary>  ``` [SQL: INSERT INTO     schema.table     (col1, col2, col3, col4, col5, col6, col7, col8, col9, col10, col11, col12, col13) VALUES     (%(col1_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col2_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col3_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col4_m0)s::VARCHAR,      %(col5_m0)s::TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE, %(col6_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col7_m0)s,      %(col8_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col9_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col10_m0)s::VARCHAR, %(col11_m0)s::VARCHAR,      %(col12_m0)s::JSON, %(col13_m0)s::JSONB),     (%(col1_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col2_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col3_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col4_m1)s::VARCHAR,      %(col5_m1)s::TIMESTAMP WITHOUT TIME ZONE, %(col6_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col7_m1)s,      %(col8_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col9_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col10_m1)s::VARCHAR, %(col11_m1)s::VARCHAR,      %(col12_m1)s::JSON, %(col13_m1)s::JSONB),     [...] ON CONFLICT ON CONSTRAINT table_primary_key DO UPDATE SET

body: ### Describe the bug  sqlalchemy.engine.url.URL's [render_as_string](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/main/lib/sqlalchemy/engine/url.py#L629) function [url encodes](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/main/lib/sqlalchemy/engine/url.py#L910C39-L910C43) some but not all characters for passwords.  I expect the output of `render_as_string` to url encode all necessary characters for a db url.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  1.4.41  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  n/a  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  n/a  ### Python Version  3.8  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import create_engine import urllib  password = urllib.parse.quote_plus("notareal[password]") db_url = f"postgresql+pg8000://scott:{password}@localhost:5432/mydatabase" print(db_url) # postgresql+pg8000://scott:notareal%5Bpassword%5D@localhost:5432/mydatabase  engine = create_engine(db_url) print(engine.url.render_as_string(hide_password=False)) # postgresql+pg8000://scott:notareal[password]@localhost:5432/mydatabase # The password is no longer url encoded. ```   ### Error  I am using AWS xray which monkey patches `Session`. The [monkey patched code](https://github.com/aws/aws-xray-sdk-python/blob/master/aws_xray_sdk/ext/sqlalchemy_core/patch.py#L17C27-L17C28) uses `urllib.parse.urlparse` on the string returned by URL's `render_as_string`. title: sqlalchemy need to relax certain server capacities assumption and better handle the errors to work with more databases
body: ### Describe the use case  A fix will allow sqlalchemy to work with some database servers implemented enough postgres wire protocol but not all the PostgreSQL features assumed by sqlalchemy.  ### Description sqlalchemyattempted to use queries in   ```  engine.default.get_server_version_info()  engine.default.._get_default_schema_name()  engine.default..get_default_isolation_level() ``` and ```  dialects.postgresql.PGDialect.self._set_backslash_escapes() ```  to probe and enable features for PostgreSQL and compatible databases. While there are good reasons, they could fail with unhandled errors for database servers that support enough postgres wire protocol and features but otherwise doesn't support these particular functionalities. In particular, sqlalchemy assumed the error would always be NotImplementedError in get_server_version_info() and proceeded to use  server_version_info without further check the None condition arise from NotImplementedError. However, for drivers like pg8000, errors like ProgrammingError would be thrown instead. To make sqlalchemy usable for the many different drivers and servers combinations, it is desirable to make sqlalchemy as lenient as possible without detrimental side effects.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  A fix is tested with arcadedb 23.10.1 with pg8000. It is possible this will also fix for other servers implemented enough postgres wire protocols  ### Example Use  After the fix, the following code works ``` from sqlalchemy import create_engine import pandas as pd  engine = create_engine(     'postgresql+pg8000://' + os.environ['DB_USER'] + ':' + os.environ['DB_PASS'] + '@localhost:3333/arcade_testdb', isolation_level="AUTOCOMMIT",     connect_args={'ssl_context': None} ) df = pd.read_sql_query("select * from schema:database", con=engine) engine.dispose() ```  ### Additional context  _No response_

body: Since version 1.4 that added support for relationship refresh, the implementation is sub-optimal, since it will always perform a query to the model table, followed by a query to the related table.  ```py from __future__ import annotations  from sqlalchemy import create_engine from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey from sqlalchemy import select from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase from sqlalchemy.orm import lazyload from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship from sqlalchemy.orm import Session   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class A(Base):     __tablename__ = "a"      id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     bs: Mapped[list[B]] = relationship("B", lazy="raise")   class B(Base):     __tablename__ = "b"     id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     a_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("a.id"))   e = create_engine("sqlite://", echo=True) Base.metadata.create_all(e)  s = Session(e)  s.add(A(bs=[B()])) s.commit()  a1 = s.scalar(select(A))  s.refresh(a1, [ 'bs']) print(a1.bs) ```  In the above script the refresh runs these two queries. ``` 2023-11-09 19:29:41,979 INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT a.id FROM a WHERE a.id = ? 2023-11-09 19:29:41,979 INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00013s] (1,) 2023-11-09 19:29:41,980 INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine SELECT b.id AS b_id, b.a_id AS b_a_id FROM b WHERE ? = b.a_id 2023-11-09 19:29:41,980 INFO sqlalchemy.engine.Engine [generated in 0.00013s] (1,) [<__main__.B object at 0x0000015C12C010A0>] ```  The objective of the issue would be to remove the first one. title: Confusing documentation on delete cascades and many-to-many relationships.
body: ### Describe the bug  In the documentation on cascades, the [*Using delete cascade with many-to-many relationships* section](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/cascades.html#using-delete-cascade-with-many-to-many-relationships) contains this text:  > The `cascade="all, delete"` option works equally well with a many-to-many relationship, one that uses [relationship.secondary](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/relationship_api.html#sqlalchemy.orm.relationship.params.secondary) to indicate an association table.  The whole section then repeatedly references `cascade="all, delete"`. Given that `all` already includes `delete`,  I found this text confusing. Why not simply talk about using `delete` in  `cascade`, mentioning that `all` includes `delete`?  Next, I think it needs to be made explicit on what to use when you *don't* want objects on the opposite side of the many-to-many relationship to be deleted. This would be the case for *most* many-to-many releationships, given that the opposite object can be part of multiple such relationships. The use of `cascade="all, delete"` in this section might give the impression that using `cascade="all"` without the `delete` would be sufficient to prevent this. I'd prefer it if the documentation were to make this more explicit  (e.g. use, at most, `cascade="save-update, merge, refresh-expire, expunge"`). title: create new string subclass for bit strings for PG drivers
body: the behavior of the BIT type, given a value like "3", uses these conversions right now for the different drivers:  ```py         dialect_map = {             "asyncpg": lambda value: testing.db.dialect.dbapi.asyncpg.BitString.from_int(value, length=3),             "pg8000": "{:03b}".format,             "psycopg2": "{:03b}".format,             "psycopg": "{:03b}".format,         } ```  all drivers except asyncpg use a specific bitstring, asyncpg requires a special type that is not actually compatible with strings (an odd design choice):  ``` >>> BitString.from_int(value, length=3) == "{:03b}".format(3) False ```  We will make our own BitString in the spirit of how we did [range types](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/commit/fce1d954aa57feca9c163f9d8cf66df5e8ce7b65) which will be handled by the asyncpg driver and also *compare equally with strings*, so that people using plain strings retain compatibility.  it should likely be a string subclass.     The BIT type for asyncpg should accommodate on the bind side all three of: plain string, sqlalchemy.dialects.postgresql.BitString, and the asyncpg BitString type.  it should return the SQLAlchemy BitString type.  For all other dialects, the bind side should accommodate plain string and sqlalchemy BitString, returning BitString.  BitString itself is a string subclass that is basically the string, like '011' for the value 3.  it should compare/ hash to other BitStrings and to the plain string version.   it likely can't hash against asyncpg.BitString since the hash values are very different:  ```py >>> b = BitString.from_int(3, length=3) >>> hash(b) -3219509243244691321 >>> hash('011') -1632922142275036455  ```  our own BitString should have from_int classmethod like asyncpgs and to_int.  this issue continues from #10532 where we are just getting BIT to work for our current round trips.

title: Conflict in Instrumentation between SQLAlchemy and Pydantic Leading to AttributeError
body: ### Describe the bug  When using SQLAlchemy with Pydantic's dataclass integration for defining ORM models, there is an inconsistency in the behavior of object instantiation and relationship setting. The issue arises when creating multiple instances of a SQLAlchemy model and setting relationships via the initializer (constructor). The first object instantiation and relationship setting work as expected, but subsequent instantiations lead to an `AttributeError`, specifically stating that the object has no attribute `_sa_instance_state`.  This issue appears to be related to the way SQLAlchemy and Pydantic apply instrumentation to the class. SQLAlchemy applies dataclass instrumentation first and then its own ORM instrumentation. However, after the first instantiation, Pydantic seems to interfere and reapply its instrumentation, which leads to conflicts and results in the error for subsequent object instantiations.  ## Steps to Reproduce:  - Define SQLAlchemy ORM models using Pydantic's dataclass integration. - Create an instance of a model and set a relationship via the initializer. - Commit this instance to the database. - Create another instance of the same model and set a relationship via the initializer. - Observe the `AttributeError` on the second instantiation.  ## Expected Behavior:  Multiple instances of a model should be instantiated and relationships set without encountering an AttributeError, regardless of the order or number of instances created.  ## Actual Behavior:  The first instance is created and committed successfully. However, creating subsequent instances with relationships set via the initializer leads to an AttributeError, indicating a conflict in the ORM instrumentation applied by SQLAlchemy and Pydantic.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  _No response_  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.22  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  aiosqlite  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  SQLit

title: support NULL passed through literal_processor
body: right now a None value that's passed through the compiler for literal_processor() is passed in, and none of the handlers expect None and just return None, where the compiler then renders nothing.    Changes should be as follows:  1. the compiler, when it sees the value is None, returns the string NULL or otherwise uses a render_null() method of some kind; it does **not** send the data to the literal_processor() for the type, **unless** should_evaluate_none on the type is set 2. all the types that have literal_processor() and do not have "should_evaluate_none" can assume the value passed is non None 3. tests for JSON/JSONB doing "evaluate none" style tests should be added; the base test_literal_round_trip() suite should do a NULL round trip for all datatypes  this could be a 2.0 thing or a 2.1 thing

title: Duplicated table constraint names for tables using naming convention and extending from an abstract table
body: ### Describe the bug  When creating multiple tables which inherit from an abstract table, table constraints which use the `table_name` token are assigned the value of the first table name.  I.e. If there is an abstract class `MyBaseTable` which defines a check constraint to be `ck_%(table_name)s_%(constraint_name)s`, the expectation is that for tables `alpha` and `beta` which inherit from `MyBaseTable`, that the constraints would be named `ck_alpha_my_constraint_name` and `ck_beta_my_constraint_name`, but the result is `ck_alpha_my_constraint_name` for both tables.  In SQL Server, this causes an error, because a constraint name must be unique within the database.  The stack trace below is from where it generates an error in **SQL Server** and was run on **SQLAlchemy 1.4.49.**  The code to reproduce the error uses **SQLite** and was run on **SQLAlchemy 2.0.21,** which does not generate an error, but the problem can be seen in the output of this code provided under "Additional Context", where `ck_alpha_my_constraint` should have been `ck_beta_my_constraint`.  ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/constraints.html#configuring-constraint-naming-conventions  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  2.0.21 and 1.4.49  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  pyodbc and sqlite3  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  SQL Server 2016 and SQLite 3  ### Python Version  3.10  ### Operating system  Linux  ### To Reproduce  ```python from sqlalchemy import (     create_engine,     Integer,     Column,     CheckConstraint,     MetaData, ) from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base   # As found in the example at https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/constraints.html#configuring-a-naming-convention-for-a-metadata-collection constraint_naming_conventions = {     "ix": "ix_%(column_0_label)s",     "uq": "uq_%(table_name)s_%(column_0_name)s",     "ck": "ck_%(table_name)s_%(constraint_name)s",     "

I followed the example and added the classes. Post this I ran the `alembic revision --autogenerate` to auto generate the migration scripts. This generated the migration scripts.  I tweaked the example a bit and moved this composite column definition to a base unmapped class and had a concrete mapped class extend this class. Post this the auto-generation fails.  **Expected behavior** I expect the auto generation to work when I define a composite column on a base unmapped class.   **To Reproduce**  Example 1 works, example 2 doesn't work.  ```py import dataclasses from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, MappedAsDataclass, composite, mapped_column  class Base(MappedAsDataclass, DeclarativeBase):     pass  @dataclasses.dataclass class Point:     x: int     y: int  # Example 1  # as per tutorial in https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/composites.html#composite-column-types # added composite columns start and end # auto-generation works for this  class Vertex(Base):     __tablename__ = "vertices"      id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)      start: Mapped[Point] = composite(mapped_column("x1"), mapped_column("y1"))     end: Mapped[Point] = composite(mapped_column("x2"), mapped_column("y2"))  # Example 2 # moved composite columns start, end to base unmapped class # added a concrete mapped class that extends this class # auto-generation fails for this  class BaseVertex(Base):     __abstract__ = True      id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)      start: Mapped[Point] = composite(mapped_column("x1"), mapped_column("y1"))     end: Mapped[Point] = composite(mapped_column("x2"), mapped_column("y2"))   class NamedVertex(BaseVertex):     __tablename__ = "named_vertex"     name: Mapped[str] = mappe

title: When using sort_order inside Annotated[...,mapped_column()], it doesn't work.
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10363
Originally posted by **ClanEver** September 19, 2023 code ```python from datetime import datetime from typing import Annotated from sqlalchemy import BigInteger, DateTime, String, create_engine, func from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column engine = create_engine( f"postgresql+psycopg://{DB_DICT['user']}:{DB_DICT['password']}@{DB_DICT['host']}:{DB_DICT['port']}/{DB_DICT['name']}", pool_pre_ping=True, echo=True, ) pk = Annotated[int, mapped_column(BigInteger(), primary_key=True, autoincrement=True, sort_order=-100)] create_at = Annotated[datetime, mapped_column(DateTime(timezone=True), default=func.now(), sort_order=100)] update_at = Annotated[datetime, mapped_column(DateTime(timezone=True), default=func.now(), sort_order=101)] str_50 = Annotated[str, mapped_column(String(50), default='')] class BaseModel(DeclarativeBase): create_at: Mapped[create_at] update_at: Mapped[update_at] id: Mapped[pk] class Video(BaseModel): __tablename__ = 'video' name: Mapped[str_50] BaseModel.metadata.create_all(engine) ``` result ``` CREATE TABLE video ( name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, create_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL, update_at TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE NOT NULL, id BIGSERIAL NOT NULL, PRIMARY KEY (id) ) ``` It looks like sort_order is ignored. Is this a bug? SQLAlchemy Version: 2.0.21
To resolve the general id would be: - ensure that sort_order is copied from annotated - add a test that automatically checks that all args of `mapped_column` are tested to be copied / not supported with a warning / error of some kind

title: with_loader_criteria not applied to explicit ON clause in ORMJoin
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10364  ```py from sqlalchemy import orm from sqlalchemy import select from sqlalchemy import String from sqlalchemy.orm import declarative_base from sqlalchemy.orm import foreign from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column from sqlalchemy.orm import relationship  Base = declarative_base()   class Tenant:     tenant_id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column("tenant_id", String(), primary_key=True)   class A(Base):     __tablename__ = "a"      id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)      bs = relationship("B", primaryjoin=lambda: A.id == foreign(B.a_id))  class B(Tenant, Base):     __tablename__ = "b"      a_id: Mapped[str] = mapped_column()   crit = orm.with_loader_criteria(             Tenant,             lambda cls: cls.tenant_id == "1",             propagate_to_loaders=True,             track_closure_variables=True,             include_aliases=True,         )  stmt1 = select(A, B).join(B, A.bs).options(crit) stmt2 = select(A, B).join(B, A.id == B.a_id).options(crit)  # criteira is applied print(stmt1)  # criteria is not applied print(stmt2) ```  so this patch makes stmt2 work, but then stmt1 gets double criteria, leading me to think this conditional has unintended side effects:  ```diff diff --git a/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py b/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py index f22a798803..f142f3b326 100644 --- a/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py +++ b/lib/sqlalchemy/orm/util.py @@ -1884,7 +1884,8 @@ class _ORMJoin(expression.Join):                      {"parententity": parententity}                  )   -        augment_onclause = onclause is None and _extra_criteria +        #augment_onclause = onclause is None and _extra_criteria +        augment_onclause = bool(_extra_criteria)          expression.Join.__init__(self, left, right, onclause, isouter, full)            assert self.onclause is not None  ```

title: need to somehow back-off subtype checks in strategy options to suit the selectin_polymorphic() subclass load case
body: we document this pattern:  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/queryguide/inheritance.html#combining-additional-loader-options-with-selectin-polymorphic-subclass-loads  ```py from sqlalchemy.orm import selectinload from sqlalchemy.orm import selectin_polymorphic stmt = (     select(Employee)     .order_by(Employee.id)     .options(         selectin_polymorphic(Employee, [Manager, Engineer]),         selectinload(Manager.paperwork),     ) ) objects = session.scalars(stmt).all() print(objects[0]) print(objects[0].paperwork) ```  What's awkward there is we are allowing `selectinload(Manager.paperwork)` to exist in a query that's against `Employee`.  Trying to do this for any kind of pathing obviously fails:  ```py stmt = select(Company).options(     selectinload(Company.employees).options(             selectin_polymorphic(Employee, [Manager]),             selectinload(Manager.paperwork)     ),  )  ```  and  ```py stmt = select(Company).options(     selectinload(Company.employees).selectin_polymorphic(Employee, [Manager]),     selectinload(Company.employees).selectinload(Manager.paperwork) )  ```  with, as expected:  ``` sqlalchemy.exc.ArgumentError: ORM mapped entity or attribute "Manager.paperwork" does not link from relationship "Company.employees".  Did you mean to use "Company.employees.of_type(Manager)"?  ```  that's an important error.  We need to raise that, that's a major path people need to know about. title: Support `Final[Mapped[...]]` in the ORM
body: In some cases generics are consired invariant since the mapped descriptors are not declared as final. While this use case for this is likely very small, it should not be too hard to support the following form: ```py from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship   class Base(DeclarativeBase):     pass   class Parent(Base):     __tablename__ = "parent"      name: Final[Mapped[str]] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     some_other_col: Final[Mapped[str]] = mapped_column()   class Child(Base):     __tablename__ = "child"      name: Final[Mapped[str]] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)     parent_name: Final[Mapped[str]] = mapped_column(ForeignKey(Parent.name))      parent: Final[Mapped[Parent]] = relationship()  ```  This core currently raises the following error ``` sqlalchemy.exc.ArgumentError: Type annotation for "Parent.name" can't be correctly interpreted for Annotated Declarative Table form.  ORM annotations should normally make use of the ``Mapped[]`` generic type, or other ORM-compatible generic type, as a container for the actual type, which indicates the intent that the attribute is mapped. Class variables that are not intended to be mapped by the ORM should use ClassVar[].  To allow Annotated Declarative to disregard legacy annotations which don't use Mapped[] to pass, set "__allow_unmapped__ = True" on the class or a superclass this class. (Background on this error at: https://sqlalche.me/e/20/zlpr) ```  Other than this, the most notable thins is that `some_other_col` requires a value assigned to it using an empty mapped_column()

title: Allow  InstrumentedAttribute  in corresponding_column
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10325
Originally posted by **CaselIT** September 8, 2023 Currently InstrumentedAttribute is not a KeyedColumnElement so trying to use `corresponding_column` and similar raises a typing error This does not seem correct since at runtime it it seems to work ```py from typing import TYPE_CHECKING from sqlalchemy import Select from sqlalchemy.orm import column_property from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase from sqlalchemy.orm import Mapped from sqlalchemy.orm import mapped_column class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass class Widget(Base): __tablename__ = "widget" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) data: Mapped[int] if TYPE_CHECKING: foo: Mapped[int] Widget.foo = column_property((Widget.data + 1).label('foo')) q = select(Widget) print(q) s = q.subquery() print(s.columns.corresponding_column(Widget.foo)) print(Widget.data.key, s.columns.corresponding_column(Widget.data)) ``` the above prints ``` SELECT widget.id, widget.data, widget.data + :data_1 AS foo FROM widget anon_1.foo anon_1.data ```
### Mike suggestion: KeyedColumnElement is a ColumnElement that has a string .key attribute. InstrumentedAttribute objects are not ColumnElement objects. it's technically not correect to send InstrumentedAttribute to .corresponding_column() right now since the latter does not use coercion, it just "happens" to work by accident right now. .corresponding_column() can be improved to formally accept objects with coercsion added, in which case it would accept something like roles.ColumnArgumentRole, something very basic like that. of coruse if we add coercion to .corresponding_column(), all the internals should be switched to use a private version that does not have this performance overhead since this method is fairly performance critical

title: Allow using Enum with length=None
body: ### Describe the use case  When using string-based enum types, i.e. `Enum(python_enum,  native_enum=False)`, the default behavior is to use `String(N)` with N set to the length of the longest enum member name. This can break if new enum members are added in the future with longer names. If the default behavior cannot be changed, the issue can be solved by explicitly passing `length=None`, which removes the string length limit. This almost works, except that it breaks the check here: https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/09d247d57ffb6329739deae89019c9e7ad3b9e7f/lib/sqlalchemy/sql/sqltypes.py#L1454 This can be further worked-around by passing an undocumented argument `_disable_warnings=True`. It would be nice if the latter was not required. title: Reappearance of Deleted Rows while Versioning with a History Table
body: ### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10259  <div type='discussions-op-text'>  <sup>Originally posted by **PHvL** August 18, 2023</sup> We are using the [Versioned class from history_meta](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/examples.html#module-examples.versioned_history) for tables that are synced from some external source. Sometimes rows disappear in the external source and later re-appear with the same primary key,  The result is that both the history table and the original table contain a row with `version=1`, resulting in a violation of the primary key constraint of the history table at the next update (or deletion) of this row.  I've hence changed the default value of the version column in the history table to get the maximum of the version already present in history columns +1  I don't know if this is the most elegant solution, but maybe it helps someone with the same issue.  ```diff @@ -11,6 +11,9 @@ from sqlalchemy import inspect  from sqlalchemy import Integer  from sqlalchemy import PrimaryKeyConstraint  from sqlalchemy import util +from sqlalchemy import select +from sqlalchemy.sql.expression import func, and_ +from sqlalchemy.engine.default import DefaultExecutionContext  from sqlalchemy.orm import attributes  from sqlalchemy.orm import object_mapper  from sqlalchemy.orm.exc import UnmappedColumnError @@ -146,8 +149,15 @@ def _history_mapper(local_mapper):  				super_history_table.append_column(col)    	if not super_mapper: +		def default_version_from_history(context: DefaultExecutionContext): +			current_parameters = context.get_current_parameters() +			return context.connection.scalar(select(func.coalesce(func.max(history_table.c.version), 0)+1).where(and_(*[getattr(history_table.c, c.name)==current_parameters.get(c.name, None) for c in inspect(local_mapper.local_table).primary_key]))) +		# Set default value of version column to the maximum of the version in history columns already present +1 +		# Otherwise re-appear

title: Request to make NullPool the default - fixes massive footgun with Render.com and DigitalOcean
body: ### Describe the bug  Hi there, I found a nasty bug that is affecting literally ALL of our projects for the org that I work for. I did it, the contractor that work for us did it. So I wanted to bring this up for discussion.  # SQL Alchemy uses a connection Pool by default  So what's the big deal? Well, both DigitalOcean and Render.com kill these connections at the os level after a certain amount of time has passed. SQLAlchemy then *blindly* attempts to use these dead connections and bombs out the server request with an error 500. My expectation as a developer would be that SQLAlchemy could auto-recover from this but it doesn't, and this is surprising.  # This bug is nasty and sporadic and infrequently happens during development  During an app redeploy, all connections are cleared out and the pool is torn down and then reinstantiated when the app is brought back online. As a result, these dead connections are largely hidden from the developer and go away as soon as they start pushing code, for example adding logging to investigate. Then after a length of time the app starts to degrade again. I caught this issue because I added logging in the proper place and was able to see the server logs to see the error:  ``` (psycopg2.OperationalError) SSL connection has been closed unexpectedly ```  # New apps don't need a connection pool until they start to scale  And when apps need to scale, developers are willing to put in the time and energy to find these optimizations. title: inspect.has_table() with SQLAlchemy 2.0's MySQLDialect leaves transaction open
body: ### Describe the bug  After calling `insp.has_table()` using sqlalchemy 1.4, the connection passed to `inspect(connection)` does not have an open transaction, according to `connection.in_transaction()`. However, performing the same steps using sqlalchemy 2 results in an open transaction on the connection following the call to `insp.has_table()`.    ### Optional link from https://docs.sqlalchemy.org which documents the behavior that is expected  https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/core/reflection.html#sqlalchemy.engine.reflection.Inspector.has_table  ### SQLAlchemy Version in Use  1.4.49 and 2.0.19  ### DBAPI (i.e. the database driver)  mysqlclient  ### Database Vendor and Major Version  MySQL 8  ### Python Version  3.10  ### Operating system  macOS  ### To Reproduce  ```python # Run using `sqlalchemy==1.4.49`, then `sqlalchemy==2.0.49`  from sqlalchemy import create_engine from sqlalchemy import inspect  engine = create_engine(url="mysql+mysqldb://root:password@127.0.0.1:3306/") with engine.connect() as conn:     insp = inspect(conn)     ret = insp.has_table("missing", "default")     assert conn.in_transaction() is False ```   ### Error  The issue does not produce an error, only a behavior change.  ### Additional context  I can't be sure this isn't user error, but the documentation doesn't specify here and the behavior change broke something of ours dependent on the 1.4.x behavior. We're in the process of migrating to 2.0, and if it's not a bug, I was hoping to at least get clarification on why/how best to handle this change.  I noticed the function changed significantly across major versions, from https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/a7438bba206f5ffa2a14cd9398354ba78fed7b6e/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/mysql/base.py#L2640-L2660 to https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/9e89d2cbbf7ccef05579472b94c90124a1ecf9e3/lib/sqlalchemy/dialects/mysql/base.py#L2684-L2727  Thank you!

title: Reuse of bindparams with literal_execute in positional dialects overwrites past values
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10141
Originally posted by **tmrlvi** July 25, 2023 When using `bindparam` in `literal_execute`, I get wrong output if I reuse the same bindparam twice. I suspect it is a bug. For example, ``` from sqlalchemy import select, create_engine, bindparam conn = create_engine(f"sqlite://").connect() a = bindparam("a", value="abc", literal_execute=True) b = bindparam("b", value="def", literal_execute=True) c = bindparam("c", value="ghi", literal_execute=True) print(conn.execute(select(a,b,a,c)).fetchone()) ``` **Expected:** ('abc', 'def', 'abc', 'ghi') **Actual:** ('def', 'def', 'def', 'ghi') Note that `print(conn.execute(select(a,b,c)).fetchone())` and `print(conn.execute(select(a,a,b,c)).fetchone())` works as expected. The problem is repeating `a` after `b` or `c`. I was able to track it down to `SQLCompiler._process_parameters_for_postcompile` where in `replacement_expressions` the value are overwritten incorrectly, but the root cause is somewhere else.

title: Support for mysql syntax "for share skip locked"
body: ### Describe the use case  Currently, `select().for_update_clause(read=True)` generates the query `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`. There are 2 ways to accomplish that in mysql: LOCK IN SHARE MODE and FOR SHARE. LOCK IN SHARE MODE doesn't support SKIP LOCKED, so `.with_for_update(read=True, skip_locked=True)` will generate  LOCK IN SHARE MODE SKIP LOCKED which is invalid, and will cause the mysql server to return an error. if LOCK IN SHARE MODE was changed to FOR SHARE, it would work properly.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  Mysql 8.x  ### Example Use  `select(...).with_for_update(read=True, skip_locked=True)`  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: object not in collection warning not emitted for pending backref members
body: ### Describe the bug  A bi-directional relationship will not be kept in sync if the many side is unloaded, and the one side sets a value. However, if the many side is loaded, then they stay in sync. I am not sure which is intended, but it seems odd that the loading strategy can have this effect. title: Local connection pools do not work with multiprocessing
body: ### Describe the bug  According to this documentation, it should be possible to pass an engine to a multiprocessing pool, as long as the connections are properly disposed. However, the documentation assumes that the engine is a global variable and can be pickled. I am attempting to pass an engine that is a local variable to a process pool, and it is resulting in a pickling error, which looks like it may be because of some unpickleable local functions in the engine. title: Possibility to use callable for relationship.back_populates and ForeignKey.column
body:
### Discussed in https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/discussions/10049
Originally posted by **AlexanderPodorov** July 1, 2023 Given this option we could make existing mapping more robust and reliable for refactoring. Current code, example from [here](https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/orm/basic_relationships.html#declarative-vs-imperative-forms): ```python class Parent(Base): __tablename__ = "parent_table" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) children: Mapped[List["Child"]] = relationship(back_populates="parent") class Child(Base): __tablename__ = "child_table" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) parent_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("parent_table.id")) parent: Mapped["Parent"] = relationship(back_populates="children") ``` Suggested example code: ```python from __future__ import annotations class Parent(Base): __tablename__ = "parent_table" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) children: Mapped[List[Child]] = relationship(back_populates=lambda: Child.parent) class Child(Base): __tablename__ = "child_table" id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True) parent_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey(lambda: Parent.id)) parent: Mapped[Parent] = relationship(back_populates=lambda: Parent.children) ``` In the above example if we rename any of attributes, the mapping will still work. No need to manually rename `back_populates` and foreign key column name. Please note that `lambda` is kind of required here to enable forward references and lazy evaluation of attributes. What do you think? Thanks.

title: Patch 1.4.x with improved mapper derivation
body: ### Describe the use case  In the process of upgrading `flask_sqlalchemy` we discovered an issue where mapper is not derived inside the session for legacy query API (I am not sure if this is also the case for new style API because codebase is too large to check). In particular we use UNION operator and subsequent query fails to find appropriate mapper for this.  A complete test is described here: https://github.com/pallets-eco/flask-sqlalchemy/issues/1231  Briefly, it appears that `bind_arguments` do not contain a `mapper` and bind resolution using `clause` does work. Upgrading to sqlalchemy 2.0.17 this is resolved. Unfortunately other libraries we have have a hard pin of `sqlalchemy<2` E.g. `sqlalchemy-bigquery` and these guys don't have an ETA for v2 upgrade (https://github.com/googleapis/python-bigquery-sqlalchemy/issues/510)  In particular I traced the fix to be in 2.0.15 (2.0.14 fails the test I have reported in https://github.com/pallets-eco/flask-sqlalchemy/issues/1231). Looking at the comparison between the two tags (https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/compare/rel_2_0_14...rel_2_0_15) most likely fix was done by @zzzeek to deal with https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/issues/9805 issue.  Can we port this fix to 1.4.x?  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  I have tested with postgres and sqlite, however I think all backends will be affected.  ### Example Use  Unfortunately I was not able to create pure sqlalchemy example, see https://github.com/pallets-eco/flask-sqlalchemy/issues/1231 for usecase  ### Additional context  _No response_

title: SQLAlchemy asyncpg dialect doesn't support mutlihost connection string
body: ### Describe the use case  You should be able to setup DSN connection string for multiple databases. Like: ```python url_str = "postgresql+asyncpg://user:password@/dbname?host=host1:5432&host=host2:5432" engine = create_async_engine(url=url_str) ```  host1:5432 - is main db connection host2:5432 - fallback connection   ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  `postgresql` `asyncpg` dialect  ### Example Use   ```python import asyncio from sqlalchemy import text from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine  async def async_main() -> None:     engine = create_async_engine(         "postgresql+asyncpg://user:password@/dbname?host=host1:5432&host=host2:5432"     )      async with engine.begin() as conn:         res = await conn.execute(             text("select 1")         )      await engine.dispose()  asyncio.run(async_main()) ```  ### Additional context  This works for `postgrsql+psycopg2`  Section: `Specifying multiple fallback hosts` https://docs.sqlalchemy.org/en/20/dialects/postgresql.html#specifying-multiple-fallback-hosts  Found old issues in asyncpg Driver https://github.com/MagicStack/asyncpg/issues/840

title: PyODBC for PostgreSQL support
body: ### Describe the use case  For short - Literally want to use PyODBC on PostgreSQL dialect.  I am using AWS RedShift, which speaks PSQL protocol.  And my code runs in a protected environment, I cannot touch public network without proxy.  The feasible solution for me is to use AWS's official [ODBC driver](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/redshift/latest/mgmt/configure-odbc-connection.html), but currently we do not have PyODBC support on PSQL.  I know there is [sqlalchemy-redshift](https://github.com/sqlalchemy-redshift/sqlalchemy-redshift/) project - they bring [redshift-connector](https://pypi.org/project/redshift-connector/) to sqlalchemy. I didn't see an official document using proxy so it isn't work for me.  ### Databases / Backends / Drivers targeted  - Database: AWS RedShift - Dialect: PostgreSQL - Driver: PyODBC  ### Example Use  For general use cases:  ```py postgresql_engine = create_engine(     "postgresql+pyodbc://scott:tiger@hostname/dbname", ) ```  For personal use case:  ```py import urllib connection_string = (     'DRIVER=/opt/amazon/redshift/lib/amazonredshiftodbc.dylib;'     'SERVER=example.redshift.amazonaws.com;'     'PORT=5439;'     'DATABASE=mydb;'     'UID=root;'     'PWD=(whatever);'     'ProxyHost=proxy;'     'ProxyPort=3128;' ) params = urllib.parse.quote_plus(connection_string) connection_uri = "postgresql+pyodbc:///?odbc_connect=%s" % params ```  `ProxyHost` and `ProxyPort` are special connection string consumed by [Amazon Redshift ODBC Data Connector](https://s3.amazonaws.com/redshift-downloads/drivers/odbc/1.4.65.1000/Amazon+Redshift+ODBC+Connector+Install+Guide.pdf)  ### Additional context  I feel it could be achieved by adopting [PyODBC connector](https://github.com/sqlalchemy/sqlalchemy/blob/main/lib/sqlalchemy/connectors/pyodbc.py) to PSQL dialect.  If no further concern, I could work on PR.

title: Saving a configuration mutates its Enum values and empty dictionaries
body: ### Describe the bug  `BaseConfig.to_dict()` converts values in `self.__dict__` in place. Saving a `ClusterConfig` to JSON or YAML therefore also replaces its Enum attributes with strings and its empty configuration dictionaries with `None`. Code that edits the same configuration object after saving can then fail.  ### Reproduction  ```python from accelerate.commands.config.config_args import ClusterConfig  config = ClusterConfig(     compute_environment="LOCAL_MACHINE",     distributed_type="NO",     mixed_precision="no",     use_cpu=True,     debug=False, ) print(config.dynamo_config)  # {} config.to_dict()             # also happens with to_json_file / to_yaml_file print(config.dynamo_config)  # None config.dynamo_config["dynamo_backend"] = "eager" # TypeError: 'NoneType' object does not support item assignment ```  Expected: serialization leaves the original configuration usable and unchanged. The output dictionary should contain the converted values. Nested dictionaries are also mutated today, so a shallow copy is insufficient.  ### Environment  - Accelerate 1.16.0.dev0 from main - Python 3.13.13, PyTorch 2.14.0, macOS arm64 - Local CPU reproduction; no distributed launch or saved Accelerate configuration required  A fix and regression tests are ready: serialize a deep copy of the attribute dictionary. Tests exercise dictionary, JSON, and YAML serialization, nested Enum conversion, empty mappings, and output independence. All three new subtests fail before the patch. Afterward, `tests/test_cli.py` reports 35 passed, 9 skipped, and 8 subtests passed.  AI assistance was used to investigate, implement, and test the patch.

title: split_between_processes crashes on tuples when apply_padding=True
body: `split_between_processes` documents `tuple` as an accepted input type, but combining it with `apply_padding=True` raises a TypeError on every rank:  ``` TypeError: can only concatenate tuple (not "list") to tuple ```  The padding gets concatenated to `result` as a list, but `result` is a tuple slice, and `tuple += list` fails even when there is nothing to pad, so this fails no matter how the data divides up.  Repro with `torchrun --nproc_per_node=2`:  ```python from accelerate.state import PartialState  state = PartialState(cpu=True) with state.split_between_processes((1, 2, 3), apply_padding=True) as out:     print(out) ```  Lists work fine, tuples die on both ranks. Seen on main (1.16.0.dev0) with torch 2.5.1, on CPU and CUDA.

title: [Bug] FSDP2 + fp16: load_state() does not round-trip the GradScaler state
body: ### Fixes  #4291   ### Summary  Under FSDP2 with `mixed_precision="fp16"`, `Accelerator.load_state()` does not restore the `GradScaler` state it saved.    | When `load_state()` runs | Symptom | | --- | --- | | In a fresh process (the normal resume) | The restored loss scale differs from `scaler.pt` with no warning. | | In a process whose scaler has already been used (train → save → load) | `AssertionError: _growth_tracker initialized before _scale` |  The cause is that `load_fsdp_optimizer` hands torch's optimizer DCP API an`AcceleratedOptimizer`.  `torch.distributed.checkpoint.state_dict._init_optim_state` materializes an empty optimizer state by calling `optimizer.step()`, and through the wrapper that dummy step runs `scaler.step()` and `scaler.update()`, which advances the very scaler state that was just restored.  The workaround currently in `load_state` ([`accelerator.py:3863-3876`](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/b795b4838eb33bde60eb398649c4ab006874e3e9/src/accelerate/accelerator.py#L3863-L3876), added in #3671) pre-initializes the scaler so that `scaler.step()` does not hit its own `_scale is None` assertion. title: `PrefixedDataset` violates the `Mapping` contract
body: ## Description  `accelerate.utils.offload.PrefixedDataset` wraps a mapping and exposes only the keys under a given prefix. Two of its `Mapping` methods are inconsistent with `__getitem__`:  - `__getitem__` expects *unprefixed* keys (`dataset[f"{prefix}{key}"]`), but   `__iter__` yields the raw, still-prefixed keys of the underlying mapping.   Iterating a `PrefixedDataset` therefore produces keys that raise `KeyError`   when passed back to `__getitem__`, and `dict(prefixed)` / `prefixed[key]` /   `key in prefixed` are unusable. - `__len__` returns the length of the whole underlying mapping, not the number   of entries under the prefix.  ## Reproduction  ```python from accelerate.utils import PrefixedDataset  dataset = {"block1.weight": 0, "block1.bias": 1, "block2.weight": 2} prefixed = PrefixedDataset(dataset, "block1.")  len(prefixed)          # -> 3, expected 2 list(prefixed)         # -> ["block1.weight", "block1.bias"], expected ["weight", "bias"] dict(prefixed)         # -> KeyError: 'block1.block1.weight' ```  ## Expected behavior  `__iter__` should yield the keys with the prefix stripped (so each yielded key can be passed to `__getitem__`), and `__len__` should count only the entries matching the prefix, making `PrefixedDataset` behave as a proper `Mapping` view of the prefixed sub-dictionary.  Note: the current single use site (`attach_align_device_hook`) only calls `weights_map[name]`, so this is a latent correctness bug rather than an active crash, but any `Mapping` consumer (`dict(...)`, `.keys()`, `in`, `len()`) misbehaves today.  ## Environment  - `accelerate` version: 1.16.0.dev0 (main, f13f7c1) - Python: 3.11

body: `find_executable_batch_size` re-raises on the first MPS out-of-memory error instead of lowering the batch size.  `should_reduce_batch_size` (`src/accelerate/utils/memory.py`, lines 108 to 116) matches on `" out of memory."`, with a trailing period. title: Add ep_size to ParallelismConfig so FSDP2 can compose with expert parallelism
body: ## Summary  `ParallelismConfig` currently has `dp_replicate`, `dp_shard`, `tp`, `cp`, and `sp`. There is no expert-parallel dimension. MoE training that wants FSDP2 on non-expert weights and a separate expert mesh has nowhere to put that axis, so every rank map and every `fully_shard` mesh has to be built outside Accelerate.  This is the Accelerate-side half of the FSDP2 × expert-parallelism work that #4178 / huggingface/transformers#48204 / huggingface/trl#6869 are driving. Those changes need a stable `DeviceMesh` with an `ep` axis; they should not each invent one.  ## Why this belongs in ParallelismConfig  `total_size` is the product of the configured sizes and is checked against `num_processes`. Without `ep_size`, a 2-way FSDP × 4-way EP layout on 8 GPUs cannot be expressed, and `prepare_data_loader` cannot treat EP ranks as a non-data-parallel group (same batch, like TP/CP).  FSDP2 preparation already does:  ```python mesh[tuple(accelerator.parallelism_config.fsdp_dim_names)] ```  `fsdp_dim_names` is `dp_replicate` + flattened `dp_shard_cp`. Expert weights must **not** sit on that mesh or they are sharded twice. The expert mesh has to be a sibling dimension, not a flatten target.  ## Proposal (config + mesh only)  Add `ep_size` (env `PARALLELISM_CONFIG_EP_SIZE`, CLI `--parallelism_config_ep_size`), default `1`.  - `total_size` and `non_data_parallel_size` include `ep_size` - `non_dp_dim_names` includes `"ep"` when `ep_size > 1` (same batch on all EP ranks) - `fsdp_dim_names` / `dp_shard_cp_dim_names` do **not** include `"ep"` - mesh order: `dp_replicate`, `dp_shard`, `cp`, `sp`, `ep`, `tp` (only enabled dims appear)  Expert placement (which modules are replicated vs sharded across `ep`) stays with the model / transformers. Accelerate only owns the mesh and the dataloader rank mapping. body: ## Summary  `Accelerator.prepare(dataloader)` always assumes the incoming loader is a *global* view of the dataset. In a distributed run it then wraps the sampler/dataset again (`BatchSamplerShard`, `IterableDatasetShard`, or `datasets.IterableDataset.shard()`). If the user already partitioned by rank, that second cut is silent data loss: each process keeps `1 / num_processes` of the shard it was given, the loss curve still looks normal, and there is no warning.  This is the same request as #4075 (closed stale) and the same idea as #4087 (closed stale, no review). #4144 documents the iterable path only. The code path is unchanged.  ## What happens today  In `prepare_data_loader`, when `num_processes != 1` and `dispatch_batches` is false:  1. **Map-style.** The `batch_sampler` is wrapped in `BatchSamplerShard`. A rank-aware `DistributedSampler` (or any custom per-rank sampler) is sharded a second time. 2. **Torch `IterableDataset`.** The dataset is wrapped in `IterableDatasetShard`, which iterates the *entire* underlying stream on every rank and keeps `1 / N`. A dataset that already yields only the local shard is cut again. Every rank also rereads the full source (`num_processes`× read amplification on remote/streaming data). 3. **HF `datasets.IterableDataset`.** If `n_shards >= num_processes`, Accelerate calls `.shard(...)` itself. A dataset the user already sharded is sharded again.  The usual workaround is to skip `prepare` on the dataloader. That also drops device placement, `set_epoch` forwarding, and dataloader state tracking.  ## Proposal  Add an explicit opt-in on `DataLoaderConfiguration`:  ```python accelerator = Accelerator(     dataloader_config=DataLoaderConfiguration(already_sharded=True) ) loader = accelerator.prepare(loader) ```  When `already_sharded=True`:  - do not wrap with `BatchSamplerShard` / `IterableDatasetShard` - do not call `datasets.IterableDataset.shard(...)` - still return `DataLoaderShard` so device placement, `set_epoch`, and state tr

title: Proposal: tutorial for sample-stable image augmentation across workers and resume
body: Hello Accelerate maintainers,  Would you be open to an optional tutorial showing how to make each image augmentation depend on the sample and epoch, rather than on whichever worker happens to request the sample first?  The current [`complete_cv_example.py`](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/main/examples/complete_cv_example.py) is a good setting for this problem: it trains on Oxford-IIIT Pets with four DataLoader workers, distributed preparation, checkpointing, and resume support. Accelerate can make the sampler sequence reproducible and can restore DataLoader position with `use_stateful_dataloader`. A third-party augmentation pipeline, however, can still own a separate random stream. If its next crop or flip is selected by call order, changing the worker/process schedule or resuming through a different path can give the same sample a different augmentation.  This is not an Accelerate bug, and the proposed tutorial would keep Accelerate's current seeding, sampler, and DataLoader-state mechanisms. It would document the remaining boundary: Accelerate decides which sample comes next, while the augmentation pipeline decides which transformation that sample receives. The existing [internal-mechanism guide](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/main/docs/source/concept_guides/internal_mechanism.md) already notes that RNG synchronization can affect random data augmentation; the tutorial would turn that warning into a runnable image example.  ## Proposed tutorial  I suggest a focused variant of the existing Pets example:  1. Keep the model, optimizer, `Accelerator.prepare()`, checkpointing, resume flow, and deterministic validation transform unchanged. 2. Use the image filename as a stable sample ID and combine it with the base seed and epoch. 3. Pass the derived value as AlbumentationsX's per-call `invocation_seed`, so the same `(epoch, sample_id)` receives the same crop, flip, and color realization regardless of call order. 4. Finish the AX pipeline

title: get_max_memory() adds a separate cpu entry on integrated CUDA GPUs, double-counting shared RAM (GB10 / DGX Spark)
body: ## Summary  `get_max_memory()` already treats shared memory correctly for MPS, but the same reasoning is not applied to integrated CUDA devices, so on those the returned budget counts the same physical RAM twice.  Current code (`src/accelerate/utils/modeling.py`, around L822):  ```python # allocate everything in the mps device as the RAM is shared if is_mps_available():     max_memory["mps"] = psutil.virtual_memory().available else:     max_memory["cpu"] = psutil.virtual_memory().available ```  The comment states the principle exactly: when RAM is shared, do not hand out a second pool. An NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark) shares its RAM the same way, but it is a CUDA device, so it takes the `else` branch and gets a separate `cpu` entry alongside its device entry.  Measured on a GB10:  ```python >>> import torch >>> from accelerate.utils import get_max_memory >>> torch.cuda.get_device_properties(0).is_integrated 1 >>> get_max_memory() {0: 73446760448, 'cpu': 87132405760} ```  73.4 GB + 87.1 GB = **160.5 GB advertised**, on a machine with:  ``` $ grep MemTotal /proc/meminfo MemTotal:       127535336 kB        # 127.5 GB ```  There is no separate device VRAM on this part. `torch.cuda.mem_get_info(0)` reports `free=74.1 GB, total=130.6 GB`, and those are the same bytes `/proc/meminfo` describes, reached over NVLink-C2C rather than PCIe. The two entries alias one pool: allocating against either shrinks the other, which the returned dict cannot express.  ## Why it matters  Everything downstream inherits the number. `infer_auto_device_map` and `device_map="auto"` treat the entries as independent capacities, so a model sized between the device entry and the sum can be planned to "fit" across a split whose halves are the same memory.  The hardware is not niche. body: ### Feature Request  I would like to request an option to tell Accelerate that a `DataLoader` is already sharded across processes, so that `Accelerator.prepare(dataloader)` can skip automatic dataloader sharding while still keeping the other `DataLoaderShard` features.  ### Motivation  Accelerate currently assumes that the input `DataLoader` represents a global view of the dataset. In distributed mode, `prepare_data_loader` wraps the original `batch_sampler` in `BatchSamplerShard` so each process receives a different subset of batches. title: [FSDP2] auto-exclude incompatible Params4bit from fully_shard to prevent silent QLoRA corruption
body: ## Summary  When FSDP2 is used with a QLoRA model using default `bnb_4bit_quant_storage` (uint8), `fully_shard()` either crashes or silently produces incorrect training results (`loss=0.0`, `grad_norm=nan`). There is no warning or error guiding users to the correct configuration.  `fsdp2_prepare_model()` already detects `Params4bit` and skips meta device movement. This proposal extends that pattern to also exclude incompatible `Params4bit` from sharding via `ignored_params`.  ## Library Info  - `torch`: 2.8.0+cu128 - `bitsandbytes`: 0.48.2 - `transformers`: 4.57.2  ## Context  Most QLoRA users don't set `bnb_4bit_quant_storage` explicitly, which defaults to uint8. The [official FSDP-QLoRA path](https://huggingface.co/docs/bitsandbytes/main/en/fsdp_qlora) requires setting it to a floating dtype (bf16/fp16/fp32) to make `Params4bit` compatible with FSDP sharding. title: activation_checkpointing=True uses *a lot* more memory than gradient_checkpointing=True *with FSDP 2.0* (FSDP 1.0 is fine)
body: Comparing models wrapper in FSDP-1 and FSDP-2  the issue seem to be that FSDP 2.0 wraps all *sub-modules* of transformer layer (for Qwen in my case, but same happens for other models) and it's certainly done on purpose (some interplay with sharding, @S1ro1  perhaps would know for sure?)  https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/db8835cc150c116f359122e6bc9dd66a9e480c37/src/accelerate/utils/fsdp_utils.py#L599           parent_module = model.get_submodule(parent_name) if parent_name else model         if auto_wrap_policy_func(parent_module):             layer = checkpoint_wrapper(layer, preserve_rng_state=False)             parent_module.register_module(child_name, layer)  so we get MLP and attention wrapped *separately* (as well as layernorms), while in FSDP-1 only whole transformer layer was wrapped (which is much more memory efficient in this case).  Falling back to activation_checkpointing=False and gradient_checkpointing=True fixes the issue for FSDP-2, but is not advisable (@SunMarc ) ? https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/30404

body: # Feature Request: Add API to Materialize Meta Tensors for Device Movement  ## Summary  Provide an API to materialize all meta tensors in a model loaded with `device_map`, enabling subsequent `.to()` device movement.  ## Motivation  ### Use Case: Fast Model Swapping with CPU RAM Parking  When using `device_map="auto"` or custom device maps for large models that exceed GPU VRAM, `accelerate` creates meta tensors as placeholders. This is excellent for memory efficiency during inference.  However, users with large system RAM (256GB+) want to:  1. Load model with device_map (fits in available VRAM) 2. Run inference 3. Move entire model to CPU RAM (freeing GPU for other models) 4. Later, move model back to GPU (faster than disk reload)  This "CPU parking" pattern is common in multi-model workflows.  ### Current Limitation  When calling `.to()` or `.cpu()` on a model with meta tensors:  ``` RuntimeError: Cannot copy out of meta tensor; no data! ```  The meta tensors have no actual data - they're placeholders that get populated on-demand from disk/CPU.  ### Real-World Example  Testing with Hunyuan Image 3.0 (25B parameters, ~160GB BF16):  - GPU: 96GB VRAM (model doesn't fit without offloading) - System RAM: 387GB (can easily hold the full model) - Disk reload time: ~2-3 minutes - Theoretical RAM→GPU time: ~20-30 seconds  **Current workflow**: Delete model, reload from disk each time  **Desired workflow**: Park on CPU RAM, restore quickly  ## Proposed API  ```python from accelerate import dispatch_model, materialize_meta_tensors  # Load with device_map (creates meta tensors for offloaded parts) model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("large-model", device_map="auto")  # Run inference... output = model(input)  # NEW: Materialize all meta tensors (load from disk to CPU) model = materialize_meta_tensors(model, target_device="cpu")  # Now model has no meta tensors, can move freely model = model.to("cpu")  # Works!  # ... use GPU for other models ...  # Restore to GPU model = model.to

title: collect_epoch_for_metrics — stream step outputs, auto-dedup, optional trim/shard
body: ## Summary / problem With even_batches=True (default), Accelerate keeps ranks aligned by duplicating a few samples at the tail. The docs recommend accelerator.gather_for_metrics(...) to gather per step and drop those duplicates. In practice, many users want an epoch-level result equal to len(dataset) without writing the same gather-append-concat boilerplate (and occasional final slice).  ## Proposal Add a helper that streams per-step outputs, uses gather_for_metrics internally, and returns an epoch-level tensor (exactly expected_len if provided). Optional: a callback to stream shards to disk instead of keeping everything in RAM.  ##utils collect_epoch_for_metrics(     accelerator: Accelerator,     step_iter: Iterable,     step_fn: Callable[[Any], torch.Tensor],   # returns [b, ...] tensor per step     *,     cat_dim: int = 0,     expected_len: Optional[int] = None,     stream_to: Optional[Callable[[torch.Tensor, int], None]] = None, ) -> Optional[torch.Tensor]  ##convenience method Accelerator.collect_epoch_for_metrics(...)   ## Semantics  Calls gather_for_metrics() each step → dedups tail automatically. On main process: accumulates CPU chunks, torch.cat(..., dim=cat_dim) at the end. If expected_len is set (or user passes len(dataset)), slice once as a final guard. If stream_to is provided, call it with each gathered chunk and return a small summary (e.g., {"steps": k, "count": n}) instead of a giant tensor.  ## Why useful  Collapses a very common eval/inference idiom into 1 call. Reduces foot-guns (forgetting dedup/slice; holding everything on GPU). Keeps low-level primitives (gather, gather_for_metrics) unchanged.  ## Backwards compatibility Purely additive. No behavior changes to existing APIs. Test plan (CPU & single-process) Concats multiple step outputs and returns sum(b_i) rows. Honors expected_len by slicing. stream_to gets called with correct step indices and shapes.

I’d like to propose parallelism_info method, which returns a dictionary containing all configured parallelism  sizes in a unified way. Thank you for your time and consideration!

title: [REQUEST] Exposing Parallelism rank as environment Variable for integration with profiling tools like CUPTI
body: First, thank you for your amazing work on this project and for being open to community feedback.  I would like to propose a small enhancement that could significantly improve compatibility with low-level profiling tools such as NVIDIA CUPTI or Intel VTune.  Motivation)  Tools like NVIDIA CUPTI rely on environment variables by Torch like RANK, WORLD_SIZE, or LOCAL_RANK to understand the role of each process in a distributed training job. However, It is not easy to know the DP Rank from accelerate easily.  Proposion)   After initializing the process group (e.g., via torch.distributed.init_process_group or Accelerator()), each process can set the following environment variables (locally) just once:  ``` import torch.distributed as dist  if dist.is_initialized():     os.environ["DP_RANK"] = str(dist.get_rank())     os.environ["DP_WORLD_SIZE"] = str(dist.get_world_size()) ```  This would allow external profilers to correlate collected GPU kernel events with the Data Parallel rank of each process, which makes User understanding the bottleneck of Training.  Thank you once again for your time and for considering this suggestion. I'd be happy to submit a PR if this is aligned with your design direction.  Best regards, [Woosung Myung]

title: Deferred initialization support
body: I wonder if it is possible to do deferred initialization with `accelerate`, specifically with FSDP2.  For FSDP2, `torchtitan` [recommends](https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan/blob/main/docs/fsdp.md#meta-device-initialization) loading weights after sharding. The recommended steps would look like  ``` 1. meta-device init 2. AC and FSDP2 wrapping etc  3. move tensors to devices and load weights ```  With `accelerate`, the above steps would map to  ``` 1. init with accelerate's init_empty_weights 2. accelerate.prepare(model) with FSDP2 3. move tensors to devices and load weights ```  However, from `accelerate`'s FSDP2 [implementation](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/d2e6b0313d696be62fe69d19f15bf3098effbad2/src/accelerate/accelerator.py#L1482), it doesn't seem to support  this approach.  cc: @S1ro1 @SunMarc

title: [Docs] Update low-precision training docs for MS-AMP
body: Hi team, I wanted to suggest updating the low-precision training docs, esp related to MS-AMP, which seems to no longer be maintained. When I was trying to get this working I ran into a few issues:  - MS-AMP requires a container with it pre-installed. While they provide base images, they are built on much older CUDA versions (11.8/12.1), so using newer CUDA versions requires building from MS-AMP from source - MS-AMP requires MSCCL for multi-gpu communication with FP8, which is a fork of NCCL, but it uses a much older version of NCCL and hasn't been updated in 2-3 years. This leads to symbol conflicts when using more recent versions of pytorch built against newer NCCL  Are these valid? If so, I would recommend flagging MS-AMP as deprecated and directing users to TE or other approaches.

title: `datasets` Iterable Dataset sharding support
body: When I'm using huggingface `datasets`, I think a good faeture is the IterableDataset create by `load_dataset(..., streaming=True)`. It has `shard`, `shuffle` and `state_dict`, which is useful in multi node training. I can just call `shard` to make different node with different data, easy to randomize and recover.  However, it failed when working with `accelerate`. when passing dataloader with IterableDatset `accelerate` assume that the dataset instance is all same in different rank. and the `IterableDatasetShard` class is doing a overhead sampling by sampling n batch in all rank and yield out the sub batches belongs to the coresspoding rank [src ref](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/v1.6.0/src/accelerate/data_loader.py#L265).  Not prepare the dataloader is a temproary solution in this case I think. But I think is nice to have the auto shard and shuffle in accelerate prepare. So I'm writing the issue for this. title: DeepSpeed ZeRO Stage 2/3 incompatibility with no_sync context manager
body: When using DeepSpeed with ZeRO stages 2 or 3, the [`no_sync()`](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/63168b151fa15987064a22c77b8b8ec72946f54e/src/accelerate/accelerator.py#L1018) context manager in the Accelerator class causes an assertion error. This happens because DeepSpeed's ZeRO gradient partitioning requires gradient reduction, which conflicts with the purpose of [`no_sync()`](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/63168b151fa15987064a22c77b8b8ec72946f54e/src/accelerate/accelerator.py#L1018) that disables gradient synchronization.  See [this](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/issues/6793#issuecomment-2517916093) comment and issue for more details.   ## Current behavior ```python @contextmanager def no_sync(self, model):     context = contextlib.nullcontext     if self.use_distributed:         context = getattr(model, "no_sync", context)      with context():         yield ```  This implementation doesn't account for DeepSpeed ZeRO stages 2/3, leading to the following error: ``` AssertionError: no_sync context manager is incompatible with gradient partitioning logic of ZeRO stage 2 ```  Similar issues are:  - [transformers/issues/34984](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/issues/34984) - [DeepSpeed/issues/6793](https://github.com/deepspeedai/DeepSpeed/issues/6793)  ## Proposed solution Add a condition to check for DeepSpeed with ZeRO stages 2 or 3:  ```python @contextmanager def no_sync(self, model):     context = contextlib.nullcontext     if self.use_distributed:         if self.distributed_type != DistributedType.DEEPSPEED or self.state.deepspeed_plugin.zero_stage < 2:             context = getattr(model, "no_sync", context)      with context():         yield ```  This ensures we only use `model.no_sync()` in compatible scenarios and fall back to `nullcontext()` when using DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 2 or 3.

title: estimate-memory gives ~64GB for meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct instead of anticipated ~140GB
body: With: * accelerate: https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/commit/f07649558051a9332a383dedfdb70918a55345de * https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/commit/8d73a38606bc342b370afe1f42718b4828d95aaa  Accelerate's `estimate-memory` gives 64.73GB for meta-llama/Llama-3.1-70B-Instruct at fp16 precision instead of anticipated ~140GB, i.e. `num_params * num_bytes_in_dtype`. title: Separate `backward` and `step` in `deepspeed` wrapper
body: Hello. I have a request to separate the two operations. Right now it prohibits from using a feature from deepspeed to access gradients in a model. See this issue: https://github.com/microsoft/DeepSpeed/issues/5199#issuecomment-2545973162.  My specific use case is fine-tuning a subset of weights in embedding and lm_head modules when initializing new tokens. I wanted to implement this logic in [on_pre_optimizer_step](https://huggingface.co/docs/transformers/en/main_classes/callback#transformers.TrainerCallback.on_pre_optimizer_step) callback in `transformers` library, which is right in between of `backward` and `step`.  There I want to use [safe_get_full_grad](https://deepspeed.readthedocs.io/en/latest/zero3.html#deepspeed.utils.safe_get_full_grad) from deepspeed to get the gradients. It has a condition that it should be called after `backward` and before `step`. But since `accelerator.backward` [(usage link in transformers.trainer training loop)](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers/blob/da334bcfa8ff7feb85138ce90ca7340e4fc6e704/src/transformers/trainer.py#L3702) has these two operations merged ([here](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/200c9eb7833cfa505907f6f224ebf5a275aa6d92/src/accelerate/utils/deepspeed.py#L255)) when used with `deepspeed`, using `safe_get_full_grad` is impossible.   Here is a [small example](https://gist.github.com/ummagumm-a/feef6e25771e4fd9dc3a90d8449e343f) to reproduce this issue. Please see the link attached earlier in deepspeed issues to see a discussion about it.

title: [FR] Support config torch.compile()/TorchDynamoPlugin with dynamic=None
body: Hi accelerate devs.  The `dynamic` parameter in torch.compile() has 3 values. True/False/None. According to the torch documentation, the default value is "None".  Doc: https://pytorch.org/docs/2.5/generated/torch.compile.html#torch.compile  > dynamic ([bool](https://docs.python.org/3/library/functions.html#bool) or None) – Use dynamic shape tracing. When this is True, we will up-front attempt to generate a kernel that is as dynamic as possible to avoid recompilations when sizes change. This may not always work as some operations/optimizations will force specialization; use TORCH_LOGS=dynamic to debug overspecialization. When this is False, we will NEVER generate dynamic kernels, we will always specialize. By default (None), we automatically detect if dynamism has occurred and compile a more dynamic kernel upon recompile.  If my understanding is correct. Currently accelerate can only config it as True or False.  https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/cb8b7c637a8588668c52bd306f9b2828f69d9585/src/accelerate/utils/dataclasses.py#L964-L965  https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/cb8b7c637a8588668c52bd306f9b2828f69d9585/src/accelerate/accelerator.py#L1613  In our development environment, using dynamic = None has slightly better results. It would be nice if accelerate can support it out of the box, and maybe have the same default value/behavior as torch.compile().

title: [CPU offload hooks] hooks with overlapped transfers and computations
body: `diffusers` relies on `cpu_offload()` a lot for implementing [`enable_sequential_cpu_offload()`](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/fdec8bd6754f8ae5428fb542f08707e0a5aba24e/src/diffusers/pipelines/pipeline_utils.py#L1092). It offloads the modules of a model to CPU when they are not being used and only pops them on to the GPU when it's needed for computation. As one can notice, the cost of these frequent transfers blocks the underlying computation and hence it leads to quite a bit of increased latency. But it also tremendously helps in running very big models on consumer hardware (very important as a good diffusion model is actually composed of multiple big models). So, the question is _can we overlap communication with computation_? https://gist.github.com/gau-nernst/9408e13c32d3c6e7025d92cce6cba140 implements a hook that leverages CUDA streams to implement the same functionality as `enable_sequential_cpu_offload()` but is significantly faster. See the results: As @SunMarc and I were discussing, it'd be extremely cool to have a similar hook supported in `accelerate` so that we can make diffusion models, in particular, more accessible without having to completely give away speed. Cc: @DN6 @a-r-r-o-w as well.

title: 🚀 Feature Request: Improve `stateful_dataloader` by passing `snapshot_every_n_steps`
body: Thank you for integrating stateful dataloaders into the `accelerate` framework! This feature could be incredibly useful for large-scale data state recovery.  In the latest version of `torchdata`, a new arg `snapshot_every_n_steps ` has been added to the `StatefulDataLoader` class. Here are the details: ```text Defines how often the state is transferred from the dataloader workers to the dataloader.  By default, it is set to ``1``, i.e., state is transferred every step.  If the state is large, this value can be increased (and ideally set to the frequency of training checkpointing)  to reduce the overhead of transferring state every step. ``` I believe this feature could significantly reduce the overhead of handling data online, especially for very large tensors or ndarrays.  With `snapshot_every_n_steps = N`, if we need to save states of intermediate steps $i\in[1, N)$, we can easily restart from step 0 and fast-forward the loader to $i$ to obtain the snapshot. And ideally, we need to save only one snapshot when saving the checkpoints by setting `N=saving_steps`.  This approach represents a clever trade-off, providing additional flexibility for users who face slow I/O or data handling issues. While this could be a simple modification to the existing state loaders in accelerate, I'm not familiar with the internal APIs and am unsure of the best elegant way to add new parameters to Accelerator.  Are you interested in exploring this further? Looking forward to hearing your thoughts. Thank you!  cc @muellerzr @byi8220.

body: Some parts of the codebase use [`str_to_bool`](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/bf4572b6ce0a534a9d73537485a0edf1d68144b8/src/accelerate/utils/imports.py#L199) to do case-insensitive parsing of bool environment variables, while others use [`parse_flag_from_env`](https://github.com/huggingface/accelerate/blob/bf4572b6ce0a534a9d73537485a0edf1d68144b8/src/accelerate/state.py#L1219).
